text: My boyfriend and his sister are lifelong vegetarians, so we were excited to check out a place where everything on the menu was an option. There were lots of sandwich varieties to choose from, the guys behind the counter looked sufficiently hippy-ish, but more towards the hipster end of the spectrum, and the cooler was stocked with scrumptious-looking cakes. In hindsight, I probably should have gotten cake for dinner. I ordered the sloppy joe ($5.50), and though I was thrilled when it arrived on a kaiser roll rather than on a wrap as promised, my dish was the only one that didn't come with a pretty little side salad of baby greens. I stole a friend's, and added the undressed lettuce to my sandwich. The greatest disappointment was the discovery that this particular sloppy joe was made to look and feel like chicken rather than ground beef, something I have never experienced and don't really hope to partake in ever again-- inauthentic, to say the least. The sauce was homemade, which is great, but it lacked any real resemblance to the sloppy joe sauce of my youth, other than the fact that it was tomato based. I slathered it with hot sauce. The grilled vegetable sub ($7.95) Boyfriend ordered came on a long roll expertly cut by the cook like a hibachi chef or a teenager into food amputation, with the ends hacked off in one quick slam of the knife from above. This was probably the most entertaining thing to happen while we sat at the counter waiting for our food, since no one attempted to engage our group in any form of conversation whatsoever. Bartending candidates they were not. Maybe they were shy. The veggie sandwich was... veggies. Sliced up. On a roll. Though colorful, they were generally unseasoned and bland. My Mexican friend ordered the chimichanga ($7). He's so daring. And unpredictable. This was another disappointment, basically rice and beans on a wrap. We couldn't really identify the subtle nuance of the spices, which was surprising since that's something I'm usually really good at. Overall, this was a bland and starchy, but filling, sandwich. More hot sauce, please. I didn't get a chance to taste the vegetarian chicken cheese steak ($7.95), but I gotta say, that one looked good to me. Peppers, fake chicken, cow cheese, good lookin' roll... Boyfriend's sister was the only one among us who, as far as I know, never partakes in any meat or fish of any kind, so this should have been right up her alley. Well, she didn't finish hers. Don't bother trying this place, unless you are perhaps a vegan with no tastebuds who is desperate for a meal.
label: NEG

text: Having stayed at more than my fair share of hotels, I have a theory that you could tell the quality of the hotel by the number (and fluffiness) of bath towels they have available in the bathroom. I proved this theory when, in my last stay at the Palace Hotel in SF, I noticed the number of towels went from 4 to 2 - and it was all downhill from there: the Internet connection didn't work, the hair dryer short-circuited and the TV remote control was nowhere to be found. The same theory applies to Fess Parker, where upon inspection of the guest room I found two lone, well-worn towels on the metal rack above the bath tub. Which was slightly disappointing because, for the price that I was paying, I was expecting much, much more. Granted, it is Santa Barbara, it is in a prime spot right on the beautiful coastal line, and it is a last-minute getaway decision made by two people who are utterly sick of 70-hour workweek. But still. I wasn't expecting to see fading carpet, old furniture, tired-looking hotel bars, and paper-thin walls. Nor was I ever prepared for loud boisterous kids running around, screaming and knocking on random guestroom doors just for kicks. Nor did I appreciate the sound of Amtrak which runs on the track about 3 feet away from the property. A painful reminder as to why I've been avoiding any Hilton-branded hotels during my travels.

text: This is quite possibly the worst cajun creole food on the planet. I can only say possibly because it's the worst I've ever had and I haven't been to every cajun restaurant in the world. But I'm pretty sure I could get away with making the claim of it being the worst period without catching too much flack. Where to start? I had some questions before ordering and the young lady (YL) behind the counter wouldn't let me finish a question before blurting out an answer to what she thought my question might be. YL: Are you ready to order? Me:I have some questions. Can you... YL: I can give you samples of stuff. Me: Thanks, but what I really would like to know is... YL: It's all on the board if you want to try it. Me: What is the... YL: blah blah blah blah blah I finally gave up. The chicken and mushroom etoufee tasted like someone had rushed to make milk gravy and accidentally spilled some rice in it. Imagine gravy made with too much flour and then undercooked. This is so far from a roux, that I thought we were at Bob Evans. The seafood gumbo looked and tasted like beef barley soup, complete with shredded beef and rice instead of barley. Still can't quite figure that one out. We sifted through it, looking for something that resembled seafood in the peppery beef broth and finally gave up. The jambalaya was watery, bland and had no cajun flavor characteristics. It was literally like someone made uncle Ben's rice and at the last minute said, "darn, we forgot the sausage and all that other jambalaya type stuff. Quick, throw some in it before you serve it." The crawfish casserole was...um...well, just read about the jambalaya above and replace "jambalaya" with "crawfish casserole". Shrimp Po'boy. It's supposed to be on a hard bun, not a soft one. The shrimp and the side of hush puppies had the same flavor. I'm assuming there is deepfry'omatic 3000 in the kitchen where everything goes in one end and comes out the other. It was about the only edible thing in our meal. Certainly the only thing we finished. Tea is out of the fountain, not brewed and tasted like a mud puddle. Long story short, it get's one star only because you can't give a place negative stars. For $7 less, we could have gone to Yats and had larger portions of the best cajun creole food outside of New Orleans. No offense to Mia, but this is not what cajun creole food is supposed to taste like. We really hoped this would be good, because it's so close to our home compared to Yats. We'll happily make the extra drive. I need to add this after the fact. i went to their website and looked at the menu. The pictures of the dishes are nothing like what was served to us. Extremely misleading to say the least. Edited on 6/27/08 to add the following: I'm not affiliated with any restaurant, let alone a competitor of mudbugs. My taste buds are just fine and able to differentiate between all kinds of flavors, textures and consistencies.. When I was there almost a year ago, both the food and service were horrible. Perhaps in the last 11 months they've gotten their act together. If so, kudos to them. They had a long way to go and it wouldn't have been easy. Judging by the other reviews, you'll either love the place or never go back a second time.
label: NEG

text: For the most part Liquid Charm is great. I think my main gripe with the place is that they still allow smoking inside. Gripe to me, but that might be a huge plus for you. Its nothing fancy, I guess its kinda like a "dive club". The cover is always cheap, drinks are inexpensive, tasty enough & definitely do the trick. The dance floor isn't huge but there's enough space in the rest of the club that non-dancers don't totally take up the floor - they hover around the bar, chat near the pool tables, or snag one of the seats along the dance floor. For the past year or so at least, it seems that alot of drum n bass nights have been getting play in the club. Almost every Saturday or Friday it seems like theres some really good DNB (seriously, REALLY good) & I'm often hearing about DNB nights on their weekdays, too. text: Don't stay at the Best Western South Coast Inn! We are posting this here to warn you and we are filing a complaint with the Better Business Bureau as no one should be subjected to what we endured. This is a hotel where the owner and the manager have demonstrated they don't care about their customers. During our second stay at this hotel we were in a room where the toilet wouldn't flush. It wouldn't flush even if the toilet was empty. We had to call the front desk twice to get it fixed, and each time they sent a new maintenance person, and each time we were told the problem was fixed. When it wasn't fixed for the third time, I called the front desk in frustration. After being put on hold for a long time, the front desk person offered us the use of the bathroom in a room about 10 doors down from ours. We couldn't just move into that room because it had only one double bed. We were four people in a suite with a king and a sofabed and no working toilet. No other rooms were available for that night. I couldn't imagine getting up in the middle of the night and walking outside in my pajamas to use the bathroom. We weren't camping here. We were paying lots of money for a hotel room for four nights. So, I explained how I didn't see how the two rooms could work being so far apart and I said in frustration, "How about just comping us a couple of nights and bringing us a plunger." I added that I had to think about what we were going to do here since we had been told that most hotels in the area were sold out. After a few minutes, I called the front desk back and accepted the offer of the second room for the toilet. We were also offered a new suite room to move to the next day, which we gratefully accepted. We thought everything was all resolved. We would have a new room with a working toilet and everything would be fine. .....but it was not to be. We were meeting friends for dinner so we had to leave. When we returned, the same front desk person knocked on our door and told us maintenance had snaked the toilet so it was working now. I wish maintenance had done that after our first call. We thanked him and gave him back the keys to the second room. I was told to talk the front desk the next morning about the situation. The next morning I talked to a new desk clerk about the nonworking toilet and he said he knew about it and the owner had heard and we were told we were required to vacate the premises immediately that morning and we were never going to be allowed to stay there again. I was in shock. We have been staying at hotels on a regular basis, including many Best Western's, with no problems. And during our prior stay at this hotel the front desk person said our file said "really nice people" and how we must have made a great impression. Now, because we were frustrated that we were in a room without a working toilet, we were told we were required to leave. It didn't make sense. We still had two nights on our reservation. This new clerk told us that last night's front desk person relayed to the owner that I had demanded to be compensated for two nights when all I did was ask as a suggestion in frustration. The desk clerk was apologetic and made excuses for the owner telling us he was under stress because of the renovations and also how the main computer system had gone down that night. We asked to talk to both the hotel manager and the hotel owner but we were told neither could be reached and the situation wouldn't change even if they could be reached. There was apparently no way to get this miscommunication undone. He was sympathetic and he did comp us $30 which we appreciated, but there was no way we could connect to the two decision makers, the hotel manager and the hotel owner to get the situation fixed. This is not the way you treat a customer. No one talked to us except the front desk person who was accusing us of demanding something we only asked for in frustration and as a suggestion. Plus, shouldn't a hotel do something more when your toilet doesn't work? The broken toilet wasn't the only problem. The cold water at the faucet only turned off at a precise point that took a while to find. The shower had very low water pressure. And, the next morning, the toilet wouldn't flush again. Plus, we heard another customer complain about how a hotel staff person walked in on them in their room really early in the morning. In the end, the owner did us a favor. We found Pacifica Suites. It is closer to our Goleta destination. The toilets work and work and work!! The rooms are much cleaner. The breakfast is better. The people are nicer. And we are very happy to give them our business - we have many trips we will be making each year to Goleta. Do yourself a favor and don't stay at the Best Western South Coast Inn.
label: NEG

text: Came in on a recommendation from some vegan family members, and I was not disappointed! My gf is a meat-eater, so we both had a chance to try what we wanted, and both of us did great. We shared the hummus sampler, which came with 4 different types of hummus, and they were all fantastic. I especially like the jalapeño variety, as it was light, fresh, and almost dancing on my tongue, and we both agreed that the fresh basil hummus was the best we'd ever had. I expressed my interest in spicy foods, and our waitress (very sweet, friendly, and all around cool) totally hooked me up with some spicy chili sauce that was friggen awesome. For our main course, I had the falafel plate, and the gf had the gyro plate. She had never had spit-fired steak before, and she was very impressed. She said the meat was flavored great, and very juicy. She slammed it all down without even taking time to burp :P My falafel were really good. Really. I try making falafel and it never, ever turns out this good. They were served with house hummus, a tahini sauce of sorts, and praise god, my awesome server brought out a couple of roasted (HOT) jalapeños. We were so stuffed that there was no room for any of the awesome looking deserts, but alas, that means next time we'll make sure to leave some room, and take the rest to go. That may be a challenge, though, cause they keep bringing oven-toasted bread to the table, which sits for about 30 seconds before being devoured. For our two meals and appetizer, we only spent $25, and the $5 tip was well earned... The hummus sampler was only $4!! On a side note, the head chef, Maurice, made a few rounds, checking on customers, making sure everything was up to snuff, and generally adding an atmosphere of friendly caring to the place. It was really nice. Umm... what else? The music was good, the service was fast, caring, intuitive, the decor was groovy... All in all, a great place to eat!

text: As chain restaurants go, "Houlie's" is pretty decent. But this particular location's service is so touch-and-go, I can only muster up 2 stars. The good: the food quality is pretty high, lots of choices on the menu and they're prepared well. I'm partial to their chicken tortilla soup, the steak and wedge salad, and the "fancy spaghetti". Their desserts are really tasty, they do a single-serving pecan pie that is out of this world. I also like that they now have a separate menu with smaller-sized dishes, so you can order a few different things and try them all. The bad: the service. This place is always busy, and I totally get that on a busy night you're not going to have the server's 100% devoted attention. But there's a huge difference in service quality among the staff, some are awesome and some are much less than awesome. Take last night, for instance -- the restaurant was packed so my BF and I ate at the bar... they only had 2 bartenders working on a Saturday night to handle drinks for the entire restaurant, which meant that service was super slow. (Not the bartender's fault... the manager should schedule an extra person for the weekends.) When the bartender finally came over to take our order, I told him what I wanted and he walked away and started serving drinks to other customers... he never took my BF's order! A few minutes later we had to grab the other bartender when she walked by and ask her to put in my BF's food. When our meal came, we marveled at how big the portion size was -- we had ordered several things off of their new smaller-portion menu, and the "fancy spaghetti" we each got was huge. We discovered later that they had ordered us each the regular-sized version of the dish instead of the small size we had asked for, which was double the cost and more food than we had wanted. This has been an ongoing problem in the years we've been coming here... we'll stay away for a long time because of bad service, then come back and have someone decent so our faith is restored... then the next time we come the service is slow and our orders are messed up, so we stay away again. My recommendation: if you want to come to this location, do it on a slow night or maybe come for lunch. And cross your fingers that the server they give you is a decent one.
label: NEG

text: While feeling adventurous on my best friend and mines 2nd annual trip to New Orleans, we felt getting out of the French Quarter could be a fun adventure. She had heard great things about the Spotted Cat so we sought it out. As we entered the bar it was pretty packed but we found 2 seats right up front at the bar immediately and ordered a drink. The band was an eclectic mix of guys belting out zydeco tunes. It had rained the entire weekend, but on this particular night we were entering monsoon territory. As the rain literally poured down and tiny rivers flowed right by the open front door, the band didn't even flinch. It really created this electric mood. I liked to pretend it was back in the 1920's and we were all escaping the rain by hiding out in a speakeasy. The torrential downpour didn't stop anyone from coming. I loved to watch new patrons enter the building by means of running or hopping while gripping their umbrellas like their lives depended on it. With each new person that entered, the room became more and more full and more and more warm. It really made for a magical evening. The music was great, the club was great and it was really a night I will never forget. I would love to go back on this years trip, I wouldnt even mind if it rained.

text: Maxercise is one of those little gems that once you find it, your torn between telling everyone so that they can experience it too and the desire to keep it all to yourself so it doesn't get too over-crowded. Apparently, Maxercise was the first gym in the US to feature kettlebells and every instructor here has years of experience in teaching and using kettlebells. For the first time in my life, I have muscle definition in my arms and shoulders. I love it! Gym- it's small and unassuming but I feel more comfortable working out here than anywhere else in the city. Nobody bothers me and I don't feel like I'm getting checked out by the guys. Everyone here is just focused on getting in shape and I've never felt judged for my flabby thighs or my girl-gut. Personal trainers- Reasonable rates, each instructor will develop a personal fitness plan for YOU and not some weird outline that they expect you to change your daily life for. For instance, they're not going to demand that you buy a medicine ball or kettlebells for your home, you tell them what your goals are and what you have available (as in, not at the gym) and they'll work around that. Ask for Alma, she's a godsend. She's helped me lose weight and stay on track, something that I haven't been able to do, well, ever. Also, for people who have kids, they are super nice to babies, and are genuinely interested to find out about your life and family. It's just such a great place. Last time we were there, there were some seriously american old people, who appeared to taking their even-older parents out to dinner. It was quite excruciating to listen to them talking to the waitstaff (they wanted things that weren't on the menu, and kept asking what was in other peoples' food on their plates), but the waitress was patient, kind, and eventually cut them off and said "okay, great!" and went into the kitchen. text: The Regency Cafe is a welcome addition to Lansdowne's business district. It's become the best lunch spot in the entire town. Not content with the diner options provided by other Landsowne mainstays, Regency offers up a great selections of salads, soup, and gourmet sandwiches. I particularly enjoy the Lansdowne Farmer's Market Salad, and the grilled vegetable sandwich has always been good. The coffee is good, and they have a large selection of flavored drinks (I like the honey steamer myself). They also keep a selection of newspapers for those who haven't forgotten the pleasures of daily print news. The Regency is located right next to Cinema 16:9 and the work-in-progress that is the Lansdowne Theater. These three establishments will make Lansdowne Ave an exciting place to watch over the coming years,

text: So lovely to look at, and a name that's so bold, but prices are shocking, and the food - well the food's just boring. Yes I know it doesn't rhyme, and that same sense of discord that you get from reading my bad poetry is a shade of what I experienced after eating here. Twice. I was so happy to see a higher end sushi bar going into Collingswood. Sagami has needed a little challenge on its home turf and the little chinese restaurant across from Wawa just wasn't doing it. Surprise! It turns out these are the same owners (as the little chinese place) taking on a new, upscale venture. It's a darn shame it's all pig and lipstick. Now I've read the reviews and I agree it's very pretty, and the staff is pleasant, but I ultimately don't care about any of that if the food is good. Let's face it - we've all eaten at a jersey dive at 2am and had the food practically thrown at us - but who cares - it was what it was and the attitude was the 'charm' of the experience. I was not charmed. Let's start with the appetizers. The sunomono was nice, but I would have prefferred more vegetables in mine. It was priced well for the portion of fish I received, but sunomono should be pickled fish AND vegetables, not fish with vinegar dressing and some seaweed for color. Sorry if you think that's a small deal, but I really like my sunomono and this was a poor effort. The Tako Su (Octopus Salad) suffered from the same affliction. On to the main course. Sushi for two. $40. Ok - I've paid that (and more) before, so let's look, we have two (each) shrimp, salmon, tuna, herring (bleah), squid, and eel. Tuna rolls (4 pcs), check. California roll (4pcs), check. That's it! This was like a $16 special at AOI in the city. Heck I could have got this at Wegmans for like $25. Was the fish fresh, yes, but there sure wasn't $40 of it. Plus look at it - Herring! Squid! Where am I - Wegman's kosher counter? Where's the Uni, or some White Tuna, or a nice Hamachi. This was boring - spell it with me - B.O.R.I.N.G. Add to that a king crab handroll, one, for $10 that was half the size of the one I usually get at Mikado or Fuji mountain, and both of then charge $6 and $7.50 respectively. Our bill came to $110 when we factored in tax and tip, and it was, frankly, shamefully overpriced. They should have called me the next day or sent me flowers to screw me over like that, and I received not bloom one nor has my phone jingled. Now I love sushi, and I've spent $300 a person at Morimoto's for a chef's tasting that left me so full I could still taste fish the next day, so to go here and pay for adequate (not interesting) fish in small portions at easily 40% more than Sagami or Mikado just makes no sense. Frankly, I wanted to give one star but I was concerned about the flaming, so I've cut my losses and given it two. After all, the fish, what little there was of it, was fresh. So I'll not be returning for a third try. I'm so disappointed at the lack of effort and overpriced food that I won't waste one more dime on them.

text: Everything about Dante's is fresh & local - the food, the drinks, the staff and even the restaurant itself. So fresh & local we ate there twice - once for dinner & then for brunch on Sunday. The board at the front doesn't show the specials - just a long list of "What's Local". Repeatedly, the staff were overheard describing with pride where or how or why something was on the menu. They have a passion for what they do, and it shows. The menu changes every two weeks or so based on what's available, and creativity is everywhere on it. While the obligatory shrimp & grits were good, the lump crab salad with cucumber and cantaloupe on field greens exemplified this. The combination was so unusual I had to try it, and it more than just "worked". The lightly dressed & salty greens melded the other ingredients into something more that the sum of it's parts. Simple, creative, and delicious. My redfish on the half shell was cooked perfectly, topped with a crab & fresh chopped herb mixture. The topping complimented the fish, but was a little to leafy for me. Lots of crab & less herb would have still done the trick, but again it was simple and creative and tasty. My wife's eggplant napoleon was excellent, and frankly would also make a fantastic side dish. From what they told us, the chef is also doing double duty as pastry chef, which can be a real workload. He's pulling it off, because the fresh blueberry pie was the best I've ever had. If it's available, get it without hesitation. Yummy. Brunch was yummy, too. The place was full, with a short wait around noon, but they get the food out fast. My Debris & Eggs Benedict was another combination I'd never thought I'd try, and they were great. Blueberry pancakes didn't need syrup they were so tasty. Portions are small so don't hesitate to double up and try a few other items. Like the spoon bread. All in all, we really enjoyed Dante's. Right across from the stodgy Brigstens, they are vibrant, fun, and passionate about their focus on fresh & local food. Worth the trip uptown, we'll be back again. It seems like the kind of place that doesn't get old.

text: Happy to be the first to review Teri's! This place is tremendous. About one month ago, they began serving dinner as a BYO (Wed - Sun); formerly, they were strictly breakfast/brunch/lunch. They put candles on the table and (good) jazz through the speakers. The space really took on a different atmosphere...slightly upscale, but still very down-home and comfortable (think diner booths with candles and jazz). Our server, John, was sweet as pie and professional...and I haven't had a meal that tasty in months. The menu is French-inspired, but not all French. We began with the duck confit appetizer ($9). A simultaneous "oh my God" literally came from our mouths. Incredibly good and enough for two. We then both decided to get the butternut squash ravioli (homemade, $15) but wanted a veggie, so we ordered a side of asparagus as well. Once again, amazing. The ravioli were superb--and the sauce! So good! Asparagus was done simply in butter and garlic and was excellent. I don't even want to know what the calorie/cholesterol count was for our meal but really, something this good is worth it. We literally cleaned our plates. The chef, Davis (last: Denick...I looked it up), came out to introduce himself and seemed like a really nice guy. Our server told us that Davis formerly worked at Coquette. It's really hard to find french/french-inspired food this good at such a reasonable price in Philly, especially in south philly.

She also kept telling us things were out, but then returning to our table to say they weren't. Also when 3-4 different people keep checking in on me when I'm dining , it doesn't make me feel pampered, it makes me feel harassed. I tried their melon infused vodka. text: Before I start, let me make it clear that I am reviewing a Kitchens with a Mission class I enrolled in, NOT the general courses or education offered by L'Ecole, nor its student-run restaurant. I was thoroughly disappointed. I took the Indian cooking class, expecting to learn tips and secrets that would change the way I cook Indian. A couple years ago, I got just that when I took an Indian class at the Kitchen Conservatory. There, the instructor was an actual head chef at an Indian restaurant and he showed us how to toast and grind whole spices to get the most "wow" out of them, secrets to getting perfect rice, and other things that made me better at cooking Indian in general. L'Ecole offered the opposite experience. There was no depth to the lesson, and basically ended up being $75 for a bad dinner. First off, the instructors, while nice and friendly, were not Indian and as far as I could tell had never worked in an Indian restaurant. This isn't necessarily bad, I guess, but it was a bit of a red flag of what was to come. The first dish was a thoroughly Americanized "chicken curry." We walked into the kitchen to start "cooking" and saw table after table lined with pre-measured McCormick spices (they didn't even tell us what they were), pre-cut chicken pieces, pre-measured chicken stock and yogurt, prepared garlic, onions, tomatoes and ginger. The student's role was essentially: brown the chicken (in olive oil, btw, which to my knowledge is not authentic), throw all the ingredients that were prepared for you into the pot, and let it simmer til it's done. Okay, I didn't need to spend $75 to learn that, a $3 box of Hamburger Helper has the same instructions. Second dish: naan. In my other class, we made it from scratch, and it turned out pillowy, buttery and delicious. That's not how they do things at L'Ecole, apparently. Someone brought out a platter of pre-made naan dough balls, and we rolled them with a rolling pin and watched the L'Ecole assistants heat them on a skillet. And that was the extent of the "hands-on" cooking. After an hour of that, the instructors pulled out a big tray of cooked rice, a paneer dish, and a lime relish and date chutney as condiments. Even if the student's role was minimal in the preparation, I could excuse it if the food was mindblowing. You probably already can tell that it was bad. The chicken curry had a cliche, vaguely "Indian" flavor with nothing interesting about it. It's the sort of "Chicken Curry" dish I'd expect to see in a 1970s Good Housekeeping magazine. The naan was just bad, completely bland, and not cooked properly. The paneer was the best item, but its flavor was just off somehow, like it was just a muddy slop of spices with no highlights or lowlights to fill it out. The relish and chutney weren't good, either. Other students in the class said they liked it, so maybe I'm just too much of an Indian food snob, but if I were served the results of the class at a restaurant, I wouldn't come back. One of the other students at my table said he had taken a L'Ecole class before and it was similar, in that most of the work was done for you. In my opinion, if I'm paying good money to go to a cooking class at an esteemed culinary school, I expect more than this Rice-a-Roni approach. Sadly, the food wasn't even good, so I won't even use the recipes they handed out. I acknowledge that half of the proceeds go to charitable causes, and that's a good thing, but I won't take another class here. I'll go back to the Kitchen Conservatory. I still make restaurant-quality dishes from that class to this day because they were so good. Sorry if this review was a bit long-winded, just trying to hit all the different points where the class let me down.
label: NEG

text: This is your classic tale of a restaurant that has a pretty gorgeous interior, solid (if still obviously very new) staff, and a kitchen that cannot live up to its billing. First, it's in the Ritz, so the place is immaculate. Huge columns, night club-style lighting, holographic light walls...all pretty cool looking. I liked how the club lighting contrasted with the old-world columns. The circular wine cellar in the middle of the lobby/restaurant was amazing. I want one. We were seated immediately by a very nice hostess. Very professional. The restaurant was nearly empty at 8:45pm on a FRIDAY...eh, that's a bad sign 99% of the time. Our server asked if we wanted Fiji or Pellegrino. Did not even ask if we wanted tap. Bad sign # 2. We were promptly brought menus and the water came out quickly. The wine list is just average. The prices were absurd. A bottle of 2005 Duckhorn sauvignon blanc sells for $24 at Total Wine. They had it for $85! Terrazas Malbec sells for $11. They had it for $42. We're talking four times mark up on wine here, people. That is simply unacceptable to me. I settled on a toreador cocktail. It was fine but it was also $15. Oh, and she brought us the wrong drink the first time, the second time she said they don't have it, and the third she returned with it. I can excuse that because she's pretty new, I'd assume. We ordered an order of the pretzels with three sauces from the lounge menu ($10), the salmon rilette ($13), two of the flat iron steaks ($26 each), the bouillabaisse ($28 I think), and the striped bass "Grand Mere" ($34) and a side of mac and cheese ($10). The pretzels were good, if too salty. The dipping sauces were good but nothing special. In fact, this appetizer was something that tasted pretty similar to what you'd get at Auntie Anne's pretzels but with a bit harder shell. They did come with a jalapeno jelly that I liked a lot. I didn't try the salmon but our guests seemed to like it a lot. The steaks came a la carte. This was a bit surprising, but I guess it shouldn't have been as the menu didn't say anything besides "shallot sauce." One steak was ordered medium and one medium rare. Both came out the exact same degree of doneness. Awful. You're a "top" restaurant! Learn how to cook a steak! The medium steak was done rare in the center. My girlfriend wouldn't even finish it as it was cool and red in the center. The other steak was the same but our friend likes rare steak so it wasn't a big deal. The steak was pretty tender and carried a nice flavor. The bouillabaisse was incredibly fishy. The shellfish were good according to our friend but the striped bass was overcooked to the point of being almost inedible. Dry, chewy, ruined. Also, the waitress could not specify what sort of shellfish were in the dish (as our friend is allergic to scallops and wanted to avoid them...there weren't any but the waitress didn't know for sure). The Grand Mere was probably the best dish at the table but it still had its flaws. Two pieces of bass were served in a slightly bland broth with various vegetables (fingerlng potato slices, asparagus, snap peas, haricot verts, sun dried tomato, all fresh). The smaller piece of bass was tough while the larger piece was cooked perfectly. Obviously, they were cooked for the same amount of time and the smaller one just became overcooked. The mac and cheese was so salty that I could not eat it. It had a sea salt crust on top (at least the bread crumbs had a lot of sea salt in them). Who does that? We did not stick around for dessert. I'd probably not recommend. I'd not go back any time soon.

text: "The Best Sandwich in America is in Indianapolis." Those are sweet-everythings I whisper to myself as often as I put on a pair of shoes. Those aren't just my words folks, google for proof that Bon Apetit magazine agrees that the Batali from Goose the Market is the must-have sandwich. I'd hock & hiss like a mad goose if this place were taken away from us. Thankfully, it's thriving. For good reason to: beginning with the pleasant, knowledgeable staff. Cheery, open for q&a and clearly they indulge in the sandwiches they craft. The seating is limited on the colder days, but most of the time there are 6 tables that wrap the corner sidewalk. While waiting for your sandwich order...head below to the cellar of fine, fine wine & micro & import beer. At first it'll seem like it would all be over-priced, but due to Indy's high prices any way...it's relative to your standard corner store. Creating your own 6 pack is recommended. I've found beers here from the West that don't make it to this side of the Mississippi too often (that is...something like specialty Rogue brews or Great Divide seasonals). They call it a "Market" for a reason b/c you could conceivably shop here for most of your kitchen essentials: all local, seasonal vegetables, breads & cheeses. Ever find yourself salivating at the late-night Travel Channel's HD Rabbit Terrine? Or wholesome Chorizo? Welp, it's here. Really, terrine in Indy! Holla back Anthony Bourdain! Holla back! "O, so your meat-eating foodie wants to drag you to this place, and you're just not in the mood to bite into duck huh? Well..smack your lips over some strawberry gelato, or any gelato!" Yep. Gelato. Coffee. Or turn around and stick your head in that fridge and you'll find a jug of Milk or Yogurt or Root Beer you can't find anywhere else. Or just go get cozy on the back patio with the Market Pooch. If for no other reason...go in here and see what a chalk board should like and to hear a lunch-time worker-bee spout, "what!? you think you're ordering the Batali without the gardiniere? That's the whole point of this sandwich?" To a complete stranger....Cheers to that gumption! Cheers to this place giving the much-maligned Goose a good name.

text: All through senior year, people would ask what I was going to miss the most from St. Louis when I packed up and moved to Boston (or Melbourne as it turned out for first semester). I gave the cheesy answers of friends, family, and just the familiarity with the city. Then I realized I wouldn't have Ted Drewes, or any other of my favorite hang outs. I returned home from aboard three weeks ago and just didn't have the chance to get down to Ted Drewes until today. It was just like how I left it, with the addition of the holiday specials. As many before have said, the possibilities are endless. One thing I didn't pick up in the first few reviews, is that no one mentioned how cheap it is! for the amount of ice cream you get, so here's the scoop. A mini (their small, which it's not - I rarely finish a mini) is 2.10! Then their regular at just over 3, which is at least 12 or 16oz. Then the large comes in at 4.20 (I think), and its bigger than a Venti coffee from Starbucks. Now why was I eating ice cream with my family in the middle of December? Because we also got the Hanukkah Bush / Christmas Tree today silly. Yes. All through December, Ted Drewes is home to the absolute best trees and wreaths. The trees range in price from 50 to 200 depending on the breed and footage, but they are worth it. Living in U. City, we have many other options, and without I-64/40 getting to Ted Drewes this year was not easy, but would weren't going to back down on our favorite trees and icecream. In the holiday months, I opt for the Great Pumpkin - which is literally a pie of pumpkin pie blended into their vanilla custard with whipped cream. It's AMAZING. In the summer, friends and I pile into one car (usually my SUV) and head on down to eat icecream in the true STL fashion: sitting in the trunk of my car. In those times, I get a simple chocolate chip concrete. Friends get the Hawaiian, or Reeses and strawberry, or cookie dough, or pineapple, ect.

text: Wow, what a terrifically disappointing experience. It was Labor Day morning --- and what a gorgeous morning it was. The sun was shining bright, the sky was blue, it was Monday and I wasn't stuck in my cubicle at work... it was going to be a great! day. My boyfriend and I were in St. Louis for Stage 1 of the Tour of Missouri. We left our downtown hotel and headed out on foot. Our mission... breakfast. We had read and heard many good things about Crepes in the City, so that was our intended destination. Somehow we missed the part that they aren't open on Mondays. We found out quickly when we arrived and the place was dark. Not a big deal, we just kept walking --- someplace was bound to be open. Eventually we found 12th Street Diner. What a cool-looking little joint! Unfortunately, that's the only thing it had going for itself. When we were seated we were optimistic about getting in and out relatively quickly because the majority of the tables were empty, and it's not a real big place. Our optimism grew dim when it took the wait staff 15 minutes to figure out which of them (out of five) was going to take our table. Finally, after watching the same staff walk back and forth by us practically twiddling their thumbs because the place wasn't busy at all, I asked the young gentleman --- standing out in the middle of the floor doing nothing --- the obvious question (in a nice manner) --- "excuse me, who is going to be our server?" My heart sank even further when he told me it would be him. He came over, took our order, and was back 5 minutes later with our coffee. Thinking to myself: Okay, so it took a little while to place our order, but our order is in now and we'll be eating in no time. Wrong! 30 minutes later when no food had arrived and we had watched folks come in the diner, eat, and leave during the time we were there, I was not happy. Our server, God bless his heart, was walking around the diner... doing I don't know what... trying to stay awake. Every now and again, another server would hand him dirty dishes to take to the kitchen and then he'd reappear, to do... nothing, but stand around. When I got his attention and asked him where our food was, he came over and said he'd forgotten to put the order in. And that wasn't all, he asked to take our order again! We'd been there for 45 minutes, not tucked in a corner, not behind a wall, right out in the open, next to the kitchen, and this guy forgot to put our order in and didn't know what we ordered to begin with --- what! I got up, I said "that's fine, we're leaving and I'm not paying for the coffee." He said, "that's okay, I'll take care of it." Umm, so am I supposed to thank you for that? I don't think so... especially since it tasted like poo in a cup. I had a word (it was civil, mind you) with the manager before we left, but I can assure you we will never set foot in that restaurant again.

text: Decided to compare the 2 best known cheesesteak places in Philly. Since Geno's and Pat's are just across from each other, I ordered a cheesesteak from each place with a bottled water and chomped away. The bread: -- Bread from Pat's was way too tough/. Not only did I have to bite into the bread, but I had to literally tear the bread in order to take any bites. The bread from Geno's was way easier to tolerate. The steak: -- The portion of meat from Geno's was much smaller than Pat's. Also, the meat from Pat's was much more seasoned. I'm not sure if Geno's seasons their meat with anything 'cause it basically tasted like unseasoned roast beef. The filling: -- I got Whiz With (with cheese whiz and with onions) at both places. I liked Geno's onions better, but the whiz was better from Pat's since Geno's was very skimpy on the whiz. The whiz is easily visible on the Pat's cheesesteak, but Geno's put a VERY TINY amount at the bottom of their cheesesteak. I almost went back to ask if they had forgotten to put it on. The price: -- It's same at both places. $8.25 for cheesesteak. ***CASH ONLY*** Service: -- Service at both locations sucked big time. I guess it's part of the whole "lure" to be rude and even curse at the customers. But I am not into this whole dumb idea of "Hahhahaa. I just got cursed at at a tourist trap. I can't wait to post it on Facebook and Twitter!" I still expect people to be nice, especially people who are servicing customers. Personally, both places sucked. The food wasn't all that bad but it wasn't anything close to what I was expecting. I expected more flavor, more meat, more cheese, and most importantly, more taste. It's cool to check out if you are a tourist. Geno's totally had the look of seedy old Las Vegas decor going on.

text: I learnt of this place at the Taste of Edmonton last summer. Their selection of value wines was memorable, especially considering the sub par wine tasting conditions involving those little plastic mock glasses and a hot, non air-conditioned tent. During the festival, I discovered one Cab so good I googled the store location to find it. I was pleased to learn this midsized liquor store is conveniently located on 99th street (and on my way back home from South Edmonton Common). Tucked in a large strip mall of miscellaneous stores, the plain white sign can be easily missed if you're not paying attention. Although I must give them credit on the name - clever enough not to be easily forgotten. And so I remembered the store again, this time on a cold Saturday afternoon. I found myself the only customer in the store, with a middle-aged gentleman greeting me right away. I told him I needed a cooking wine that was good enough to drink off with my puff pastry chicken pot pies - a dry, full bodied white. Naturally, he suggested a couple of oaked American chardonnays, one in the $15 range and the other in the $20. I went cheaper, but (really) should have known better - good chardonnays cost. It was not "buttery" enough of a match for my puff pastry, but a decent value nonetheless. And isn't value all that a buyer can really ask for? It's when a $20 bottle tastes like it should have cost $12 instead - that's when one has a problem. This time, like during my previous visits, the customer service was very good. So when the sales clerk asked if I needed anything else, I admitted I could use a couple of reds in the $20 range to replenish my depleted, post-holiday stocks. I confessed I was drinking a lot of Malbecs lately, and he poured me a generous glass of a Malbec blend he had going at the tasting bar. The wine, an incredible value at $11 (called Fuzion, by the way) was a well blended Shiraz-Malbec. And I thought the only thing a person could get in that price range Boon's! Not that I drink Boon's; I haven't had any of that stuff since that camping trip in high school... I also ended up getting another Argentinean Malbec he recommended, but since it hasn't been corked yet, I cannot report if it's worth its price. He packed my three wines into a snazzy Keg'n'Cork tote bag - a complimentary gift "to get me into the store more often", he said. A smart customer service move - it worked. I will stop by to stock up on my value wines, whenever I take that route back home from South Edmonton Common. And for those of you that are not value wine drinkers, and prefer something both a little stronger and a little more expensive, they carry a good selection of scotch. Some are of collector price range at hundreds and even thousands of dollars. Maybe that's the kind of scotch that could make me a convert. Or not! I'm sure I would enjoy a $1200 bottle of Malbec too...
label: POS

text: Don't waste your time, seriously. I know it's free but you'd still be overpaying. It's a self guided tour that overlooks the production of coins 60 or so feet below the glass windows. The production runs aren't that often so you'll probably end up going on a day that the plant is practically empty except for maybe a small batch of pennies moving around at the end. There are a few tiny 10" TVs placed along the way that have videos made in the 70s or 80s explaining some things about the production; unfortunately only about half the TVs are working. It doesn't look like they really did anything from a tourism standpoint in at least 3 decades. It's a cool place to go if you're a die hard coin collector, there are some real unique coin displays along the way. The gift shop is tiny and has very few unique Mint items. If you just want to go to see coins being made, learn a lot about the process, or buy something cool then you'll be disappointed.

text: I am allergic to fragrance, and this is the first pedicure I've been able to get in over ten years. While some other reviewers are frustrated at not being able to bring their own polish, I LOVE that about this place. It's great for being fragrance-free and totally wonderful for the chemically sensitive. When they say "organic" they really mean it. It's not cucumber scent in the cucumber scrub or something that greenwashes itself by claiming to be "98% natural"--it's actual cucumbers spun in a blender. It's not shea butter infused with something to make it smell good--it's just shea butter. It took me about 20 minutes on the phone to confirm that I really truly wouldn't be allergic this place. Justin steered me toward the cucumber-sea salt pedicure over the citrus one on the off chance I'd be allergic to the essential oils used in the citrus pedi. Karina did my pedicure, and we talked about my allergy and she was fine with eliminating the one commercial product that had fragrance. I subjected my pedicure to a week of sand, salt water, and equatorial sun--still going strong. So excited to have found this place!!
label: POS

text: Crap... I should've yelped the place from our hotel before letting my folks convince me that we should just drive around for a burger place in Reno. Its unanimous..it's a 1 star joint. I somewhat feel like I'm doing a public service to the people and tourist of Reno. 7 YELPING STRANGERS...1 STAR RATING.. COMMON DENOMINATOR. DO NOT EAT AT JOES! You know how people say, don't judge a book by it's cover? Well they're right. From the looks of things Joes is a happening, retro-themed diner that's actually well decorated and fully staffed. The restaurant itself is clean and orderly. When we first pulled into the parking lot, there was just one empty spot which raised my hopes that we might have actually found a decent lunch spot off the strip away from all of the annoying flashing lights and lingering cigarette smoke. Our 6 top table was seated promptly in a nice comfy booth. We had tons of elbow room but that's where the positive comments stop. Our waitress was slow, rude and never to be seen when we really needed her. I ordered the club sandwich which was horrible. The bread was stale, and the the bacon was black. So get this.. we're having lunch and my mom runs off to the bathroom to fix her glasses and as soon as she got up, our waitress came in and without asking took my mom's basket and cleared her food. My mom got back to the table, noticed her food was gone and then flagged down our waitress. The chick was never around the refill our waters but the moment my mom gets up from the table, she's there to busily bus our table? We all were still eating so I don't know where she gets off thinking we were done. My mom complained to the manager and they made up another burger for her but by that time.. she totally lost her appetite. So despite the crap-ass service, the prices are up there along with Red Robin burgers! I don't mind going to Red Robin and paying $9.99-$12.99 for an awesome burger and bottomless steak fries but there's no way I'd ever come back to Joes and pay $9.99 for any of their burgers or sandwiches.

text: I was going to preface this review with a defense of Starbucks, but changed my mind and decided to not get into the politics and simply stick to reviewing. (Though I will say - politics does influence where I will spend my money.) In some ways, a Starbucks is a Starbucks. At least if you are at a Company Store and not a Licensed Location (of which there are thankfully few.) However, in the world of "the same" this location stands out as wonderful. The Baristas are uniquely friendly. They also do seem to try harder to be helpful than at other locations. I have on a few occasions needed to speak to a manager, not for problems, but to get information, and the woman who seems to be the store manager is knowledgeable and responsive. She also seems to have a good rapport with the staff, which may account for the quality of service. The store, and specifically the restroom, is always clean, and when I have found it lacking in a paper product, they are quick to fix the problem. Although the lines can be long, service doesn't dawdle. On the other hand, when it isn't busy, staff is happy to chat about coffee, or movies, if you are interested and don't interfere with their work getting done. There are plenty of tables, and four areas which have power outlets, which is more than most locations, so it is truly possible to be there and get work done. It does get crowded at times, especially during exam weeks at Drexel and Penn, but I have only once, out of many visits had to leave because I couldn't find a seat. This is not the ONLY Starbucks in Philly that I like, but it is my favorite! On a Company-wide note - they now use NO High Fructose Corn Syrup in ANYTHING. Desserts are back on my menu!

text: Wow.... "Fine dining and sushi" is quite a bold statement for this new restaurant. Reno's culinary image is stepping up with more and more imports bringing in a crowd that can support new restaurants and introduce top quality cuisine to Reno. Wasabi will not be one of those establishments. We decided to drop in last night for dinner after seeing a movie at the Summit. There was no wait and about 1/2 the tables were full when we arrived. The bar had about 16 seats total and all but one was taken. We took this as a good sign. It wasn't. My girlfriend and I both decided to give all you can eat a shot at $21.95 so we could get a real feel for the menu. Again, bad idea. Though a few of the items on the sushi menu jumped out to us, most lacked appeal and seemed just average at best. We decided on a few rolls to get started... 2 for each of us. After waiting over 15 minutes, our first rolls were delivered. Mine had to be sent back because they left avocado on them after I requested it be left off. Almost 10 minutes later my rolls arrived again, and AGAIN with avocado. I just skipped trying to fix those and ordered ones that wouldn't require anything to be left off. Overall theme, they all lacked flavor. Even the spicy crab roll that my girlfriend ordered was so mild I could eat it (I don't do spicy). It had no "spice" in the spicy crab roll. Ingredients did not seem fresh - even the fish had a weird after taste to it. The restaurant itself was slightly odd - the decor had no central theme. One wall had a cattle horn plaque that said "Out House" as you were directed towards the bathrooms and the rest of the walls were decorated with photos of flowers. Only one busboy was working the whole restaurant (not too big, but too big for only one guy) and tables sat dirty for most of our meal because the busboy simply had too many tables to clear at once. Management seemed frantic at best. I know the restaurant enviro. can be stressful and chaotic but don't show the customer that. The owner led us to three tables before finally choosing one for us and allowing us to sit. The wait staff seemed inexperienced and dropped alot of things, ran into each other, etc. Worst even of the night was that the bar stools sit on such a slippery surface that two people fell onto the ground when attempting to slide their chairs back. Thankfully both were ok, but i'm really glad we opted for a table and not the bar. I will NEVER go to the restaurant again and I would recommend that, unless you have a very strong stomach and like wasting money, you don't either. So much for having a sushi spot on this side of town.
label: NEG

We ask the bus boy for it, he looks at us like we spoke English (right, we did instead of Spanish!) and then leaves. 15 minutes later the waiter comes and we get sour cream for our baked potatoes. The food wasn't bad. I had the stuffed sole. It was $21.95 with a soup, baked potato, veggies, and bread. My hubby had seafood alfredo (20.95), and aside from the ridiculous bread they claimed was garlic, it was good. My sister did the 1lb crab and she seemed happy ($18.95). My brother in law did the "jumbo" shrimp and fries baskets, and didn't feel that 5 "medium" shrimp and a whole plate of fries was worth $17! The waiter came and took our plates when we were done for about 10 minutes, and then didn't come back for 20 minutes to "see how we were doing". Check please!! We instantly put the cash on the receipt tray and sat and waited for our change...and waited, and waited, and waited. I had to get up and walk to the bar where him and the manager were hanging out and ask for him to take our bill and get change...and the manager just looked away! So did we feel bad leaving a penny tip? No. I am actually a phenomenal tipper, but its called a tip because you have to earn it. Give me great service, I will be happy and leave you 25% no problem. None of the staff serving us last night deserved a dime for a tip. They couldn't even do their job correctly...too bad you can't deduct from their hourly wage too!

text: Located on Banks Street in Mid City (just a couple of blocks up from Jesuit High), you know Crescent Pie and Sausage is in the neighborhood as soon as you get out of the car. The smells from the grill hit your nose and draw you in like a siren's call. I'm not going to go into any more details on the food at Crescent Pie and Sausage, though. The service I received was so bad that talking about the food might convey the impression that it mitigates the way I was treated by the front-of-the-house staff. I arrived at Crescent Pie and Sausage about 1:15pm. They were pretty busy. I usually try to make my way to the bar when I'm a single; no need to take up a 2-top, and usually bartenders make for good conversation. Alas, the bar was full, so I stood, not sure if this was a wait-to-be-seated or a seat-yourself place. Crescent Pie and Sausage isn't very big, so it could go either way. There were two servers, one guy, one gal. They both kept walking past me, without as much as a 'hello.' Now, I know places get busy, but when you've got this big fat guy standing in your doorway, he's pretty hard not to notice. After the male server walked past me to check on the five-top on the patio, I figured maybe it's a seat-yourself place. I sat at a 2-top for a few minutes, watching the activity around me, trying to catch the eye of one or the other of the servers. I watched a guy come from out of the kitchen and bus the 4-top in front of me, I was wondering if I was invisible. The gal server actually bumped my knee as she passed between my table and the one to my left. She apologized politely, then proceeded to head to the bar, still not even noticing that I'm just sitting there. As the clock on my phone went from 1:29pm to 1:34pm, I was answering e-mails and such, still trying to catch the eye of someone on the staff. When the male server sat two people at the now-bussed 4-top and brought them menus, I asked him if he could bring me one as well. He said, "did someone seat you or did you seat yourself?" I replied that I waited at the door for a bit, then seated myself after he had passed by me on his way to the patio. He brought me a menu and cleared the table. When he came back to wipe the table off, I ordered a sandwich and an iced tea. By this point, I think they realized I wasn't a very happy camper, because after my Crescent Pie and Sausage sandwich came out, someone came from the back to ask if I was doing OK. I nodded and said I was allright. I finished the meal, and the female server brought me the check. I left $14 for a $11.50 tab, and one of my "mini-moo" @YatPundit cards. I probably wouldn't have written this Crescent Pie and Sausage article had it not been for the tweet I noticed at the coffee shop a bit later which said: "I had the *ahem* pleasure of serving @yatpundit at work today. I don't think he's ever been to a busy New Orleans restaurant." OK, ya know, I realize that a $2.50 tip isn't all that much, but it was only a $11.50 tab. Still, it's 20% of the bill, and that's the conventional wisdom for a lunch tip. Maybe this guy's a part-owner of the place or some such. I hope so, because then I'd feel no remorse about calling this behavior out in such a public place. Still, you don't treat people as poorly as Crescent Pie and Sausage did me, then insult them on Twitter after the meal. It'll be a while before I give Crescent Pie and Sausage another shot.
label: NEG

text: Since the local sushi place we wanted to visit was closed, we wound up giving Kobe a shot. The three stars are blended total for the overall experience, not the sushi itself. And because she didn't really seem to care when I mentioned it, what was already average service took a dive. Most of what I had was tasty. Nicely salted edamame (4 stars) and the Mexican roll had plenty of flavor (4.5). The unagi was fine (3) but the Hawaiian roll (3) was lacking a punch: the spicy tuna really wasn't spicy, and the avocado didn't rise to the occasion. That gives us a weighted average of 3.5, because the edamame ranks lower, and from there, the indifferent service and missing dish got a 1, so we split the difference and end up at a high 2. Would we go back for the teppanyaki? Possibly. Teppanyaki is better suited to chains than sushi -- and it's hard to get bad service when you're sitting right in front of the chef. As for the sushi, we'll time our next trip to Kaisen better when we're in that part of town.

text: I LOVE LAZAROS!!! When I first graduated from college, I lived in a cramped row house with two roommates at 18th and South. I had no clue how to cook. I have learned since then, but in those early months, I became a serious client of Lazaros Pizza House. Lazaros is staffed by amazing people. It is always nice to have take-out people who know your name and order when you walk in the door and don't judge you for it. I appreciate good service. These guys rock. The pizza is flawless. It is definitely not gourmet brick oven pizza. But it is delicious. It has a thin, crispy crust that buckles and folds toward the bottom. The sauce is mild and applied ever-so-thinly, just to lubricate the pie. The cheese is simple, fresh, and delicious, perfectly and evenly distributed across the surface. I think the key to good pizza is the ratio of sauce to cheese, and they have this down to a science. They will usually make up a fresh pie for you if what you order isn't already prepared, but if you order a slice they have on display they will sprinkle some fresh cheese on top. A nice touch. And the toppings are good too. I usually just get black olives, but I have tried the pepperoni and mushrooms and chicken. All are good choices. Their white pizza with ricotta is excellent too. So are their garlic knots. I also enjoyed the chicken parm sandwich. Their wings are so-so. But honestly, this is the best pizza in Philly! When I lived over that way I went at least three times a week. Now I don't go as often but it is worth the trip every time. Disclaimers: pick it up there. I moved across the city, and every time I order I am disappointed. The crust doesn't hold up very well in the delivery car. It is worth the walk. Also, they aren't open very late (I think 10 or 11), so make sure you order early!
label: POS

text: I've been in Tucson for about four years now and have experienced the ups and the downs of cuisine in this town. While I have not been to sushi happy hour at this establishment which seems to have gotten some excellent reviews my experience in the eat-in restaurant section has been sub-par at best. This sentiment has only solidified over time. I agree with the analysis that this is less like Japanese food and more like 70's vegetarian style preparation/cooking/philosophy. I was amazed to find my vegetable yakisoba dry and tasteless with a faint hint of dish soap and even more surprised to find that my partner's salad was replete with wilting greens and a gnarly hair from someone in the kitchen. I once had to send back a roll because it was completely inedible, tasting as if it had been sitting out for many hours. My vegetable ramens of the past have always been rather gamey with scrappy vegetables. There is always a problem with freshness. This again was in the dine-in section, so I speak for only this part of the establishment. Yoshimatsu could be one of my favorite places in Tucson if quality control was better in the kitchen. There are wild fluctuations in the preparation style here -- your vegetable yakisoba may be the bizarro counterpart to the real stuff and the end result is often confusing and bland. I'm not saying here that Yoshimastsu should try to emulate authentic Japanese dishes, but if you're going to "innovate" do it well. Yoshimatsu does so many things right -- the ambiance is amazing, the music is always at good levels, the staff is generally amicable, the gift store is super cool, and of course karaoke on Fridays -- if only the food were better.
label: NEG

text: So, I finally checked out the long awaited and highly debated SugarHouse casino. I'd been putting it off due to the recent muggings and my slight gambling addiction, but I couldn't fight the temptation any longer. I arrived at around 2:15A on a Saturday night and stayed for exactly 36 minutes. Being a lover of all things Vegas, Atlantic City and Black Jack, I knew that SugarHouse would be different but not in the ways I expected. For one, it's just a casino. Yeah, I think that "for one" may be my deal breaker, right there. You've got your slots, your tables and slightly sketchy crowd just like every other casino, but where are all the fun extras? Can we get one awesome restaurant? Maybe a few bad lounge singers? How about some scantily clad cocktail servers pushing coffee and Red Bull and Vodkas? Most importantly, where's the cheesy, pop music blaring through the sound system? As a matter of fact, all you you can hear is an occasional cheer, the cha-ching of the slot machines and that voice in your head saying, "You should have quit while you were ahead." On the bright side, It is still really shiny and pretty. I'm sure I'll be back when I have a little extra moolah to burn, but it won't be the second home I predicted.

text: Danger!! Keep away!! You'll be killed then BLAMED for your own death. Do not get your flat tire or anything else repaired here on a Sunday in late October. Better yet, never go near a Canadian Tire service centre at all. While on her way to Lloydminster from Calgary, my daughter Claire went here in desperation on a Sunday afternoon, Hallowe'en actually. After a long wait the Canadian Tire boys finally took a look at her leaking Michelin tire on a 2007 Pontiac Torrent, patched it and sent her down the road. Within 30 minutes of leaving Canadian Tire the low tire pressure alarm sounded. It's a good thing she has TPM (tire pressure monitoring) on that vehicle. Claire managed get back to the Fort Road Canadian Tire to have the tire fixed properly and what does she hear? "It's too close to closing time to do anything? Sorry miss?" That was the story but they did remove the tire to perform a quick soap bubble test, declaring the tire to have 5 separate leaks now. Oh no! Panic! Got to go to work Monday in Lloyd. "Too bad chica, we're punching out." So they put the tire back on the Torrent without doing further repairs and sent Claire on her way... to DOOM. Within blocks Claire decided something was wrong and luckily stopped. It turned out the Canadian Tire boys had re-installed her wheel using only one wheel nut. That's one of the 5 wheel nuts they had just removed. Question: If she survives, what's a young working girl supposed to do in Edmonton on a cold dark Hallowe'en Sunday evening with one leaky tire, 4 missing wheel nuts, stranded at the side of the road 2 1/2 hours drive from home? Oh right! Call your dad in Calgary, he'll know what to do. I wanted to choke someone when I heard what had happened. In desperation we decided to borrow one nut from each of the other three wheels, then jack up the problem wheel and install the 3 borrowed nuts. I cleared this solution with my BIL (brother in law) Terry in St. Albert, a mechanical engineer. On the phone, Claire told me she hadn't thought to inspect her RR wheel before leaving CT; before driving off. How tragic. Here is a young girl thinking she is somewaht to blame for the negligence of CT. I wonder how many drivers think they should inspect the work of their car mechanic. It cannot be many, or wouldn't we be doing our own auto repairs? So, was this criminal NEGLIGENCE? Maybe some lawyer out there could say, but I know one thing, it's GROSS INCOMPETENCE. It shows a complete lack of concern for the safety of the public. Next day, still in Edmonton, now missing a day of work, Claire went downtown to Central Tire and had the tire expertly repaired by real tire people. They assessed the patch by Canadian Tire as AWFUL and professionally repaired 2 punctures, not 5. No further problems. Oh yeah, earlier in the day Claire went back to the Fort Road Canadian Tire, and when informed they had failed to properly reinstall and torque up the RR wheel nuts they REFUSED TO ACKNOWLEDGE THEIR GROSS ERROR. Hypocritically, they suggested my daughter must have removed the wheel nuts herself. WOW!!! A new LOW benchmark for personal and professional ethics is established. I like Canadian Tire for their merchandise but for goodness sake, any enterprise with TIRE in their name has to be better with TIRES. This dreadful performance could easily have turned tragic. I wonder, what will it take to get the management of Canadian Tire to wake up? YELP maybe?

Okay, fine. And then the colored lens is going to cost an extra $100. Again, fine. I was splurging. Well, a day or two later I get this voicemail from Carlton. Remember Precious' mom? Yeah... This woman tells me that A.She has no record of a revision being made in my order, and that there is no note to give me a refund. B.They don't GIVE refunds anyway, and C.She can't help me. I *tried* to explain to her the difference between a refund and giving somebody's money back because you don't have what they paid for, but she was having none of it. So I left, and I called the city's licensing office to find out who owns Philadelphia Vision Center. Which ultimately lead me to their nearby location on Chestnut Street. This location is cleaner, more attractively laid out, quieter and overall feels MUCH more like an actual medical facility. The people there gave me the owner's number, I called him, he got back to me and of course he was mortified. The woman at the Chestnut location told me that they don't MAKE non-colored versions of my prescription in the brand name that I had initially ordered, so I ended up with more expensive non-colored lenses. Which just makes no sense to me. Someone should have told me that they were changing to a more expensive brand when they changed my prescription to non-colored lenses, so *I* could decide what I wanted to do. Anyway, I guess I learned a $50 lesson, which is that you should spare no time or expense when finding something as important as vision care. text: The name of this business should be unavailable, unprofessional and incompetent plumbing. My husband and I recently purchased a home. An agreement of that purchase was that a draining issue in the bathroom would be corrected. We had a quick settlement so there was not time for the job to be completed prior to settlement which left us with a check payable to available plumbing for completion of the work. My husband called Randy (the owner) the day after settlement to get the work scheduled, Randy was on vacation. The following monday I called again to schedule the job, I was told that the soonest he would be able to start would be that Friday and that he could come out and meet with me thursday morning. This led me to believe that he would be starting work on my home that friday, but I was wrong. When he came out to meet with me, on a job he had already started, he informed me I would need to get tile before he could procede. I left a message with my name, the address of the house, and the date that I would like him to start the job if he was available. He never returned the call. Monday afternoon I called again, slightly unpleasant this time because he hadn't returned my call, and left essentially the same message. About an hour later he called my office, one of the girls i work with answered the phone and he said "yeah this is the plumber" he couldn't even remember the name of the person he was calling, and when the call made its way over to me after some assessing, he asked me what day I wanted him to start (i'd left that in 2 messages) I gave him the date and he said he would have to check his schedule and get back to me. I told him that was unacceptable, we needed to be out of our apartment by the 31st and that simply didn't allow enough time. He went on to say that it wasn't his fault my tile guy took a week, well i said, that isn't but if i would have known from the start that i needed tile, that would have been done. text: Ever have one of those restaurants where you ate the food, looked around at a relatively-empty place, then wanted to find whoever was responsible for their marketing and smack them upside the head? Welcome to the Doghouse. Following our Xmas shopping, the wife and I decided we wanted a quick bite to eat before heading home. Any restaurant within a 1 mile radius of Exton mall was packed solid, so we decided to finally give Doghouse Gourmet Burgers a try. This is the small sister shop to the Firehouse restaurant. When we first walked up, we didn't think it was open. No one inside, and quiet as could be. The doors were open, so we decided to head in. Pretty cool look to the place, no-nonsense in the seating area, with a line of very cool barstools that would swing out from the eating area for folks to sit on. Three items stood out for me as we ate: 1) The onion rings were top-notch. Nice, thick, and fresh tasting, without the crust falling off. I like good onion rings, and these definitely rated. 2) My wife ordered sweet potato fries. Rather than coming out with shoestrings, she gets this plateful of steak / wedge cut fries. Perfectly crisp on the outside, with the great sweet potato flavor from the inside. 3) Finally the burger. I ordered the Mastiff, which comes with lettuce, tomato, fried onions, onion rings, and queso with a chipotle sauce. This was, by far, the best burger I've ever tasted. The burger was moist and delicious. Rather than going with a over-the-top chili-packed queso, this one stuck pretty much to its roots and was simply a creamy cheese inside an onion ring volcano. Absolutely delicious, and I can't think of a better burger at around $6. Which brings me back to how I started: How can we have been the only ones there?? The burgers are outstanding and deserve more customers than what we saw. Don't get me wrong - I like places that can be "our little secret". But they are never fun if they go out of business....

text: I moved to New Orleans earlier this year from San Francisco, the Tenderloin to be exact. Therefore, my weekly trips for Indian food to Jones & O'Farrell (Lahore, Chutney, Shalimar, Sultan, even Naan n Curry on Van Ness) consisted of my favorite weekly comfort food of my life. When I moved to NOLA, I knew comfort food would switch to cajun/creole - but I had no idea it would be so hard to get an adequate Indian meal. When you come here, don't expect traditional Indian. It bills itself as "New Orleans Indian". And, for what it claims to be it, it delivers. I have been in many times for the extensive and varied wine selection in the store, but had not tried the Indian food. I ordered the lamb spicy vindaloo. Like others, I was a little disappointed in the lack of sheer heat at first. But the flavor, while unlike any other Indian I tried, was outstanding. It was a little sweet - my wife's chicken curry was a lot sweet. No potatoes (is that everyday?), but that was always my secret least favorite part of vindaloo (more lamb!). Naan was pretty good. Papar was a little greasy but a perfect compliment to the Vindaloo. Portions were perfect for a dinner and prices were outstanding. This wouldn't be a 4 star Indian restaurant in San Francisco, but in New Orleans - as a super-funky place in the middle of one of the best neighborhoods in all the world - it's close to a 5.

text: Went to Hiroba last wednesday with two friends who recommended it highly. They also happened to have a free bottle of sake for everyone in your party. Not a bad way to get your day going. The place was packed to the gills, but we were greeted within 10 seconds of walking in the door, and seated at the bar in less than a minute. Take note other sushi restaurants in town. This is the first example of what you could be doing better. The first thing that struck me about the overall experience is the great energy that the sushi chef's have and put into their craft. I hesitate to call it work, because everyone seemed to be having so much fun. This comes in sharp contrast to the lackadaisical (and sometimes angry) service of restaurants like SP2. The fish was fresh, which should be a given at any place worth its salt. What made it noteworthy was that the portions of fish were actually suited to the small ball of rice in the nigiri sushi. I can't tell you how many of these all you can eat chop shops slam half a cup of rice under each butterflied tiny shrimp to fill you up. None of that happening at Hiroba. They had some fun new rolls I hadn't tried before, and many of them contained traditional japanese ingredients. Also, a number of their creations come with contemporary touches like crushed macadamia nuts and mango sauce. Definitely worth getting out of your usual godzilla-roll grind for. My friends love quail egg and tobiko shooters and we had a few rounds. OK I had a few rounds, and they had 9 each. Hahah. I liked them better than most, but I'm not a gigantic fan in general. Another great benefit to Hiroba is that you can get appetizers and dessert included in your all you can eat price. I find that to be an awesome bonus. They even have a dessert roll that might strike your fancy. The overall quality of the experience as a whole package was very high. I think I prefer the fish at Jazmine slightly more. But they are definitely different restaurants, both of which are perfect for a certain mood. Bottom line: Great Service, Reasonable price, good food. Go here.

Honestly - it felt like a place that has gotten popular enough that they don't need to impress anyone to get the business anymore... which is a really bad idea when you're located two blocks from Morning Glory and Sabrinas. Bottom line - in brunch, growler and bottle sales I've spent enough money there that I'd be surprised if the staff didn't recognize me... and I still felt flat out ignored as a customer. It's rough when you find a pace you fall in love with and watch it go down hill... and I really want to love Hawthornes. However this was my third bad experience there in a row.
