text: So all of the other reviews are pretty much on the right track here, this place is awesome. The owners are two of the nicest people I have ever met. They chat with you and really make you feel at home. This place really does feel like exactly that, a home. Has a really nice and comfortable outdoor seating area in kind of a garden setting, just a really nice place to relax and eat a mid day meal. Little bit off the beaten path but well worth the trip, no matter where you're coming from. You order up front and can sit outdoors and then one or two, or both of the owners will bring your food right out to you. Probably their most popular dish are their "Lomito" sandwiches. They are INCREDIBLE. I have never had anything like them before. I ordered the original Lomito and my girlfriend got the mini-lomito. They were so good. Big fluffy potato bread bun, with steak, ham, tomato, cheese, lettuce, spiced mayonnaise and fried egg, all on one sandwich. One of the tastiest sandwiches I have ever eaten. The only downside to their dishes are that they come with what you order, nothing else. No side fries, no pickles, nothing, just the sandwich, for around $7 I normally would expect something on the side, but you know what, it was so good so I really didn't care. We also ordered a side of papas fritas, with salt and pepper. Oh my god, seasoned perfectly, and full of flavor. Only had about 7 slices of potato on the dish, but they were SO good. The ketchup they bring out is also their own, it's slightly spicy like it's mixed with some sort of hot sauce, and it makes everything taste even better. We got a couple iced coffees to go with our meal, $2 each and they were huge. The coffee you can just tell is amazing quality. Big plus for this place here, iced coffee refills are just $1! That's amazing. Also, we were about to leave and we were going to take a couple iced coffees for the road, we ordered two small ones and had a chat with one of the owners (Oscar), while he was preparing them, asking about the heritage of the food and stuff (Paraguay if you're wondering). They were supposed to be $1.64 each (+tax), but after we were done chatting he was just like, "For you guys, $1 each." You know, it really makes you feel special and appreciated when something like that happens, they truly are a nice couple, and a pleasure to dine for. For two people, including the iced coffees to go, the bill was like $24. That's $12 a pop for a big GREAT sandwich with a side of potatoes and two huge cups of iced coffee, honestly, you really couldn't ask for more. I WILL be going back here, no doubt in my mind, if only just to talk with Oscar again, he's the man! And to get more of their fantastic unique sandwiches, I have to try them all before I die, because they all looked crazy good. By the way their menu isn't limited, they have all sorts of breakfast and lunch foods including eggs prepared anyway you want, salads, really everything you could want from a brunch place. The only thing they didn't really have was regular breakfast foods like pancakes and french toast, but who cares, it's not that kind of place, it's better. Do yourself a favor and try this place out, you won't regret it.
label: POS

text: Like Jerry S., I think that Arch Gourmet could improve if they added some simple options. I was thinking a Scottish theme - maybe do something fun like put a "Mc" in front of everything. I definitely think they should offer more types of food than just deli sandwiches, like hamburger sandwiches and fried foods. They could even patent a special "magic" sauce that would be just a simple combination of condiments. In all seriousness, Arch Gourmet is a great asset to the neighborhood. It's staffed by attentive, friendly and hard-working people. I don't think it needs to become Salad Works (Jerry S.) OR McDonald's to improve. I don't know how many corner deli's Jerry S. has been to, but I'd definitely put Arch Gourmet in a higher caliber, and I don't think adding a Salad Works style bar would make it more gourmet. The store stocks a wide range of foods, including the all-important drink mixes and garnishes (including celery for your bloody mary), a large selection of chips and snack food, from the standard Lays and Herrs to Pop Chips, Terra, Pirate Booty, Dirty Chips and more. Likewise, they offer a wide selection of frozen foods - meals, vegetarian/vegan options and edamame, vegetables, etc. What makes something gourmet is subjective based on personal taste, however Arch Gourmet clearly makes an effort to provide a variety of products in addition to a variety of choices. text: Third Degree is incredibly unique (as Stephanie E indicated), not just because of the glass blowing but also because the space hosts many cool St. Louis events, including the Rock 'n Roll Craft Show, which was going on this weekend! RRCS is not your granny's craft fair...there were no Kleenex box covers in sight! What the craft show did offer was 1) art/crafts by local designers 2) Schlafly beer 3) live music - all of which were organized by a group of St. Louis crafters who wanted a way to show off what their friends/colleagues in the city have to offer! In the background of the crafts and music, Third Degree glass blowers were offering demos where audience participation was encouraged. At Third Degree, they want to make glass blowing accessible to people of all ages. I would encourage anyone to check out a class there! Also, have you been in the bathrooms at Third Degree? They are gorgeous! The sinks are custom made and the glass tile is beautiful. Yes, a public restroom is beautiful. The only drawback to the Third Degree is that the parking is limited. They do have their own private lot, but it's small and fills up quickly during big events. You are allowed to park in neighboring lots but it's kind of confusing to find a spot. Also, there's not a lot of seating during events...besides the demo area. After standing on concrete floors for several hours, I just wanted to sit down and take a break...and there was nowhere to do so. But I also have a bad back and should probably stretch before events like this. Fun place, locally owned and not found "just anywhere", Third Degree is a must in St. Louis!

text: We played the Karakung course today. As Beth K. said, I'm sure at one point it was really nice. There are some pretty vistas and landscaping, and you don't really feel like you are in the city. But, the course is in terrible shape. The grass was completely clogged with clover and weeds, and very brown. The fairways were so dry and unkempt that when the ball hit, it would bounce and roll in completely unpredictable ways. Because some of the holes are blind when you're teeing off, this made for an inordinate amount of time spent searching for balls. I'm a beginner, but my partner shoots in the low eighties and has played a lot--he said it was the worst course he's played on in his whole life. Some other specific issues: the lack of women's tees. The scorecard suggests that they exist, but they were nowhere to be found. You have to drive your cart across very busy roads multiple times. Cart paths were flooded, nonexistant, or extremely potholed. Some tee boxes were so worn down that there was no grass at all for about five feet. You also had to drive behind the driving range (which has no net) to get from one hole to the next. Little scary. Finally, random people just kept walking, jogging, and riding carts through our fairways. It was the strangest experience I have ever had playing golf. We did appreciate the extremely friendly staff, and the Olde course, which runs alongside much of Karakung, looks much nicer. It was also extremely cheap ($22 per person including the cart). No bathrooms or food on the course--and the turn is nowhere near the clubhouse--so be prepared!
label: NEG

text: What's there not to love about a menu with over 30 Grilled Cheese Sandwiches in a retro-Fifties motif diner with the implied promise that there would be food that appealed to both young and young at heart? In this new gastro-destination of South Jersey, a promise made is not always a promise kept. On a beautiful 4th of July Saturday, we wandered into this popular Collingswood eatery and soaked in the cuteness of a newspaper menu, fifties rock, soda jerk hats for the kids and friendly staff. While I had no illusions that this would be the NJ equivalent of Sabrina's, the food was on par with most average diners in this state. And there are many that ought to be avoided. My coffee was pedestrian and the wife's peach iced tea was slightly bitter receiving but a hint of peach flavor. My son's grilled Philly Soft Pretzel with Cheese could have been an opportunity to meld flavors and textures previously unknown, but was an opportunity lost. It was just a two ordinary soft pretzels sandwiching barely melted blocks of yellow cheese. Not much better than the nubs of pretzels that you dip into cheese wiz goo at ball parks. My Warm Spinach Salad was big, but filled with limp baby spinach leaves and with the odd addition of sauteed onions and mushrooms. The wife's Alaskan Egg Benedict fared much better with smoked salmon taking the place of the more familiar canadian bacon. But the nondescript hollandaise dominated the flavors, masking even the smokey fish. The girls' pancakes were the highlights of our meals. These huge flapjacks were well made, somewhat light and fluffy, although the strawberry pancakes could have had more fruity flavor. Really love the concept and the service was nice. With so many viable eateries in this area, this really disappoints. If you're looking for a place that would delight both children and parents, well Pop Shop comes through for half of the family. The other half can pick at their limp salad greens and enjoy the kids having fun at this eye candy for the young.
label: NEG

text: Tasty pints and good times. I popped in here for an early dinner and a few pints last week. The service was very friendly, and the place had a cozy and comfortable vibe like a proper pub (not some knock-off, wannabe attempt like you get at other so-called pubs). Regulars and newbies, alike, filled the place with warm, but not overly loud chatter while soccer (er football) played on multiple flat screens. In addition to a couple of pints of London's Pride, I opted for the haggis, which was a good, Americanized version of the Scottish treat (the S.A. uses ground lamb sausage). If I had been more hungry, I would've wanted to started with some Scottish Eggs, which came highly recommended from my friend, but I opted to use that stomach space for more beer. Like their sister place, the Shaved Duck, I will most certainly be returning here when I make my way back to STL.

text: 3.75 stars. Some years ago, when the great love of my life was still a sapling, I stopped at Half Moon with my companion for an unexpected late dinner. I remember relaxing by the windows, gazing at an old clock's alabaster face glowing against the chilly night sky, admiring the light dusting of snow on the streets, and enjoying a comforting meal. With a dose of anticipation and glee, I stepped into Half Moon over the weekend with my companion, and prepared to indulge in its storied menu of game dishes. Unfortunately, our hostess was quite rude, and left us feeling unwelcome as we slid into a half booth close to the back. Shaking her memory from our minds, we studied the cocktail and dinner menus, deciding on a French Orchid (Grey Goose, Chambord, and a splash of pineapple), brown IPA, crab nachos, gator gumbo with chorizo, and the game sampler. Then, our faces relaxed into lazy smiles in the low candlelight, and we giggled as absurd conversations from the bar floated across the room. Hungry from an earlier bike ride in Philadelphia, we were pleased when the gumbo and nachos soon arrived. The crab nachos presentation was elegant and gorgeous. The blue corn chips and warm crab salad were layered so that the chips appeared to be lotus petals lightly cloaked in toppings, the avocado salsa's green and red colors interspersed with lumps of crab and a snowfall of grated cheese. The dish was also quite tasty, particularly the buttery, citrus-infused salsa and pungent cheese, but it was difficult to distinguish the taste of crab from the other flavors on the plate. As my companion remarked, we could have had shredded chicken and the taste would have been the same. I greatly enjoyed the comforting quality of the gumbo, but had the impression that pureed beans formed part of the soup's base. The soup's richness was nicely offset by a lingering heat, and the alligator meat's flavor was a welcome addition to the dish, but I wished that more generous portions of alligator, chorizo, and the holy trinity were added to the soup, as it sometimes felt like I was eating separate dishes when scooping from different areas of the bowl. After several bites, the soup became less interesting, and I slid the bowl across the table. The wild game sampler arrived last, showcasing filets of kangaroo, ostrich, and wild boar accented with a tart cherry sauce and a gougere. The ostrich was deeply flavorful, and perfectly cooked until it was firm but moist. It provided the night's outstanding culinary moment, and my fork locked tangs with my companion's utensils as we struggled to get the last bite. The tart cherry ver jus completely captured my palate and imagination, and I greedily dragged my spoon across the plate to discern its cinnamon, pink peppercorn, and offal flavors. The kangaroo and wild boar both had interesting flavors but were a bit chewier than we preferred. By this time we were stuffed, and it seemed a challenge to continue. If you order slightly differently (try the local goat cheese appetizer, any of the numerous local brews on tap, and an ostrich dish with cherries), I think your meal at Half Moon can be phenomenal. Our server was a sweet, spunky girl who understood our leisurely mood, and eagerly answered our questions about the chef and restaurant. The restaurant's setting was comforting and fun, with live music that started soon after we arrived. And the upstairs section, with its wrought iron tables and chairs, hanging plants, and large windows, would be perfect for a summer or winter party. Recommended.

text: This place is pretty rad (if you're into brewing and GOOD, rare beer). We opted to try and use a "local" shop for our second-ever brewing experience, and the Reno Homebrewer did not disappoint. Hidden away in the "industrial" section of Reno, next to artsy tile shops and random "new, artsy" condos, the Reno Homebrewer exists. Shelves of hops, malts, sugars, mesh bags, carboys, etc etc line the (rather small) shop. A decent selection of dried fruit and spices exists in the center of the store. On one side, you can find the wine essentials across from a 'fridge stocked with rare beer that I've only seen here. A bar sits in the front of the shop (a place to enjoy those rare beers), where they also ring up your brewing purchases. We wanted a relatively easy brew session and we wanted to follow a store recipe, so we opted to check out the recipes printed out in the back of the store to "build" a Nut Brown Ale. Basically, the recipes line the shelf and then it's up to YOU to walk around the store gathering the essentials. (It's easy-enough, though. Everything is marked remarkably well.) The price was absolutely right and on-par with anything I've seen on More Beer or Midwest Brewing's websites....but you don't have to pay shipping if you buy in-person! The store help was also exceptional. Both workers were super-friendly and not-at-all judgemental, snobby, or anything that might make a new brewer self-conscious about important questions. We bought everything we needed and splurged on a liquid yeast over a dry. We bought a new mesh bag, some new metal caps, and a $10 bottle of Alaskan's 2009 Baltic Porter Ale. Our total came out to about $50 with all of the ingredients we needed, as well as the "extras." (There is a surcharge of about $3 or so to use the credit-card machine. I felt this was a bit steep.) We found out that you can get $2 back if you return the container that the malt extract comes in (clean, of course). I only took off one star because, well, this place is pretty dirty. There was dust pretty much everywhere. I realize that you sterilize your equipment before using it, anyway, but I would expect a brew store to be a bit cleaner. I also didn't like the steep credit card surcharge or the rather high pricing for the bottled beer (Dogfish Head was about $4.25 PER BOTTLE. You can get a 4-pack for almost double that price - even in Tahoe. I'd only buy beer here if you're looking for something super-rare.....the equivalent of seeking out a fine wine for a special occasion; for this, the Reno Homebrewer rocks.) All-in-all, I think this is definitely our new spot for brew equipment and ingredients. It's more fun to pick out your brew stuff in-person and the staff is really nice. I'll be recommending this place to anyone who asks about brewing beer.

text: Hands down, my favorite place to get Dim Sum in Center City. 15 bucks will make you and your friend's tummies full for the next couple of hours. Now, I must say there are several things that ran through my mind when I read the reviews that fellow yelpers left about H.K. Golden Phoenix: 1. They must NOT be Asian 2. They must NOT have gone with an Asian 3. They definitely do NOT know what authentic Chinese food and service is all about The nature of Dim Sum (in the states and abroad) is fast service, scattered communication with servers and well, fast service. My parents and I discovered this place while walking around Chinatown when I first looked at schools up here. The Dim Sum service is fast, efficient and if you know what you want, you can order it from the waitress and they will go back there and steam it for you right away. I know communication with the servers is tough, but if you know your dumplings, then you can just repeat the specific dumpling or Dim Sum platter you're wishing to order over and over until they understand you. If you don't get what you want, stand up and walk over to another server and ask. This is how a Chinese restaurant work. They share tips so they are all willing to help out the other. Eventually you'll pick out who knows the best English. Now, I don't recommend this place unless you are familiar with Dim Sum (if you are going for Dim Sum). Go with someone that does and you will have a much more enjoyable experience. I have brought many of my "white" friends there (including my boyfriend - many, many times) and they are often times overwhelmed with the speed in which everything is ordered in, but are always pleased with the food. Alright, I know I talked a lot more about culture of Dim Sum than anything else, so let me say more good stuff about H.K. Golden Phoenix. Their dumplings are always hot, you can always order straight from the kitchen and they'll have it out for you right away. Seating is not that big of an issue as they have an upstairs and downstairs area. Although, the stairway leading upstairs is decorated perma-80's wedding ceremony. They're Dim Sum ends at 2:30 or 3:00 pm. I've never been there for dinner, but I can definitely recommend their Dim Sum. Some things to try out at Golden Phoenix's Dim Sum: 1. Ha Gow - Shrimp dumplings 2. BBQ Pork Buns (take the paper off the bottom before eating it) 3. Su Mai - Pork Dumplings 4. Shrimp Chow Fun (the Dim Sum ones). This is shrimp in large noodles 5. Pan fried turnip (they call this Turnip pudding, I think) 6. Fried taro (this will be in the cart with all the pastries) Just a note: Chinese Salted Shrimp is not supposed to be peeled. You are supposed to eat the entire shrimp with the skin on it. It is crispy and deliciously flavorful. Seriously, thinking of it is making my mouth water.

text: Right before my first Lithe class I called to see if it would be okay to visit without first taking Immersion. "How difficult can it be?" I naively thought to myself, "It's only Pilates, or evolved, or whatever. I'm a toughie, I can handle it. Right?" Wrong. After that first class, I was hurting in places I didn't even know it was possible to hurt. This is hands-down the best workout I've ever experienced. Lauren and the rest of the instructors are tough and aim to push you to your body's limits; you won't be coddled here. But that's a good thing, because the results from these classes are worth it in the long run, and even in the short run--after each difficult class, I left feeling refreshed and healthy, and not at all tired. Here are the facts, and where my unsettled stomach comes in. One week after dining at City House I reconcile my bank account and notice a large $400 debit to my account. Whah? I would probably go as far as to comp the entire party's meals. I certainly wouldn't charge her friends accounts 13 days later. Although we waited so long, the waiter was very attentive and apologized twice to us during the wait. He communicated that they made some error in the kitchen and had to re-make the chicken. This was actually good to hear, they seem to really hold up to their standards. I must say that the chicken is worth the hour wait. I had it with a side of potato salad, and the boyfriend had it with a side of red beans and rice. The breading on the chicken is very different from your usual fried chicken. It's thin, fluffy and crispy - difficult to describe, but SO AMAZINGLY GOOD. The chicken was hot and juicy. The peas that came with the potato salad were the best I've ever had, the texture is so smooth and it tasted great with the potato salad. The red beans and rice was good as well. The plate came with 3 pieces of fried chicken. BF got two wings and one breast, but I got one wing, one drumstick and one thigh... I guess they do it randomly. Every bite was heavenly. It was fresh, hot, crispy, juicy..... more than I could ever expect. The price is very reasonable for the quantity of food. 3 piece chicken with one side is $10. The decor is very simple, and had a vintage feel to it. Overall, highly recommend this place for fried chicken!

text: I will make it easy for you. If you don't care about good food but love a cool, hippy place, Chew Man Chu (CMC) is it. The decor is nice, the crowd is great. Of course, Penang or Sakura offers a much better version. three miso ramen. where is the miso??? The soup taste terribly sweet. The pork belly slices are completely dry. Last comment, both the oxtail soup and the ramen taste very similar and very sweet. The base seems to be made from a Chinese Char Siu sauce. In fact, the Char Siu sauce smell is quite pervasive around the entire restaurant. I surmise that a common stock made basically from 1 part Char Siu sauce, 4 parts sugar and poured onto half of the food. text: Milagro Modern Mexican is just that- a departure from your traditional (and traditionally average) Mexican restaurant, replaced with a modernized version. The decor, atmosphere, lighting and spacial arrangement of the restaurant was very Modern and very refreshing. Too often have I visited some hole for decent Mexican food and was forced to sit at a 3 foot table surrounded by strangers, all within arms reach of stealing the salt shaker off of my table! Not at Milagro! The tables are large and well spaced- the space overall was used extremely well imho. The service was phenomenal! It appeared to be of the same ilk as Dewey's Pizza in that we were not the culinary property of a single waiter or waitress... new servers appeared often, asking if we needed anything. Each and every one of them were extremely friendly, helpful, attentive and fast. We started out with the traditional chips and salsa- only these were head and shoulders above 'traditional.' The corn chips were thicker and sturdier than average tortilla chips, allowing us to pick up more salsa on each chip. We tried both mild and hot salsa varieties. I recommend the hot. Food service from the kitchen was also exceptionally fast. We ordered the Tostadas de Pato and BAMF! they were on the table! They were awesome- the duck was tender and the combinations of sauces made for a delicious hot/sweet flavoring. I was skeptical about the lime cabbage initially (not into cabbage, AT ALL!) but it added a refreshing element to the flavor combination. For the main course I had the Tacos al Pastor. While reading the menu the pineapple in this dish called to me and I have to hand it to my subconscious for answering that call! The marinated pork was expertly prepared (it even LOOKED expertly prepared!), the grilled pineapple was tender and juicy, the cilantro seasoning was subtle and the corn tortillas were extremely soft and tasty! The tacos were a treat, both with the salsa verde that comes with it and also the hot salsa that came with our chips. For dessert (yes! they have desserts!) Steph and I decided on the Chocolate crepes stuffed with rum soaked plantains. Imagine a light fluffy chocolate crepe, stuffed with bananas (ok, plantains, but they're similar!) whipped to a custard-like consistency and infused with the *spiced* taste of rum then criss-crossed with chocolate and caramel syrup. Now stop imagining and go get one! This magically unique creation is a reality! With whipped cream, what else could I ask for? Besides a carry out bag to make sure none of this exquisite indulgence went to waste? For a fresh, modern expedition into the rich, uncharted jungle of Mexican cuisine, let Milagro be your guide!

I would pass. - Branzino: Unique Mediterranean fish that I had never heard of, served with head, tail, eyes, everything...tasted great. text: this airport basically sucks. However, unfortunately, I do have to use it frequently, so it gets a couple of stars. Here is important info: If you are flying US AIR domestic (USA only), then you could be in Terminal C or F. Before you get to the airport, figure out which terminal you are flying out of. Next, if you are flying Southwest, know if you are in Terminal D or E. Knowing this info will help figuring out where you need to check bags, etc. getting from terminal to terminal inside the secure areas is tricky at PHL. You are better off just going to the correct terminal. You could walk from terminal to terminal on the roadside...but, it will be a long walk!! Parking in the airport is VERY expensive (short-term and long-term). So, if you are poor and have to drive, then use an off-site lot (8$ to 12$ per day) or the Economy lot. Food choices inside most terminals SUCK badly (except Terminal C). So, bring your own food if you want. Drinks, etc is very expensive, but you have no choice than to buy them here or not have a drink at all. Toilets can be hit or miss. Best used minimally. Flight delays are very common and are a rule with US AIR. Weather is often bad and low ceilings are common. The SEPTA train runs through each terminal and connects to downtown and other destinations. SEPTA rail costs $7 to downtown and $10 to Jenkintown. (one way). People (staff) are generally not friendly, since this is the northeast. You might luck out. Continental airlines usually have reasonably good staff. I fly this airline most of the time. There are not enough chairs for the number of people (especially in terminal D). This is not fun. Also, almost non-existent power outlets. There are some by the restrooms, if you want to sit close to the nasty smells. Overall, ok airport....this is going to be as good as it gets for Philadelphia. It wont be better until USAIR becomes bankrupt and stops flying. Then, we could get a different airline as a Philly hub which might improve facilities. Oh, Be VERY careful when exiting off of I-95 to the airport. Thanks to senseless road-designers, they made the airport exits as dangerous as they possibly can. Best to just take the train if you dont live here.

text: Been to Kotatsu twice and really enjoyed both meals. It's a Japanese steakhouse and sushi bar that's BYOB with a state store (wine and spirits) on the same strip. Service at the hibachi table was OK first time, much better the second time. Get an appetizer in case you have to wait for the table to be fired up -- gyoza were good. And when the chef tosses the shrimp at you, hold up your napkin just in case you don't catch it. (A friend sacrificed her sweater when she forgot to do this.) We'll be going back at some point and will try the sushi. We've heard a lot of horror stories about Hibachi -- several locations in town and in the 'burbs -- and walked out once ourselves before actually getting a seat there. Thanks to Kotatsu, we have a much better option. Highly recommended (for the hibachi at least).

text: In my head, all theaters should still look like the Bala theater. It was built in 1926 and the outside facade is all decked out in Egyptian Revival motifs that were really popular with movie theaters in the 20s and 30s. It even still has an old school style marquee that juts out from the front. The inside is even more beautiful, grand staircases up to the second floor where balcony seating used to be, and lots of handpainted murals. In the early 90s they turned the theater into a triplex, and luckily the architectural firm that did it kept the structural and historical integrity of the existing auditorium and it's still gorgeous inside. The theater plays a lot of indie and foreign films, and it's a great place to go see something after a run has ended at the Ritz. I went here to see the new Jean-Pierre Jeunet comedy, "Micmacs" which was fantastic. But I'm not reviewing the movie! Seriously walking in this place is like mini time travel.

text: This is a "SIX STAR" restaurant. Commander's Palace is as good as it gets. I have eaten from one end of the USA to the other and this is hands down my absolute favorite restaurant. Period. The menu is innovative and sometimes surprising. While emphasis may be on Creole cuisine, I would describe much of the fare as being Continental. CPR has been serving patrons since before the Civil War. The restaurant resides in an Antebellum home with seven distinctly different dining rooms in the establishment, allowing for a different ambiance from one room to the next. Each dish is prepared to perfection. Each cocktail is wonderful. What distinguishes CPR from all other restaurants is their service. It is over-the-top and they make all other fine restaurants look amateurish in contrast. The wait staff is invisible except when they are wanted. The somehow anticipate their patrons desires. I have yet to experience this level of service in any other restaurant. Do expect to spend a small fortune eating here. A sumptuous feast for two will set you back at least $150. Did I mention that their bread pudding souffle is to die for? It is the best bread pudding dish I have ever had. As talented as the likes of Emeril LaGasse, Wolfgang Puck and Paul Prudhomme are on their own merits, each started his meteoric rise to fame at Commander's Palace. Their success is in no small part attributable to this historic and venerable establishment.

text: Planning a conference trip is always an exercise in anxiety for me, knowing how much money I'm going to need to spend on conference registration, sub-par food, ridiculous hotel prices, and outrageous airfares. Upon arrival at the airport, I took the "Indy Go" (cute name) Green Line shuttle, which provides express service to downtown hotels for $7. The Omni was the shuttle's first stop. Prepared to get stuck in an $87 second-story closet over the boiler room/kitchen/bar, or next to a construction site, I was happily surprised to be placed on the 8th floor, in a room with a bit of a view, room to walk around, and a cozy king-size bed. A good friend stayed in the same hotel, had to pay the regular rates, and wasn't so lucky, getting a queen size bed in a much smaller room. If you find this piece of info helpful for upcoming reservations, #855 was the bigger room, and #422 was the smaller one. The bathroom was immaculately clean, and my only peeve was leaky faucets, forcing me to relocate all my toiletries to keep them dry. I did report the faucet problem, so hopefully someone will fix them. I did not use the room service, but the typical $10 bagel and juice, among other expensive breakfast options, were advertised on the nightstand. Skip that, give yourself extra time in the morning, and walk 15 minutes to Cafe Patachou on, I think, Capitol and Washington. There was a tempting tray of goodies on the desk, but $3.50 for a Clif Nectar bar kept me away. Glad I stuffed some Trader Joe's dried fruit & nuts in my bag before I left home. If you're looking for snack food, there's a CVS drugstore at 105 E. Ohio, about a 10-15 minute walk from the hotel. A coffee pot, along with caffeinated and decaf Wolfgang Puck coffee are in the room. A nice touch were the paper cups with lids, so I could take my beverage with me on my way out. Weekday copies of USA Today newspaper were also waiting outside my door every morning. The Omni also provides wi-fi service. Upon trying to go online, the default splash page provides three choices for access, one of which includes a $9.95 per day charge, and the other two read as if you need to pay for a membership to get the wi-fi. text: With the recent popularity of the book and film, The DaVinci Code, and interest in the Knights Templars and similar topics, it was inevitable that interest in Freemasonry, would spike . It is impossible to speak about the Masons without the discussion becoming at best political and at worst adversarial. Two things about which there can be no dispute is one, they are fiercely patriarchal and two, they are even more fiercely secretive. That out of the way we can concentrate on the magnificent edifice in the direct geographical center of the city across from City Hall, The Masonic Temple of Pennsylvania. It is arguably the most magnificent building in Philadelphia. There are 7 great rooms inside connected by ostentatiously beautiful corridors and staircases. Each room has a motif; Gothic, Ionic, Egyptian, Norman, Renassaince, Corinthian and Oriental which has woven into its design elements of the Alhambra. The walls are hung with remarkable paintings and the halls lined with extraordinary statuary, many seemingly sculpted from marble are actually carved wood. Tours are worth the $8.00, cash, and the guidelines for touring are strict. But there should be at least a few oohs and aahs.

text: The Competitor group puts on a number of marathons and half marathons throughout the country and they recently bought out the Mardi Gras Marathon/Half Marathon (this was considered the inaugural year for the Rock N Roll event). As you might expect, they have a lot of practice in organizing road races and their events run fairly smoothly. This was no exception. PRE-RACE ORGANIZATION: They did a good job in organizing shuttles from the Superdome to the starting line. The start is actually pretty close to downtown near the convention center. It's a pretty short walk from Canal street/French Quarter to the start and I personally didn't need a shuttle. For anyone planning to run this race in the future, I think that a hotel in the downtown district is fine; it's convenient to the expo and the start with shuttles taking you back this way after the finish. COURSE: I really like how they set up the course for this event. Sure, it's a flat and fast course, but they went to some pains to make it more scenic. I did the half marathon and the course encompassed a number of the sites of New Orleans. There are some nice residential sections with scenic homes, a stretch along the historic street car line at St. Charles Avenue, part through downtown and the French Quarter (I loved the hung-over spectators in shades watching me run by) as well as St. Louis Cemetary and City Park. They also had a few leftover Mardi Gras floats decorating the first few miles of the course. The marathoners also had a nice stretch through Audubon Park. This was a cooler year for New Orleans, but I think that this course would even work better on hotter days. There are a lot of sleepy trees along the course with the branches hanging over the road that provided considerable shade for the route. The one catch with the route is that the roads area bit nicked up: there's a number of potholes and irregular surfaces that you'll be running on. It felt a little bit like a trail run in this respect; I had to pay more attention to my footstrikes than typical for a road race. ORGANIZATION: Four stars instead of five overall for this. The route was well organized with plenty of water stops, bands (I loved the accordion players) and a GU stop. The post-race shuttles were a problem. Several of the staff weren't quite sure where they were located (and even were debating about whether an arrow on the sign was correct) and once we found them it was a bit of a hash. We boarded one bus, only to be told that the driver was going on break and then reloaded on a second bus. This driver said that the directions were no good and proceded to get lost in the city. It took close to an hour to get the four miles back to the hotel. On the plus side, the driver was pretty cool about letting us get off at different points near our hotels. OVERALL: A very nice race with good hospitality and an interesting course. For people considering a vacation with an easy course, this is a good choice.

text: I loved Jones! I went this past Saturday when I was back in town to celebrate my birthday with my family. I chose to come to Jones for dinner, having heard about it before, and knowing my brother comes here often with his friends. The way I see Jones, and similar restaurants (i.e. other Starr restaurants) is that you're coming here not only to get a meal, but to also have an experience. You are going to this particular restaurant because of the unique atsmosphere. That said, I also expect the food to be good with decent sized portions. Upon entering Jones we were seated right away. This was about 5:30/6 on a Saturday night. The place was pretty full, but obviously not packed since we got a booth for 5 with no wait. We sat 2 on one side, 3 on the other in our booth. It was comfortable for my parents on their side, however elbow room was a bit tight for the 3 of us sitting on the other side. It wasn't as tight as some people have described it, though. I wasn't at all uncomfortable; it just made it difficult when we all needed to cut our food at the same time. This was not a huge deal. Theme: The décor of Jones is exactly how others have described it: retro 70's, complete with avocado green booths, wood paneling, orange chairs and funky lighting fixtures. I absolutely loved it. Menu: While the menu is not huge, there are certainly a number of meals to choose from, as well as a wide variety of food from seafood, steak, pasta, and typical favorites like chicken pot pie and meatloaf. There are also a bunch of sandwiches as well. Menu is available on their website. Service: Despite what some may have said about their service, we had no problems. Our waitress even brought my dad's half eaten meal back under the heat lamp to keep warm while he got up to take an important call. Either way, I try not to judge a place based on their service unless I've gone a few times and still have a problem. You can get a bad/snobbish/inattentive server anywhere, from a 5 star restaurant to a local dive, and unfortunately unless you address that with the server or manager, it may not change. But again, we had no issues, just good service. Food: All of us were happy with the food. First of all, the portions were large so I felt the prices were justified. Secondly, despite what I've read on here, I would not put the quality of this food in the same range as a diner - it's most definitely above. While the menu items may have included diner-type meals, you can't forget that it's a part of the theme of this place. What would a retro-themed restaurant be without serving those at-home favorites? The quality of food was what I would expect for the price and type of restaurant. The 5 of us shared two orders of the pierogies as an appetizer. We all raved about how good they were, I definitely recommend them. However, while I found all the portions to be large on other foods, there were only 3 pierogies to an order. Slightly pricey for only 3, but I would order them again because they were that good. For dinner, my mom ordered the chicken pot pie which she was unable to finish due to the size. My dad ordered the pistachio crusted tilapia, and my boyfriend had the spicy jambalaya (and loved it). I went with the make your own salad - there were so many things on the menu that I wanted, but I've been on a major salad kick lately, and when I saw how huge the salads were, I was sold. I have to say, the mini clipboard/checklist sitting on the table for ordering the personal salad was a cute touch as well. Lastly, my brother, who has been here many times, never ordering the same thing twice, tried a hamburger this time. He admits that it was not the most flavorful hamburger and won't order it again, but still loves everything else he's eaten here (including the crabcake which I was considering ordering). Dessert: My dad and I each ordered the strawberry shortcake -delicious, and the boys each ordered the chocolate cake, which was actually served with a cold glass of milk. A cute idea and perfect touch! It's safe to say that I'd like to go to Jones again when I'm back in my home area sometime. I enjoyed the food, the atmosphere was fun and unique, and the prices were pretty much what they should be for this type of place. The dress code can range from casual to dressy, meaning whatever you wear in that range you'd fit in. I recommend Jones if you're looking for a fun place to get a good meal in the city.
label: POS

They roped off the rest of the restaurant, so that people looking for enough space to breathe were reduced to standing in front of the service entrances, or practically spilling into the lobby of the Comcast Center. Second, we went for Sips, hoping for the menu that they had advertised online, but when we arrived we discovered that the actual menu available was completely different: instead of a yummy-sounding mango drink, the only thing available was a variation on a cosmo made with well booze. And instead of half-priced pizza and etc, if you wanted food, you could either pay their full (steep!) prices, or pay $7 for 3 small pieces of tuna sushi. text: Pho is essentially a hot noodle and meat soup and takes hours upon hours to make. It's a time consuming process but the end result speaks for itself. I should know; I've eaten it all my life. So I enter any Vietnamese restaurant being slightly skeptical of their pho because frankly, I know a good bowl of pho from a bad one. Trust me, I've had my fair share of bad pho and it's not good at all. However, Pho Ha makes a damn tasty bowl of pho hands down. I ordered the pho tai nam gau gan sach (steak, fatty flank, tendon and tripe - yes, tripe!). It was delicious, comforting and filling - everything you want in a hearty bowl of pho. A very well flavored broth adorned by copious amounts of meats makes me a very happy camper. And at about $5 for an immense bowl, it was a friggin steal! A little tip - if you ever encounter an expensive bowl of pho (like over $9), you're getting ripped off. Pho is so NOT an expensive soup! The place is a mad house on weekends so plan on getting here either really early or really late. They keep things relatively clean and moving. Super fast service too. My only gripe is that they're cash only. Luckily, it's cheap as frick here. The parking lot is fairly big but they're located in an extremely busy strip mall (on weekends) so that too can be a bit of a pain. Would I come back? Pho sure!

text: My lady friend loves me. How do I know? She treated me to Mercato for my birthday last month. Mercato is the best overall BYO in Philadelphia. Now that I've written it, feel free to state it as fact. I will accept no arguments to the contrary because they are inherently flawed. It's literally impossible to disagree with my assessment. I ordered the Grilled Petit Tender Filet. $25. Beef Consommé, red bliss potatoes, brussel sprouts, smoked bacon. Cooked to perfection. Incredible price point. Large portions. Comfort food doesn't get any better than this. A debate between archaeologists, historians, and anthropologists has raged for years regarding the catalyst behind the shockingly accurate premonitions of the Pythia at the Oracle of Delphi. How could they know the future? What could possibly trigger their vivid hallucinations? Nerds say it's ethylene gas emanating from the earth beneath the Oracle. Dreamers claim that it's pure, unadulterated divine inspiration. I think they're both wrong and my hypothesis has the potential to shake the conventional wisdom to its core. The Oracular Statements of Delphi are clearly the result of the mind-altering aromas that wafted up from my Filet masterpiece. I didn't see Mackenzie Hilton, but I'm almost certain that she is the reincarnation of Aeschylus, brought back to spread the ancient joys of Gaia throughout the modern world. Upon reaching my olfactory receptors, the vapors drove me into a trance-like state, not unlike a coma. My girlfriend said I looked like a junkie on Intervention after a nice, fat shot of heroin. I slumped over in my chair...inert...dead to the world. However, while my body languished, my mind exploded with glorious visions of the divine and the improbable. There I sat for a thousand years, a bucket of water resting precariously atop the Great Wall of China until a nomadic Giant came along and poured me out. As I splashed across the stone and mortar, the droplets of water constituting my essence shattered into an infinite number of stars that laughed and sang their way into the nether regions of the universe...It was a spirit quest of the highest order. If only I could find Don Juan, I could piece together the puzzle that is my being. Alas, he is dead. Oh well. When I came to there was a pool of drool collecting on my sweater and my lady friend was frantically digging through her purse in pursuit of a cell phone with which to call 9-1-1. Thank God she didn't or I wouldn't have had a chance to eat. And oh boy did I eat...voraciously! Like my yokel South Carolina cousins after a long day on the farm, I tore into my dish is if it were my last meal on earth. Every successive bite was better than the last. By the time I finished I was fully satiated and depressed. Like the end of a great book or an engrossing movie, I couldn't believe it was over already. I will be back...if I can ever get a seat again!
label: POS

thought oh no, new recipe, suck ass, but when i took a bite of their pizza, still the same recipe. so why have i been eating this pizza for so long and dont think no other place out there makes it the same... their sauce is phenomenal, very tangy and has a little spice (although id prefer more, its just right so that everybody can enjoy it). they dont skimp on the sauce either, they add a lot. it also is just enough so that it doesnt ruin that t really thin and crispy crust, if you're lucky you still see them hand toss that dough in the air. they also add lots of cheese, and sprinkle pepper and oregano all over it. i usually order their supreme pizza with all the ingredients such as olives, mushrooms, meatballs, pepperoni, bell peppers, etc. lately, i have been ordering a pie with just pancetta and mushrooms. oh its so damn f#ckin good, to see all those mushrooms and red/brown spicy/salty pieces of pancetta causing you to see a shiny oil sheen all atop the pizza. ive had requests from other former residents here in vegas to freeze pies and transport it back up here to vegas. it is that good!!!! If you don't go with a large group of people, you can order pizza by the slice. the slices are bigger than a standard paper plate. i remember eating on the portions that hung over the plate as i was being driven in the car when i was a little kid. i dont recommend ordering a small or medium pizza b/c the crust wont be as thin or as crispy b/c they really load up the pizzas. get the slice instead, unless you get a large or x-large. oh yeah, you have to try their calzones. get the meatball calzone...whew its like eating a football stuffed with hella sauce and meatballs....when you first take a fork and knife to this thing, you see hot steam and sauce spew out of the crust. when you take the calzone for take away, they use a wine box. i think the last time i ate there, it took me 3 days to finish that thing...i cant wait to go there....two more weeks!!!

Another thing is they're use of the propane torch to crisp the skin on my fish.....helloooo....I can taste the propane and it's not very pleasant. And the plate of nigiri that came out was so small that I had bring out my magnifying glass to eat it. I was still hungry after that 8 course meal. Another annoying thing was the neon lit interior, the colored lights kept changing every 10 seconds, how annoying when trying to eat. text: On a recent trip to Indy we were looking for a good place to eat that wouldn't be super heavy or a big steakhouse (we had reservations at a steak house the next everning). Indy seems to be very big on steak houses, and this was the alternative we were looking for. I really enjoy tapas style eating since I tend to want to try everyone else's food anyway, so small plates get a big plus from the start from me. Our service here was great, the waiter was very friendly and helpful with drink selections. the food is decently priced and about as to be expected for tapas. We had no issues with waiting too long for food even though we got one of the steak kabob dishes. Actually, we had to be careful to not order more plates too soon or else we were ending up with a table full of food! Tha goat cheese was good. Better than similar dishes like this that I've had. the bread was crusty, but not hard, and you get a generous portion of cheese. The sause also has a very nice amount of spices added to it which took it to a higher level. The garlic shrimp were very good if you like garlic, shrimp, and spice, which I do. the empenadas were so-so. A previous review was right when they said it tasted like boiled frozen spinach. I thought the dough was very tasty though. The horseradish steak kabob was tasty and very well cooked (be wary of this dish if you like your meat well done. Ours came out med-rare which is what we like, but I didn't remember the waiter asking). We had a great experience on a casual night out for two people. I could see where it could be too loud for larger groups, but on a Thursday night it was perfect. The interior is also a bit similar to a Chilis-type interior or a lot of mexican places, but it seems to work for them and did not put me off at all. It is very brightly colored and festive, which makes a great casual night out.

text: I hope that this location is replaced by something better. It could be anything. It could be an empty office space filled with heroin junkies and it would be an improvement. My feelings towards Sprint and its employees are like the manifestation of a cruel joke, being played on me by an angry God who has decided to wreak karmic vengeance on me for every sin I've committed. This scenario is actually comforting to me, because it means I've already paid for my sins while on this earth and will probably end up going to heaven instead of hell when I die. The door functions and the temperature is comfortable for casual and business attire. Apart from these two qualities, everything about my experience here was horrible. Every single person, from the greeter to the manager, tries to pass the buck to someone else. The retail store passes me off to customer support. Customer support passes me off to order support. Order support asks me to show my ID to a retail employee to prove who I am before they tell me they can't help me. When I walk into a retail establishment and I'm told that I have to call their customer service from one of their demo phones, this is a serious problem. AT&T will crush you. text: Rock-n-Sake's sushi rolls may truly be the best I've ever had, anywhere. Reading the reviews I see a lot of complaints about the price. My faves are Calamari Crunch Roll ($9.75) for 8 large pieces, Crunchy Dynamite ($6), LSU ($13), Rebel Rice Paper Roll ($8 - oh my GOODNESS!), and Shrimp Tempura($7.25). It is only a block away from the hotel I seem to stay at the most, which is great after a 12-15 hour day working a convention. Yes, it is super crowded - every night after about 6:30. text: I have a soft spot for Morton's. Simply stated, it is a fine dining steakhouse experience. Real food, real service. I've been here a few times, always for special outings with family or some special lady. The first time I was here, it was located a bit further west tucked away. They relocated some years back to the more central location of Broad & Walnut. The elevator opens to the coat check/host area. The dining room is spacious and adorned with large bottles of wine. A few booths line the wall. After being served drinks, you will be graced with the privilege of hearing the server's rundown of the menu. This is done with visual aides, the server wheels a cart with all the different cuts of meat on it. Since there is a whole lobster on the menu, lo and behold - there is a live lobster on the cart for your viewing pleasure as well. (I know it sounds gimmicky and unnecessary, but it's cool, unique and I always enjoy it.) Like any fine steakhouse, it has a choice selection of apps & sides. Tuna Tartare, Scallops wrapped in bacon & a lobster bisque come to mind. Steaks are quality and cooked to perfection, in my opinion. I usually go with the Porterhouse - best of both worlds. Two unfortunate incidents of note, costing it one star: 1) A server once spilled a good portion of a Cosmo on my date. It took her a while to even come back with any offer to help clean up, a napkin or even to top off her drink. I understand mistakes happen. I don't sweat the small stuff, but the players involved in fine dining are supposed to bring their A-Game. High standards of service, product and overall experience are paramount. What may seem like minor mishaps DO matter within this context. Delaying in bringing relief for your mistake only exacerbates the problem. 2) I had received a Morton's gift card as a present. I took a girl out and chose to use it. As the server stood to my right, I very discreetly added the gift card to the check presenter along with my credit card. The server decided to chime in with "Oh I see we got a gift card." He saw me being discreet handling it yet he decided it would be a good idea to announce it so that my date would hear. The girl I was with wasn't superficial. We were pretty close. I didn't NEED to conceal the fact that I was using a gift card. Gentlemen don't discuss price, it was just natural discretion on my part. I don't wave my debit or credit card around when paying either. Really server man? What's your deal? The guy who's expecting to be tipped out heavily, who is supposed to be bending over backwards to keep us happy is sitting here trying to embarrass me? It was so transparent that he was doing it intentionally, for no other purpose other than being a total dick. He was a skinny, balding guy with blond hair and glasses. I don't know if he still works there. If you're reading this: F@#K YOU! That having been said, I will still definitely go back and recommend it to others. Oh, it's one of the few places I've found that served Heineken Dark too. ;)
label: POS

text: I LOVE the Hinge and often go out of my way to visit. The iced coffee in the summer is reason enough (and get something from the bakery. You will never regret it). I've only eaten dinner here once but I loved it. The bowl of roasted brussel sprouts was hard to finish because the serving was huge! My dining partner and I both got a bowl and couldn't even stop to take a breath. We devoured them. Perfectly pan-seared, not too oily, and just spicy and garlic-y enough without hitting you over the head. The "Japanese Meatballs" or whatever it was called (the menu changes monthly) sounded risky but I went with it because they're vegetarian. I was right to take the risk. Imagine Japanese soul food... and you've got these. They were everything you love about Japanese food, crammed into a ball, and lightly fried. Served with cold soba noodles, I was in heaven. My waitress provided some extra peanut sauce to dip the "meatballs" in and it was perfect. My friend ordered some sort of fish dish and loved it, tho I don't recall the particulars. Brunch, on the other hand, is something I frequently grab at the Hinge and LOVE. The breakfast burrito will keep you full all day. I don't have a single complaint or negative thing to say about the brunch here. In short, go to the Hinge. It's a BYOB with a diverse menu, friendly servers (one of them just won the annual "Best Waitress in Port Richmond" prize according to the owner), and one hell of a brunch.

I developed a serious craving for dumplings after a recent vacation in Shanghai and these dumplings fill the need. The staff can heat up your food if you desire really hot food, but most of the time I just heat up some of the things at home. Honestly-with a name like Yummy Yummy there is a lot to live up to and they do. I highly recommend this place for tasty treats, good prices, and kind service.

text: Dalessandro's was the best cheesesteak I ever had. I have lived in Roxborough/East Falls for the past 3+ years and have passed this place innumerable times - I have even patronized Chubby's Steaks across the street a couple of times. Chubby's staff was distinctively rough & unfriendly and the steak wasn't memorable. So, a few weeks ago, a friend of mine from out of town had to have a Philly Cheesesteak after a day of shopping in Chestnut Hill. I was blown away by this cheesesteak - perfection. The roll was sooo fresh. This is why Philly steaks cannot be replicated elsewhere. Everyone thinks they can throw meat on a hot dog bun and call it a Philly steak. In addition, the staff couldn't be friendlier. They served also, Frank's Black Cherry soda which my guest enjoyed - also a Philly favorite and I hadn't seen it served locally much. Good to know it's still around. The steak was no frills - prepared the mass way all the others are (there was an Eagles game that day, so I think they were preparing for a boom). Reasonably priced. Cash only, but worth the trip. I have had a good number of Philly cheesesteaks in my time, but this place deserves it's title as #1. text: I've been hearing great things about PYT for a few months, but due to scheduling conflicts (everytime I walked by it was closed.) I never got to give the burgers a test spin. I finally got a chance to stop by P.Y.T. with a few friends on Monday night. I entered in the side door and was greeted then sat immediately. The waitress immediately brought waters out and waited for the rest of the party to arrive (they were outside smoking) to take our drink order. I have to say that there were only four beers on tap, Walt Wit, Kenzinger, High Life, and I think an IPA and there was no drink menu, so if they have bottles, I'm not aware of it. There was a nice selection of food even for the vegetarians out there, but our party settled on Baby Burgers, a Cheeseburger, and Grilled Cheese. We got a round of onion rings and french fries, which for three people, was plenty. The menu was inaccurate which was irritating (the cheeseburger doesn't come with lettuce and tomato... I seriously cannot understand why restaurants do that), but the waitress pointed it out immediately, which was appreciated. Now, the food was great. My friends split the baby burgers and grilled cheese and refused to share either. From what I hear, and from the lack of sharing, I understand they were top notch. The cheeseburger was a solid, six dollar burger. It's higher quality than a fast food burger, but not a gourmet burger and not something that is craveable specifically. In other words, I'm not going to say, "I want a PYT burger." more like, "I could go to PYT or Five Guys or Carl's Jr/Hardee's for a burger." However, what really sets the burger apart is its lack of greasyness which was much appreciated. Like a gourmet cheeseburger, the meat did not soak through leaving the bread soggy. I really enjoyed the burger and I'm glad (or maybe I shouldn't be) I can walk to it from my house. As far as the onion rings go, they're not bad, I just wouldn't say they're the best I've ever eaten. I ate two and they were over battered, soggy, and bland. Call me weird, I look forward to the cooked onion part, but all the taste I got was similar to a heavy, grease-soaked tempura with onion in the middle. The fries- they were just forgettable. It's only two days since I've eaten them and all I can say is there were fries on the table, I ate some, but they probably weren't even seasoned. Our table settled for some beers on tap, but those adult milkshakes are tempting. If you're thinking about making a trip to PYT, it's worth the trip. It's a neat place with an interesting design. The prices are par with the food and the service is great. I would even venture to say our waitress (and the rest of the staff) broke the "Northern Liberties code" by smiling and being friendly. Despite the fact there seemed to be a lot of extra staff that stood around and talked, she was still attentive to our needs. The only thing I would complain about is the fact avocados are an additional $2. They ran out of them, maybe the steep price tag is a regional thing (I just moved to Philadelphia) but for that price I would hope I get an entire avocado on my burger.

text: We'd read good reviews of this place on Tripadvisor.com and thought it would be a good place to eat dinner, since we both love tapas. What a mistake! We were the only people in the restaurant on a Saturday night, which should have told us something, considering that other restaurants in the area had full parking lots. It actually reminded us a lot of the show Kitchen Nightmares, where the restaurant was deserted and the standards had slowly slipped over time (we're giving them the benefit of the doubt that they weren't always this awful). We arrived during "happy hour," which ostensibly should have entitled us to $5 tapas. After we were given the check, with full priced tapas on it, we overheard another server (not ours) tell the second group in the dining room that the $5 tapas was tapas that was not on the menu. Unfortunately, our server did NOT tell us this. He was very nice and friendly, but seemed quite callow, given the absence of his notification about the tapas specials and the fact that he didn't offer us dessert or to order more tapas, even though we said that we'd start with 3 and would probably order more. There were other strange things about the service like, with an entirely empty dining room, they gave us the table next to the bathroom. The woman who seated us didn't pull out our chairs or spread out our napkins, which was another indication of the unpolished service that we received here. The food, though, was the big problem. We wanted to start with three different tapas, but they were out of the one that sounded most appealing to us, the fried green tomatoes with crab meat. We ordered the ceviche, four crab croquettes, and the shrimp al ajillo. The ceviche turned out to be a garden salal with precisely TWO shrimp, sliced lengthwise, and a half of a bay scallop, which was cut into two pieces. Not exactly what is usually indicated by the term "ceviche," especially for $7.50. The crab croquettes, which were described as "filled with crab and cheese," turned out to be plain potato croquettes. Neither crab nor cheese was in evidence here. The shrimp al ajillo, at $7.95, was a giant rip off. This, of the three dishes, turned out to be the only one that was what it said it was: shrimp with garlic sauce. However, $7.95 at Tapas Garden buys you 6 medium-sized (26-30/lb) shrimp. Woo hoo! I'm posting a photo, though it's only got 5 shrimp, since I forgot that we were photographing the food and had eaten one of the shrimp before I remembered this. I was so irritated at this point by the misinformation and misleading descriptions that we just paid the check and left. I didn't even finish my glass of wine because I was so irked. I would definitely advise avoiding this restaurant unless you would like to pay too much for mediocre food with either excessively small portion sizes or misleading ingredients like "ceviche" or "crab" croquettes.

text: My first impression was of trying to reach this compound on foot from McGavock Pike. A sidewalk was provided; "That's thoughtful," I said to myself, since getting run over seemed a likely alternative. The more the sidewalk meandered about the grounds, however, the more doubts I began to have. When the sidewalk led me to a closed, locked gate, "thoughtful" was no longer the word I associated with it. Fortunately, an entrance (excuse me, "portico") was visible only a quarter-mile away, and at that point I disregarded the "Please follow sidewalk" signs and went for the shortest distance between two points. My second impression was of a cozy, high-class hotel lobby -- I'd entered through the Magnolia Portico. My third, as I traveled toward my meeting room, was of the enormous Delta Atrium, full of plants, brick buildings, wrought iron railings, flowing water and winding paths and overlooked by walls of balconied hotel rooms. It had a quirky, organic charm. My fourth impression was of trying to find a decent place to eat dinner. I was in a gregarious mood and happened to strike up a conversation with two other convention-goers, which is the only reason I got into Volare, which had one unreserved table left and a 90-minute (!) anticipated wait after that. (The next night I tried, and failed, to get into Wasabi, a seafood restaurant, and I balked at the outrageously expensive Old Hickory Steakhouse.) Some of Volare's entrees were appealing-looking but, at $20 to $30, out of my range. I settled for a Caesar salad and a personal brick-oven pizza, which I ate half of. When I asked to have the other half wrapped up, the waiter brought me a Pizza Hut box. He said it had come from room service, but I still had to go, "Hmmm." My fifth impression was that, once inside the compound, it was difficult to get out. I was staying in a motel just across McGavock Pike, less than a mile away, but a taxi ride from one side to the other (no way was I going to attempt to walk the distance anymore) cost $7; a ride to anywhere else in town had to be at least $15. (I discovered later that it cost twice that to get to the Vanderbilt-Belmont area.) Also -- sixth impression -- the artificiality of the place was starting to get to me. It had been cute at first, but the tourist-trap ambience of Delta Island in particular and the extremely expensive array of available shops and restaurants in general, not to mention the tacky Christmas decorations (in mid-November -- pretty soon, the World Series and the start of the winter holiday season are going to cross over each other), had eclipsed it. In two days, I'd learned my way around the labyrinth pretty well, and since my mind was no longer occupied by figuring out how to get from Point A to Point B, it now had time to notice -- and dwell on -- what a colossal pain in the ass it invariably was. It began to feel like one of those Star Trek bubble universes, where the laws of physics are different and people disappear and undulating girls in tight, skimpy black dresses sing "We Got the Beat" and "Wrap It Up" in a faux Bourbon Street bar. I was sorely tempted, more than once, to toss a wrapper on the path, just to test the level of surveillance. My seventh and final impression was that Findley's Allegedly Irish Pub was the only decent meal deal in the entire joint -- a tasty crab cake with remoulade and pub chips cost around $10. Also, if you came at night, a couple of guys (one from Tennessee, one from Leicestershire) would play Irish songs and crack jokes about how ridiculous the "Bayou-dome" was. (Not that Findley's itself escaped this ridiculousness -- among the menu items was, I kid you not, the Pail o' Sausage.) In five days, I managed to escape from the bubble into the real world only once. I can state authoritatively that the real world is better.

text: Protzel's has hands-down the best corned beef. Period. Exclamation point. I have been singing the praises of Protzel's corned beef for as long as I can remember. And every other Jewish deli I order a corned beef sandwich from has failed to live up to my standards. I don't know their secret, but even if I did, I'd still come back for the heavenly good sandwiches. My favorite is the corned beef on rye with spicy mustard. Some people like it with cheese, but not me. Prices aren't cheap, especially for the corned beef (which I think they cure on site), but whatever they're charging is but a small price to pay for the best corned beef sandwich ever! Their potato salad is also possibly the best potato salad I've ever had. It's mustard-based (but not too tangy), and the potatos have just the right texture. Their slaw is good (both the sweet and the vinegar), as is their chopped liver. The tzitzel rye bread is yummy - I wish I could eat all my sandwiches on that! Be warned - they're closed on Mondays, and can be jammed packed on the weekends, so make sure you allow ample time to savor your Protzel's deli experience. There's street parking in front along Wydown. Also, there's a few counter chairs inside, with a small table or two, and a couple tables outside - but most people just get their goodies to go.

I ate so much of that with bread dipped in olive oil that I took most of my entree home! Their menu is huge - I think almost any pasta dish incarnation you can dream up will be on it. It's very hard to decide and just sitting there sipping wine for a bit and watching the food come out of the kitchen didn't help, absolutely everything looked scrumptious! Last night I had the "Tagliatelle ai Funghi Porcini" which was pasta with porcini mushrooms, garlic, cream and onions. Oh my, if you like a deep mushroom taste try this, so good and the sauce was not thick or too heavy either. My dining partner had the chicken cacciatore which I tasted and though I would not order it, it was still very good made with boneless chicken breast with some yummy salty olives in the sauce. We split a slice of chocolate mousse cake for dessert and it was completely delicious, deep dark chocolate cake that was not sweet with a luscious rich chocolate mousse in between the layers and a lighter chocolate butter cream icing outside. I teasingly asked the owner if he baked it and he said it was from Sweet Jazmines (a local bakery, which I now need to check out!). It's BYOB so take a nice wine, the food deserves it. The only negative is how small this place is. With the exception of a few tables in private alcoves, it's mostly European type seating with lots of tables squished very close together so you are practically sharing a table with those around you. Lunch it's very quiet there but at night it is hard to get a table, so call for a reservation. This place is no where near my house but I would go out of my way to go back. Maybe I should give it a four because of the seating but that doesn't really bother me so it's a five, just really excellent food and service.

text: When you walk in the door, you'll smell the sweet aroma of cigarette smoke and desperation. Your first inclination will be to turn around. But keep going. The drinks are cheap and sold in plastic cups. Good start. On the small stage, they'll have an acoustic act playing an assortment of trailer park anthems and highschool party favorites. Getting better. At this point, if you're smart, you'll realize the night is probably a wash and accept it for what it is. Losers ain't about self-respect, baby. The crowd is extremely diverse. It runs from twenty-something songwriter/musicbiz/whatever types to fifty-something songwriter/musicbiz/whatever types. Occasionally you might see a geezer in a track suit make his way through the crowd. The MILFs will murmur: was that Kenny Rogers? Or just a geezer in a track suit? With Loosers, you never know. In the heyday of the Nashville music biz--before it imploded and began hemorrhaging money by the truckload--deals went down in these dives. Now it's mostly people trying playing the part. Nonetheless, it's still fun to watch. Whether a local or a tourist, you owe it to yourself to visit this place once. Go on in, order a Tanqueray and Tab, and enjoy the show.

Since I hadn't eaten since noon, and it was nearing 8PM, this did not bode well. -1 star They DO have outdoor seating in the alley, which consisted of four patio tables. Some people in the group enjoyed a tasty $7 Margarita before moving on to $6 shots of Patron. The bottled domestic beer was under $3 each. Once seated, service was a little slow. To be fair, it was a packed house on a Friday evening (approximately 8:30PM. Our water came only after we had been there for almost twenty minutes, and orders were taken shortly thereafter. Or meal was delivered in an acceptable time frame, and all went well. Some of my friends were a little put-off by the prices, but I thought they were fine. I had the chicken mole, which is usually all I ever order at Mexican food restaurants. The meal tasted fine, although I could feel my stomach churning an hour later. Sometime around 3AM my stomach woke me and I felt feverish. An hour or two later I was hugging the toilet and praying for mercy. Overall, my experience would have been three-stars without the food poisoning. But since I'm still clutching my stomach at 2PM the next day, I'll have to resort to a single star.

text: I took some time to read the other reviews before I wrote mine, so do not think the two stars is a snap judgment. Like many others, I've been coming to Zern's my entire life. I have been bringing my son there since he was born, and my 90+ year old Aunt tells stories of when it was new and in the middle of nowhere. But Zern's has changed, and not in a good way. I've watched the cafeteria close and never be replaced by a business that has stuck for more than a season. I've seen the flea market reduced from a huge venture to a few very old retailers hawking the same products they've been selling for the last ten years. Watched as craftsmen and real vendors have been replaced by dollar store vendors, siding salesmen, roof repair hawks, and empty stalls. Even the huge army navy store closed a couple years ago. replaced by a bunch of smaller craptastic hawkers. Spring Glenn farms, the last true purveyor of true PA Dutch food closed a few years back (Allentown Market Fair has a stall). There is only one Bakery left, and they are hit or miss with what they have, and Burts Farms, the best purveyor of meat in the market, closed this week. Years ago you'd see local farmers selling fresh produce along side their wives, who sold their jams, jellies, and fresh baked goods baked fresh early that morning. Do you remember? Zern's apparently does not. Yes - there are still some glimmers of hope. Little Richards, eternally staffed by teens still serves a decent lunch. The spice shop is well stocked and fair priced, and (some) of the fruit and veggie vendors still sell decent local produce. But the decent vendors are fast fleeing, and management seems content to let the market die. Maybe they'll put in a nice Wal*Mart - wouldn't that be grand?

text: A sophisticated treat! Delizioso! This is as authentic an Italian Gelato Cafe as you can find on this side of the Atlantic. That means when they run out, they run out. No time to make more until tomorrow. If you're not familiar with real, fresh gelato, imagine a smoother, richer, yet somehow lighter version of your favorite ice cream. But you'll need to make more than one trip to savor all these fabulous flavors. I highly recommend trying a Gnutella crepe. It's big enough to share and unlike anything I've had before. They make their crepes fresh right before your eyes (crepes are like super thin and fluffy pancakes) then they spread a a rich chocolate over top. The chocolate has the consistency of peanut butter, but it's flavored with hazelnuts. Topped with whipped cream - why not just skip dinner! Last but not least is their coffee bar - again completely authentic. I think I saw Illy's beans near the espresso machine. You must try a shot of espresso poured over top of your favorite gelato flavor. A coffee-lovers dream in a cup.

text: Sometimes things are named ironically, unfortunately, or inaccurately. Often, you see those in nicknames guys give to each other. If you listened to the previous reviews, you'd be left to believe that Doghouse is ironically named, and that is simply not the case. I do, however, think that the restaurant is somewhat inaccurately named. Confused? Read on, intrepid foodie. I've tried the food here 3 times, and found that, like a sophomore in college, it is a restaurant still finding itself. The first time I went, I was graced with a burger that only Wayne Gretsky would love... (vague hockey puck reference) it was well-done, and awful. When Shaun, the manager stopped by to ask me about the food I informed him of the problem, and he immediately thanked me and got to work on another burger. The second and third times proved to be much better. The fact of the matter is, the Doghouse serves good burgers, cooked fresh, and has beer by the bottle and on tap (Victory Brewing Company, anyone!). Their fries are good, though not for the potato, but for the seasonings. The onion rings are tremendous, and the missus loves the sweet potato fries. Now, it is time to return to the comment about ironic naming... on to the burgers (I haven't done a hot dog yet)! When one thinks of "gourmet burgers" many things can come to mind, and all of them subjective. Do you think of sauteed shallots, maitakes, and boursin on a brioche? Well, that is not this eateries modus operandi. In fact, the toppings are fairly pedestrian, but they are good. ... hence, the inaccurately named Doghouse Gourmet Burgers. P.S. - the prices aren't gourmet, either.

text: I come from a Californian town where EVERY STREET CORNER is a froyo place. Did I like this place? NO. Decor: Fro yo places are supposed to be 'cool' and 'hip'. This place was like TRYING to be. It was basically all white and light blue, but everything was all in an attempt to follow a trend rather than trying to make it a good quality-looking place. As for the customers there, it was swarming with college kids and high-school (?) kids which made a nice buzz of conversation.
