text: 10th Street Laundromat is pop music posing as alternative rock, and it frustrates me beyond comparison. Located just at the edge of South Philadelphia (just a block and you're in Center City!), a first glance pegs this joint as super hip and cool. And it couldn't be more intentional: having had the sad fortune of interacting with the owner, a lady who is far more interested in image than product, it is no small fact that you are supposed to be fooled into thinking you're at a cool coffee bar. But you're not. You're at a laundromat. A cramped, sweaty, overpriced laundromat. The foundations are no different than any other laundromat: washers and dryers are packed in so tight that you can barely maneuver your way through. There is NO seating; which is to say there are a few (3 maybe) rickety folding chairs which are rarely free for use. It is HOT and CRAMPED. Did I mention that? The only way to remain comfortable is to go sit outside, where they have put some nice wooden benches. The cost is pretty high in comparison with other places, and you can't help but figure you're paying extra to be "hip". One load of laundry is $1.25 and the dryer goes up by 6 minutes for every quarter you chuck in. Unless it's the weekend, at which point those prices double. People comment on the art that is displayed here and the live bands that sometimes play. Neither are very good. The art that is hung up is usually horrendously bad, with the occasional tolerable item gracing the walls. It screams "Freshman art student." Honestly, if they could ditch the artwork and instead make more room to move around or be seated, I wouldn't complain. The staff is a disaster. They have a penchant for hiring young-ish emo types who play Tori Amos all day and don't make eye contact. Recently they have replaced several of them with some Hispanic staff who, bless their hearts, simply don't have enough of a mastery of the English language to be in a customer service position. Just today I called to find out if they were keeping regular hours for Labor Day, and the young woman who answered my call couldn't make heads or tails out of my question. The bottom line is that Tenth Street Laundromat is nothing special masquerading as something special. In point of fact it is sub-par in terms of price, customer service and comfort. To quote Stephen Sondheim: "Nice is different than good." Don't be fooled.
label: NEG

text: I expected better out of Fairchild's, after reading reviews on Yelp. The dependability of Yelp comes through 9 times out of 10. Unfortunately in this case, I don't agree with the average 4 star rating. Fairchild's Oyster Bar is strategically put together in the casino, such that people walking by can see and smell the food. A money making ploy, most definitely. When you're seated, you're not protected from the noise of the casino, including the pulsing drum of a Chinese New Year marching band sent through the corridors. Yes, they're fun to watch when they're near you, but when they're out of sight and you can still hear the pulsing, it gets kind of annoying. Let's move on to the food. The introductory free bread is delicious. I found myself wishing it were served with olive oil, or at least non-foil packaged butter (considering the pricing of things on the menu) but alas, your only choice is the butter neatly packed in rectangle candy wrappers. I had the southern-fried catfish. Quite frankly it was pretty bland. I feel like frying a fish kind of takes away from the worry of overcooking it. However, a good fried food should have more flavor than just breading, and I think Fairchild's failed in this respect. I was disappointed, and would not recommend Fairchild's to others.

text: I'm actually sort of perplexed...people like this spot? It's the equivalent of Uno's Pizza in Chicago. Home-owned? Yes. Tourist magnet? Yes. Lackluster quality and customer service? Yes. We happened to be down this way coinciding with the Holiday Parade. So, it was busy. I would venture to guess it is often busy based on it having 171 reviews as of today (12/4/10). People go. They eat ribs and items such as that because they are in Nashville, and it is well-located and has a good reputation. I'm sure they'll continue to go...but as a tourist that tries to NOT be such a tourist, I'd tell likeminded peeps to search elsewhere. The problem? I ordered a Student Special ($7.50 for a large pizza) for my boyfriend, and for my vegan self ordered curly fries and a vegetarian pita sandwich, which wasn't on the menu, but wasn't a very hard order to request: all I said was that I'd like everything that's on the Vegetarian Pizza on a pita bread, minus the cheese. If you work in the food industry, this is REALLY a simple order to take, which I can testify due to my four years' experience working as a server and taking FAR more complex orders successfully at a much more busy hour (again, this is 10 PM on a random Thursday). I made sure to read off each topping on the pizza so that they knew exactly what I wanted: MARINARA SAUCE, MUSHROOMS, spinach, broccoli, onions, green peppers. I repeated this twice. All was good, I paid with a credit card, and waited the requisite hour or so that it ALWAYS takes to get pizza delivery at Swarthmore, no matter how simple your order. When they arrived with my food, everything seemed to be off to a good start. The pizza was piping hot and fragrant in a good way, that much I could tell from holding the box. Once inside my room, my boyfriend agreed that the pizza was very hot and surprisingly tasty for a local pizza joint (and he's New Yorker!). My curly fries were hot, crisp, not oily, and the only complaint I could really have about them is that they somehow tasted a little burnt. Then the sandwich. It was cold. Not a good sign, but I could deal. Maybe they mistakenly thought I wanted the toppings cold. Unraveled the sandwich. It was pita bread covered in raw spinach, raw broccoli, raw onion, and a slice of raw tomato. Are you serious?! For $5.25. Absolutely confounded as to how they could have though that any living human being would want a pile of raw vegetables on a dry pita bread and furious because the two things that would have actually made it a sandwich, the tomato sauce and mushrooms, were missing, I dialed Appetitos back. It rang and rang and rang, despite the fact that it was only 11:08 PM and they close at midnight. I called them for over half an hour straight, nonstop. And no one answered. Thanks for my overpriced pile of inedible vegetables, I really appreciate it, and THANKS FOR DOING YOUR JOBS by answering the phone during your business hours so that, if you didn't have the decency to remedy your error, you could at least APOLOGIZE. I'm still hungry. :(

text: This architectural landmark in Tucson has quite a twisted history...the fourth replacement for the original church of St. Augustín de Tucson (founded in 1776), construction began on the new cathedral in 1897 under the supervision of two French-born bishops (Salpointe and Bourgade), who envisioned a Gothic structure with two pointed spires (which were never completed due to lack of funds). For thirty years, the church stood unfinished, with bare-brick walls, until American-born Bishop Gercke decided to finish it in the Mexican baroque style. Inspired by the Mexican Catherdal of Querétaro, the sandstone façade and mission-style towers were completed in 1928. Structural deterioration prompted a restoration in 1966 under Bishop Green, who demolished everything except for the facade and the twin towers. The new building (completed in 1968) sadly is a product of its age...industrial acoustical tile, kitchy folk tapestries adorn the clerestory, a giant floating Jesus looms over the altar, red kitchen tile lines the floors and ceiling mounted florescent lamps cast a dull pallor over the interior. text: A buffet place that doesn't quite match up... A private party on a Sunday afternoon, Wong's Genghis Khan Kitchen was an interesting experience. On my first pass through, I see the Mongolian barbecue station, then come across the soup, then the hot foods and moving on next to the cold stuff - nigiri sushi, desserts, kim chee, and self serve ice cream from Dreyers. When I grab my plate, I peruse through their dim sum selection: tiny siu mais (pork dumplings) that were dried out and needed to be left in the steamer, har gows (shrimp dumplings) that were bigger but acceptable, and char siu baos (bbq pork buns). They also had sesame balls, egg rolls, deep fried shrimp (too much batter), shrimp with the head on still, beef and broccoli, braised string beans (good stuff), fried rice, chow mein, chow fun, beef skewers, and a few other random things that would make up their Chinese selection. When you get to the soups, they had won ton soup and what I would call a Chinese chowder soup. The soup was good, but watch out for the cross contamination of bowls. When I reached for a nearby bowl, I noticed raw meat juice in the bottom, and realized they put the bowls from the nearby Mongolian barbecue station right here. So, be wary. For the barbecue station, you fill up your bowl with raw beef, raw pork, raw chicken, raw veggies of your choice, and some sauces of your liking. They throw it all onto this giant heated surface and stir it up for you and that's about it. That's Mongolian barbecue for you. I'm not a big fan of it myself, so I passed on it. Japanese nirigi - believe it or not, I passed it on. What looked like mediocre slices of fish on giant balls of rice just didn't seem that appetizing for me. So, I bypassed the whole thing. Huge assortment of cookies and random pastries were laid out nearby, along with fresh fruit including the canned stuff like lychees. You'll also pass the forementioned kim chee just about now. Then you get to everyone's favorite spot - the self serve ice cream station. There's a nice note on the window asking you to put a disposable plastic glove on your scooping hand so you don't continue the germ spread factor already existing in the water where the ice cream scooper is, but trust me, no one reads that sign. (I happen to read it and use the glove myself, but everyone else who had ice cream didn't even notice the sign or the gloves present!) They offer chocolate, strawberry, vanilla, green tea, mint chocolate chip, and macadamia nut. The ice cream is pretty hard and you need a strong arm if you're gonna get any. (Which makes me wonder how any of the kids ever got to it.) The green tea tasted weird, maybe it was old? Overall, I probably won't be going back. It's not a place I would recommend for buffet eating in Reno.

text: If you're in New Orleans for the first time you totally have to dust off your nice dresses and dinner jackets for a meal at this Crecent City institution. The rule is "jackets preferred" -- we definitely saw plenty of jacketless guys, but my husband felt more comfortable wearing his blazer. The food was delicious and the service was excellent. If you go, I highly recommend opting for Chef Tory's Three-Course Special. For the price of an a la carte entree, you get soup or salad, an entree and dessert. My husband went for the chicken and andouille gumbo, the Crispy Soft Shell Crab and the Louisiana Blueberry Shortcake. It was the largest crab either of us had ever seen, and, well, the above-mentioned dessert probably ranks among our top five favorite desserts ever. I went for the Commander's Salad, which was basically a variation of a Ceasar salad, but 10 times better. It was hearts of romaine, Parmesan cheese, croutons, bacon, egg, grated Gruyere and creamy black pepper dressing. My entree was the Crawfish Maque Choux, which was like a thick gumbo (it included corn, okra and peppers in a crawfish bisque). And I too went for the blueberry shortcake. My husband and I consider ourselves to have quite discerning palates -- and the fact that we literally had zero complaints about our dining experience at Commander's Palace assures me that we will certainly find ourselves back there again one day.

text: Intrigued by other reviews, Hubs, kids, and Mom and I tried this place last night, and we were overall impressed. No hugs (except a grasping of Mom's shoulders by the lady who runs the place) and no kisses, but perhaps when we achieve the status of regulars... We were seated swiftly, and then the lady decided we'd be more comfortable at a larger table, so she had two other servers, a young man and woman, push two small squares to become a larger rectangle. It was a good idea and done to allow us more room. We demolished the two orders of onion pancakes, which I thought were actually over-priced at $2.75. They were such tiny little triangles! The sauce they came with was good with cilantro and fresh chiles, tangy and pungent. Next came crispy and hot, slightly oily salt and pepper fish filets, with slices of al dente onion and sliced chiles. It was a hit. Then basil beef, which had a nice chewy texture, was fragrant with the green herb, and spicy with a chile kick. White rice was warm but poor quality in terms of clumpiness, and just general flavor and texture. I asked the lady when I ordered, to recommend something from the "Chinese" menu. She suggested tofu with pork, which turned out to be a pleasant stir-fry of smoked tofu matchsticks and pork shreds in a savory but un-spicy seasoning with plenty of green onions, which when sauteed are like a nice green vegetable, only with a mild onion zest. At this point we were pretty happy tucking into these three dishes, but I started to get nervous when we were close to full and still no sign of the remaining two dishes. FINALLY, after we had enough of what was on the table, my son's request of General's chicken arrived. He thought it was worth the weight-mahogany colored large chunks of chicken, sweet, tangy, savory goodness, but oddly, for my taste, a little too flavorful. Maybe they should have kicked down the marinade just a notch with the sugar, vinegar, or salt. But then again, if the white rice had been of better quality, it would have been a great foil for the savory meat. Finally AGAIN the snow pea shoots arrived. You could describe them as spinach-like, but with a lovely snap-pea aroma, because they are the leaves that grow on the pea plant. tender, yet toothsome, with slices of fresh but not overpowering garlic. The poor timing of its arrival coincided with us diners being stuffed, so we were unable to appreciate it the way it deserved to have been. The meal ended with juicy but a little too tangy orange slices and crisp, thin fortune cookies that tasted really fresh, which was a nice surprise. the meal came out to $80 exactly, which included a $12 tip for the lady of the house, who provided very good service. The young man, however, had to be asked twice to bring chile sauce, and then I gave up and asked the young woman server. Oh well. In terms of atmosphere, it was surprisingly light and breezy inside at 6 PM on a beautiful summer early evening. Tiny dining room with perhaps 12 tables, so it might be a good idea to reserve at peak times, which it was not when we arrived, though the place was half-full by the time we left. it's located on a little side street in Old Town Goleta. It used to be Red Pepper the Thai restaurant back in the day 15 years ago or so. I would have to agree with some of the other reviews that this is the best Chinese restaurant in SB/Goleta. Do give it a try.

In the beginning miles, priests and parishioners cheer from the steps of churches, while families wave from their doorsteps. As I passed a group of gentlemen near a fast food restaurant last Sunday, one yelled out something to the effect of "keep running; you've got junk in the trunk!" I did a quick survey of my neighboring runners, and hoped he was referring to the woman on my right. Regardless, I was inspired. In the middle miles, throngs of supporters crowd the sidewalks from Arch to Ellsworth, and musicians keep the vibe upbeat. At mile 8, the Rocky theme is played from... somewhere, and the knowledge that the end of the race is near starts to set in. text: I am a picky consumer. Period. I hate large chain stores and I truly thrive on personal service when I am in unfamiliar territory. Wine is one of those territories. Sure, I am a major booze hound and have two fully-stocked bars with a myriad of exotic ingredients and tinctures for my passion, crafting cocktails. But when it comes to wine, while I do enjoy it, I really start to panic when it comes to picking a good bottle out and generally stick to what I know. Here's where the Wine Shoppe comes in. They have a compact, but deep selection. You really get the sense that there is no bottle on these shelves that was not placed there without a great deal of thought. And that holds true at all price points. I went in looking for a nice bottle of wine for a special occasion and was immediately greeted by the two shopkeepers. One of them, Saul, was immediately by my side and attentive to my questions when I asked for help. I told him what we liked and he made a range of suggestions at varying price points. He also was full of knowledge regarding the wineries and growing regions, clearly passionate about the product. The pricing was very reasonable, especially compared to some of the other liquor stores in Green Hills. They have a reasonable selection of spirits with some items that I haven't seen at some of the other stores around town. In all of the other Green Hills stores, you generally see one or two employees in a big location or trapped by a high-maintenance socialite - this was not the case here. Everyone was greeted and assisted promptly (I had to take a work phone call so I was casually observing the flow of business). Last but not least, they have a big cooler with a good selection of chilled wines which god knows during this summer is a necessity. So, bottom line, this place is a class act and even though it is across the street from the Green Hills Mall, I didn't feel like I was out of place.
label: POS

Pulpo a la Gallega: the best spanish octopus I have ever had. A must try! 4. Piquillos Rellenos: less appealing compared to other dishes we got 5. Revuelto: Loved it! It has a very nice texture and smooth taste which makes it a rather comfort dish 6. Costillas de Ternera: I wasn't too impressed by this flatbread... For dessert, we had Leche Frita and it was heavenly! In addition to bring out the flavor of vanilla and hazelnut, the dish has the perfect balance of crispiness and smoothness. I cannot wait to have it again! I would highly recommend this place to anyone who wants great food and a romantic dining experience.

text: Sweet Curry Savior! It was almost an entire month since my last Thai meal. That, my friends, is about 400 times too long for a girl who used to be able to walk down the street and have her choice of 6 different $5 rice and noodle shops. I hopped on Yelp, checked my "Thai Me Up, St. Louis" Talk thread from a million years ago and crossed my fingers. Justin and I settled on Sen Thai and headed downtown--and I'd say it was worth the trip! The setting is pretty stylish with wide windows overlooking the street (which is probably more interesting during the day when I suppose people are actually walking around, but nighttime downtown is generally pretty dead, aside from one or two streets. But I digress.). Our server was super friendly, but not overly attentive and she was happy to make recommendations. I am a creature of habit and tend to order green curry at every Thai joint I try, but our server was so enthusiastic about the choo chee that I had to get it. The presentation of this curry with vegetables dish far surpassed that of any Thai spot I've tried in the past (photo is up!); more importantly, it tasted great. Justin had the drunken noodles with chicken and was delighted that there were more chicken chunks than pieces of onion in his dish, which is typically a rarity. We both had enough leftover for lunch today and left dinner with full bellies. Sen Thai's dishes are about $4 more than my favorite Thai joints in my old 'hoodie, so I'm still on the hunt for a cheaper, delicious spot, but I know I'll be back to Sen Thai again--I need to try that green curry! Oh! How could I forget--we did have the crab rangoon appetizer before our meals. Six pockets of creamy fried goodness for $5--not too shabby. The rangoons were solid (still not as good as Ping Pong or Duck Walk, but damn, they were stuffed!) and large enough that I didn't have to stab Justin's hand with my fork to prevent him from eating his fair share. Sometimes a girl just needs 4 crab rangoons instead of just 3!

text: Move over Farmer Bob Evans. Your country breakfast has been bested by a family that did a bang up job of frying up some breakfast lunch and dinner, hot, fast, and fine as cream gravy. The e-mailman had sent me one of them new fangled electronic promos that I used to get in the mail till threatened the postman with my shotgun. Darn postman needs to keep his hands off my sheep... anyways. I saddled up the little one and got a wiggle on to see the elephant in the town of Brownsburg. As usual with any new cantina, I keep to myself and ain't bother nobody, but the real friendly lady said howdee to us and sat us right away. I usually try a basic country breakfast of eggs, hash browns, toast, and meat. I am happier than a pig in slop that I did, but next square dance I may venture into their other offerings like their banana pecan french toast. The food was yee-haw good and cooked just the way it should. The whole grain wheat toast had some giteeyup to it, and the double helping of hash browns had just the right amount of crispiness to them. I'm still feenin' for some more of that extra crispy bacon! My daughter wolfed down the whole kit and caboodle of her pancake, eggs and bacon, and then she asked for seconds! Bully for Maria's!! Although she loves it when I throw down for breakfast, she NEVER asks for seconds at home. I'll chalk it up to an ace high pancake and hopefully not another growing spurt (cause I don't think the grocery budget is ready for that !) Well, partners, Imma mosey on for the night. But you best believe I'll be back for the boss breakfast soon! A thanks to the following website for the cowboy slang terms: http://freepages.genealogy.rootsweb.ancestry.com/~poindexterfamily/OldWestSlang.html HI HO Silver! Away!!!!

text: A small New Orleans coffee shop with hipster vibe offering quality food and drinks. I agree with Chad C. that there seems to be a strong sense of community here but I also believe (or want to believe) that Hey! Cafe welcomes in newcomers like they're bffs. The front is a typical coffee shop with tables that can fit one or two people, flyers up letting you know what's going on in the area, and a some pastries on the counter. It's comfy. The shop offers coffees, lattes, teas, and even italian sodas. I was surprised that the prices were a little steep (bout the same as starbucks) but then again they aren't a huge chain and they have to support themselves. It's worth it. And if you don't want to pay $3 or $4 for a coffee drink, get a tea for under $2! I was very happily surprised to find that Hey! Cafe offers food! And not just food but even vegetarian options! I walked in starving and expecting to have to eat a sugary fat-laden muffin but i got a homemade vegetarian "chicken" sandwich that they whipped up right there. It really hit the spot. I saw one of the workers take out a huge tub of what I think was homemade hummus and spread some on a bagel- i might have to go back for that! Being that it is so small it is a little awkward if you go in by yourself to grab some food/drink and the three workers are are hanging out having fun. It just feels weird. BUT, I do hear that they have live music which is pretty awesome. I really enjoy the homemade food and I like that it's a local business, not a chain. Careful when you drive over though, parking can get tricky in that area. But, just park around the corner and walk a block and you'll be fine. Okay Hey! Cafe, you've got me, I'll probably become a regular before you know it.

text: I've been to several shooting ranges in my 4 years of gun ownership. Unfortunately, Philadelphia Archery & Gun Club is one of the most problematic. I really wanted to love this place...seriously, it has the potential... This place is located on a narrow street in South Philadelphia, which is why you'll see it referred to (erroneously) as "South Philadelphia Archery & Gun Club"...there's even another Yelp entry for that name. Parking can be a pain - especially on weekends...be prepared. The front door is usually locked and they will buzz you in when they realize - via the security camera - you're not there to rob the place. Once inside, you'll find a cramped store, overstuffed with gun accessories and two or three glass cases with handguns - new and used. Behind the cases, you'll see a rack of rifles and shotguns...mostly new. All of these weapons are overpriced. Let me say it again - ALL of these weapons...shotguns, rifles, handguns - all of them are overpriced. I have heard rumors of people occasionally finding a used weapon of some sort for a reasonable price. Now, that statement isn't a knock on this place in particular - ALL of the Philadelphia gun dealers and shooting ranges are overpriced. You've got to get 10 - 15 miles outside of the city to find reasonably priced guns or affordable shooting ranges. Alternatively, you could find an independent FFL (who usually live 10 - 15 miles outside of the city) who orders stuff directly from the distributors...that's a great way to get a good price. And finally...yes, ammunition is also overpriced. Usually by an even more unreasonable margin. I've actually decided I will never go to this range again. On Glock Day (which other reviewers have mentioned), they had advertised free range time and free gun rentals plus the Glock representatives would be there to let you check out their line-up. 9mm target ammo was $24.00 a box (50 rounds)...even at today's inflated prices, this stuff shouldn't be much more than 17 or 18 dollars at a range (and they are making a nice profit at that price). 24 dollars a box is a travesty as it is likely they buy it for 9 dollars a box or less. These guys were obviously trying to capitalize on the the "free" range time offered for Glock Day. I walked right out. With all of that said, the range it self is sort of nice. As others have mentioned, it's upstairs...and small. The target hop is really sweet. I've never seen anything like it before. You can program in exactly how many feet you want the target set at. And you can set it to auto-return to that location after pulling it back in to put up a new target or something. Yet, like many other ranges...and especially this one because it's so small...it will get hot and humid pretty quickly, so dress accordingly (especially if it's the weekend, when it gets busy). Overall, this place really strikes me as a location for people who don't shoot regularly and as a lot of the reviews on Yelp would demonstrate - are first time shooters without any reference to what the prices should be or how big a range should be. I guess the other people who go here don't want to drive anywhere (maybe they don't have a car?) but don't mind paying considerably more for a trip to the shooting range...although, I guess it's affordable if you're a regular (once week) and you get a membership (VIP = 350 dollars?...I forget, check their website), so you can bring your own ammunition. I've found most of the people who go here are LE (Law Enforcement), Federal Agents, etc. Those folks don't pay for their ammo and they get first priority on the range...if a bunch of them show up together - you'll be waiting for a long time before you get to shoot. Lastly, I've called a few times about the availability and pricing of certain shotguns and handguns...each time I was treated pretty poorly and if I was given a price - it was hugely inflated. Several times, they claimed they couldn't give me a price over the phone, which I thought was very strange because all the items I was calling about were incredibly common. I really don't understand why this place is so expensive...if it wasn't, I'd be more apt to give it a good rating. I guess so many people go here because it's close-by and because they want to shoot a gun (oh boy!) for the first time, so they are willing to pay whatever is asked. I don't think it's worth it. Check out Classic Pistol (I wrote a review) for a good place outside the city or The Firing Line, which isn't nearly as nice but is considerably cheaper for shooting purposes (I have no idea about their gun prices - they are probably equally bad).

The owner busted out pastry bags of icing to let me sample the "confetti cake batter" buttercream (mostly tasted like Amaretto, not cake batter), as well as the peanut butter (decent, but a letdown after the rich, nut-studded PB frosting at It's a Cupcake). Their buttercream is too fluffy for me - it doesn't have the langorous, sugary density of Brown Betty's and Naked's, nor does it come close to the same concentration of flavor. The chocolate, which I ended up putting on my vanilla cupcake, was the best of the three. It had a nice strong cocoa taste (But would I take it over BB's chocolate frosting? Never.) Not to mention that it skeeves me out to think that they leave out pastry bags full of unrefrigerated buttercream all day. If they really used butter, it would solidify if it were refrigerated, so that makes me think it is either full of artificial crap or kept at room temperature. I steered clear of the TCBY-like toppings and went with a purist chocolate frosting-vanilla cake combo. Most importantly, I found the cake itself to be off-putting. I hesitate to say this in case I am in error, but it sure as hell tasted like a mix to me. It had that overly-springy, overly moist texture rarely found in scratch-baked cakes, and a telltale artificial taste. In fact, it tasted exactly like a muffin from Costco. When dressed up with enough cocoa icing it tasted OK (because I couldn't taste the cake), but believe me - this is not artisan-quality homemade pastry. I'll take my $3 and go to Brown Betty. Sorry guys. I love to see creative local bakeries succeed, but I also hate wasting money and calories on inferior dessert. Prove me wrong! Until then, I'm sticking to my story.

Now, they actually LIKE going somewhere together. At first, they started going on the weekends, then it became a few nights a week. Now, I call my mom on her cell and before she even says hello, I can hear the "ching, ching, ching" in the background...the sound of money, the sound of victory (aka her favorite slot machine). Harrah's isn't all that bad...well OK yes it is. It reeks of smoke (since St. Louis still allows smoking in public places), while cute little grandma's and grandpa' with walkers wheel their oxygen tanks around the different slots machines looking for their next big win. My parents are a fixture. When I go with them (merely to appease them), we are treated like I would imagine VIP's get treated at The Palms in Vegas. But make no mistake, this is NOT Vegas. We eat free meals in their fairly decent Steakhouse and in the very popular (and better than average) Charlie Gitto's - an Italian restaurant that's probably the best thing about the entire Harrah's experience (hence the 2-stars). I'm not sure how to sum up this review other than by saying...if I sold my soul to the devil...this is where I'd expect to end up.

text: My month long stay here in Tucson has been quite enjoyable so far, until I went to this kosher deli/market. I'm not Jewish, but my husband is. It's around Chanukah time, so I thought I'd buy some treats and share them with our non-Jewish friends here in Tucson. They've never experienced any Jewish tradition, so I thought it would be a fun experience for them. This deli's website said they offered sufganiyot (jelly filled fried donuts) which were "direct from Israel". At $1.25 a donut, they'd better be. Well, they weren't. Some Jewish guy in the back fries them up and barely fills them with some tasteless jelly. When I got back to my friend's place, I opened the aluminum tray and saw 12 odd-shaped flat pucks of various shades of brown. The area of the donut where they squeezed the barely there jelly through was torn and flattened as if someone stuck a fat thumb through the donut. These 12 throw-away sufganiyot cost me over $16. For a dozen crappy donuts!!! Needless to say, I was extremely embarrassed to serve these to our friends. While at the store I was also hoping to buy some lunch and perhaps some market goods. When I looked at the prices and quantities, I was shocked to see how overpriced ALL the items were. I've bought kosher and Israeli items plenty of times before at other stores in other states, and I expect the sticker shock. However, the prices in this place seemed like they were taking advantage of their clientele. WAAAY OVERPRICED. On top of the all that, the two people working the register and counter were extremely unfriendly. There were also 3 over-dressed women customers who refused to move away from the counter to let me pay when my order came up. They were so close I swear they wanted to see what was in my wallet. The only reason I can give as to why I was given such obviously crappy donuts and was treated rudely by both the counter people and customers was because I DO NOT LOOK ISRAELI OR JEWISH. The rude customers I can overlook since I've run into their type before. However, I cannot excuse the rudeness and insult of the 2 Jewish guys who took my order and money. They intentionally gave me crappy donuts. I was dressed nicely and was pleasant during my whole encounter. I didn't even know I paid for crap until I was at my friends' home. I think the owners, employees, and patrons of this deli are not used to visitors who are obviously not Jewish or Israeli (by appearance). I find it disturbing that the owners and patrons of this deli/market portray themselves as rude and arrogant bigots. My Israeli Jewish husband says it's a "xenophobic attitude common among Jews that comes from self-preservation." Whatever the reason or stereotype, I don't believe it can justify the over-priced donut rejects I was sold and rude treatment I encountered. I hope a competitive kosher deli/market opens in Tucson since I will not be recommending this place to anyone.

My main course featured seared scallops, served with grilled romaine tossed in a Caesar aioli, with a roasted red pepper sauce alongside. Others at the table raved about this dish but I was a little underwhelmed myself. The fish special that one of the other girls ordered looked phenomenal, however. The men generously shared their dessert course with the fairer sex. A chocolate torte with crunchy hazelnuts was enjoyable, but the French press coffee I ordered stole the show. Passion fruit meringues were a dainty little treat that packed a flavorful punch to close out the meal. Fond's menu changes seasonally and there aren't many safe options for picky eaters, so leave those friends behind when planning a trip. I personally look forward to returning after the reincarnation of said menu!

text: I love this museum. Hands down, one of the best state history museums I have ever been to. I do have a bias though since I am a museum curator (therefore, I'm super picky). When I lived in St. Louis, I visited here all the time. The permanent exhibits are free. The 1904 Worlds Fair exhibit is a must see. Their current traveling exhibit, "The Treasures of Napoleon," is absolutely wonderful. I was shocked at the quality of this exhibit. I give props to the curators of both this exhibit and the permanent exhibitions. Considering the quality of many state historical societies and museums has declined in the past year or two due to budget cuts, furloughs, and having to let go of entire departments, I can say that the Missouri History Museum is still going strong. They have a variety of exhibits that reach beyond strict Missouri history and bring broader historical topics (ie: Napoleon) to the center stage right in St. Louis. "Lindbergh," "Seeking St. Louis," and "The 1904 World's Fair" are the permanent displays. If you want a history of Missouri and the making of the western frontier, might I suggest going down to the Arch for that? The Missouri History Museum doesn't need to do double duty talking about the earliest days of St. Louis and the frontier since the Museum of Westward Expansion does just that. Major props to the Missouri History Museum for bring light to different subjects in exhibits like "The Americans with Disabilities Act: Twenty Years Later," or "Home Lands: How Women Made the West." I really appreciate what they've done there. Also, "bravo" to their curators and educators for making online exhibits, holding regular public events, and allowing for more educational opportunities than just the museum.

text: OK I have eaten at the original Zona 78 before. We actually liked it. the fruit and cheese plate was tasty and the pizza we created was good. A bit expensive but not bad for a night out. We were excited about Zona 78 coming to the Eastside. We went yesterday for lunch. We did not have a good experience. Our stay there with no wait for a table was over 2 hours. The children's pizza came out about an hour and a half into the stay and about an hour and 15 minutes after the starters. About an hour into the lunch the waitress was nice enough to bring the children a plate of fruit on the house but the wait was unbearable for the adults. When the kids finally got their pizza the waitress told us that they were sorry for the long delay but they wanted to have all the pizzas out at the same time. Over a half hour later our pizza's came out. The hostess kind of disappeared from our view of the last half hour but I called her over the first second she poked her head out of the back. She asked if the manager spoke to us. He didn't She sent him over and he apologized for the long wait and offered to comp the pizza. He should have comped the whole meal. We told him we needed to take it to go. We went across the street to Udall park and ate it. It wasn't good. We ordered the Tuscany Pizza. It was small, very cold and the caramelized onions over powered the whole pizza including the sausage. Our friends ordered the Margherita Pizza and enjoyed it. I like to frequent local establishments and I like their concept of marrying Tucson area products like Wilcox apples but they need to get their act together.

text: I often come to the Tea Place before going to North Edmonton Cineplex. This place is nothing fancy, it is simply a great spot for spending some time drinking tea, coffee, enjoying light food and catching up with friends. There are only a handful of tables at this cafe which is not a problem since this place is never too busy. On the menu you will find soups, salads, Panini sandwiches, and lots and lots of various kinds of bubble tea, both with milk and dairy free. Bubble tea as well as the food is very good here. Combo consisting of soup and sandwich is always a good option considering that the Tea Place uses freshest ingredients. Their mushroom soup is to die for, especially paired with veggie melt sandwich. One other item from the menu I recommend is mandarin salad: it's like, crispy and very satisfying. The food is prepared very fast. You can not only eat and drink bubble tea at this cafe, you can also shop here. The Tea Place stocks up on loose teas and tea drinking accessories such as small pots, tea cups and tea strainers. I have never bought any tea here but I might because the selection is quite nice and ample.

text: Dear Cafe Rio, I hate you. I'm sorry to put it so bluntly. I thought that maybe I could wrap the bad news up in some trite compliments, but I can't think of any at the moment and I think it's better for both of us if I'm just straight forward with my feelings. I will say, thought, that I didn't intend to hate you. In fact, I had the best of intentions of loving you. I've been to another Cafe Rio before and vaguely remember liking it. Plus, I brought a kid with me and they gave me a free cheese tortilla thingy that was delicious and warm, and came with a strawberry. When you came to Boise I was able to more examine you more closely, sans cheese and strawberry distractions. I'm left befuddled and with a few questions that I can't answer. Like, why are you so loud?? Why do you insist on yelling everyone's order and cheering about it? Why are there so many chairs and tables in your establishment? I could barely walk to the self serve soda fountain (where I got real Coke instead of my usual diet to help assuage the headache your volume, overabundance of tables, and cliche south of the boarder decorations caused). Lastly, I have some questions about the food. Again, I'm going to be blunt in saying it's a little overdone. Baja Fresh, Costa Vida, Bajio's and like a hundred other places have the same menu. You don't do it better, just way louder. It wasn't bad....it just wasn't good. Plus, you made me and everyone else in my party sick. I will admit that this incident may have shaded my opinion of you just a bit, but spending a night curled around a toilet might do that to anyone. I think it's better if we just agree to part ways, permanently. Best of luck.
label: NEG

text: YUMMY!!! LOVE IT. There is a lot of great Vietnamese food in St. Louis. (i.e.. check out South City. duh!) but this one's in your own backyard; no need to make the drive downtown. That's always nice. The prices are a bit more than the South City spots but for one, you live in West Fucking County. You can afford the $3-4 increase in food price. Two, this place takes Vietnamese way up a notch, to gourmet levels, minus the pretentious attitude and ambiance. I recommend the Sizzling Saigon Crepe (see my take-out pic), the calamari, and of course the spring rolls (beef is best) for apps. I often get the crepe (which is more like an omlet-crepe hybrid) for an entree b/c its full of yummy protiens and served w/ their delish lime sauce. For an entree GET THE CURRY for sure. Get it with whatever protein or veggies you want. You will not be sorry. There is something so special about Vietnamese curry. It's creamy, comforting, yet light tasting. You will fall in love. I love all ethnic curries but Vietnamese is my fav. I ask them to make mine spicy and it's divine. I've tried many other items and they were all good. You can't really go wrong here I don't live in St. Louis anymore but I come back often to visit family. Last time I was there it was BYOB which is nothing short of AWESOME. My girl friends and I often get together w/ a few bottles of wine and nosh out. Makes for a great local night. Would be a great date spot too.

text: This is the cousin or maybe even brother restaurant (not sister because it has a pretty manly vibe) of the Broadway Brewhouses. I personally like the vibe and the food much better at this one. I really like to sit outside in their beer garden when the weather is nice and drink some draft Yazoos. Although the menu is almost the same as the Broadway Brewhouses, it's a little more rounded out here, and the food comes on real plates, not Styrofoam ones. I hate eating out of Styrofoam! I usually get the gumbo and house salad combo. I think their gumbo is the finest in Nashville because it's thick with small pieces of sausage, and shrimp, and it's also pretty spicy. The house salad comes with jalapeno bacon, cucumber salsa and this amazing spicy ranch dressing. They also have a great burger, which also comes with the jalapeno bacon. I just really like the laid back vibe here. It's a surprising place a little off the beaten track and it has the coldest, most delicious beer.

text: Urban Active fitness used to be a decent place to go. I first started going here when it was still Golds Gym. Then, according to my sources, the people who owned the franchise, wanted to expand but Golds wouldn't let them. So, they said bye-bye to Golds and created their own brand, Urban Active. Once the change over was complete and the 'renovation' was finished - they started offering new members much lower rates - which sort of grated on my nerves since I was in a contract for twice as much. Not only was the new rate half of what I was paying - it was a month to month contract. After a while - they decided that they were going to do a full remodel and they closed the gym for a period of time with signs on the door announcing how the gym was going to be better than ever after they renovate the gym. Then suddenly I find out - only by driving by - that they have closed the place for good. They didn't tell anyone. However, once the credit card they had on file had expired they were calling me every day to try and get a new number. I had to be less than polite when I told them that they were NOT getting a new credit card number from me because they closed by gym without notifying me...and since they closed my gym I take that to mean that my contract is also finished. They disagree and pointed me to other gyms in the city. However, they don't consider that the entire reason for joining this gym was its proximity to my home (it is across the street). Needless to say they didn't get my credit card number and finally the calls stopped. A quick stop by the Better Business Bureau you will find Urban Active has a F rating. http://www.bbb.org/nashville/business-reviews/health-clubs/urban-active-fitness-in-nashville-tn-37002954 Check other cities across the country - all have an F rating: http://www.bbb.org/cleveland/business-reviews/exercise-and-physical-fitness-programs/urban-active-fitness-in-lyndhurst-oh-12003084/ http://www.bbb.org/centralohio/business-reviews/health-clubs/urban-active-fitness-in-columbus-oh-70011953 http://www.bbb.org/lexington/business-reviews/health-clubs/urban-active-fitness-in-lexington-ky-14004664 I'm not sure why things went downhill so quickly for this company - because for all intents and purposes - its the same company that ran Golds and I never had a problem with them. Maybe it was the lower prices? Maybe it was because they were trying to appeal to the lowest common denominator. I really don't know. But whatever you do - you'd be wise to stay away OR, if you do decide you want to try it - do NOT sign a long term contract. They make it nearly impossible to cancel the contract. And, at the very least, you can get a good idea of what its like with no commitment. I think you'll find that other gyms will offer you a better experience even if it is more expensive. Better yet - just look elsewhere.
label: NEG

text: I have a college professor to thank for turning me on to this radio station as I drug my unhappy butt into my 8am MWF class freshman year. Morning edition was always on the radio while we did our studio work, and while the lull of the voices and music made me want to go to sleep, the stories eventually got to me. This was real news that wasn't laced with celebrity news every other segment. I'm now addicted. I would much rather get my news from NPR than most television stations, where they let any idiot give an opinion. This American Life and Morning Edition are my absolute favorites, and I also enjoy the puzzle shows on Sunday mornings. I've also caught my beloved David Sedaris and Jack Handy on days when I was just flipping through my programmed stations, furthering my devotion. If no shows are playing, you're probably listening to classical music, and while this age of Britany Spears seems to continue to rage on, it's nice to catch some Beethoven sometimes. Just by listening to it on the way to work I can tell a difference in my demeanor than if I just turned on the local rock station. I probably owe my good blood pressure to NPR.

Next time I go back and that will be soon, the corn casserole and fried pickles are a must try. For less than $9 I got pulled pork, 2 sides, cornbread and a drink, you can't beat that for excellent vittles. The lobster risotto is the house specialty and, as I have been told that on any given night, upwards of half of the meals served. I have never met anyone who did not really enjoy it. text: My boyfriend and I were looking for a good and affordable sushi place to take out his family, and this definitely fit the bill. We ordered edamame and tempura for starters, 6 different rolls (spicy scallop, spicy tuna and avocado, house roll, spider roll, rainbow roll, and a dynamite roll), some nigri, and beef teriyaki and a chicken teriyaki bowl for the more picky eaters. With that and a few drinks, and we barely broke $100 to feed 6 people. I was amazed. Overall, everything was good and fresh. I also liked that there were some creative roll options that I've never seen before. I would come back to try out the Pink Panther roll and Pizza Roll. The owner was also very nice and always came back to check on us. When my water had some club soda in it, they immediately replaced it and responded to every other response quickly. The only thing we found odd was that they didn't have a bottle of wine but only a glass (wonder how long that has been open). They were also out of some other things-- but I would rather have that than unfresh sushi. I would recommend giving this place, which is very unassuming on the outside, a chance.

text: The decor of this hotel is a bit antiquated, but it still retains that classy or ritzy feel and is still a nice place to rest your head. All rooms have a small balcony which is quite nice and both rooms I stayed in had beautiful views of the rising morning sun over the Mississippi River and the bridge to the Greater New Orleans area. The TVs in these rooms are not flat screen, in fact, they are actually pretty old. Then again I wasn't expecting Vegas-like amenities with an HDTV embedded in the wall and staring back at me while I'm sitting on the pot. A huge plus for the elevators being really quick. text: Ohmygod. Best Indian food I've ever had. Ever. I recommend going at the "white people early dinner" time of 6:30 PM. My family basically had the whole place to ourselves! They start you off with a delicious, featherlight crisp bread and some dipping sauces...a sweet and a spicy. Because my family is a fan of all things bread, we ordered a type of sweet naan with raisins and nuts as our appetizer. This is seriously the best naan I've had in my life. I'm going to be saying that about the rest of our meals (best ___ of my life), so for brevity's sake, I'll leave that out of the rest of this review. Once we demolished our sweet naan, we needed MORE BREAD. Regular naan this time, also a delight. I got the Malai Kofta (veggie dumplings in a "mild cream sauce" that I requested spicy). This was my first time ordering this dish so I wasn't sure what to expect, but everyone loved it (sharing is caring). My mom got the Palak Paneer. Now, I love Palak Paneer, but this stuff was unlike any I've had. Not dripping with oil, just a thick, powerful punch of spinach and homemade cheese with just the right amount of spice. If you think you've had the best Palak Paneer...you haven't until you go here. Trust me. My boyfriend got a dish that I haven't really seen at other Indian restaurants: Paneer tikka masala or something like that. Basically the homemade cheese cubes in a nice and spicy-sweet sauce. Delicious. The portions at this place are not huge, which is good and bad...good in that you can actually stand up after your meal and even have some mediocre Rita's water ice next door, and bad in that I wanted an infinite supply of leftovers because I never wanted this meal to end. Hyperbole? Maybe. Check this place out, and you tell me.

text: I wanted to go to the Ethiopian place, but was overruled. For a cohesive menu, they might restrict those to a bar menu. Steakburger ($10), weak on flavor, 5/10 8oz Prime Rib ($22), edges only were flavorful, 6/10 Green beans, overcooked & oily, 3/10 Rice pilaf, dry, tasteless, in the shape of an inverted cup, 3/10 French Onion Soup: little soup, cheese sprinkled ON the cheese ($5), 4/10 Service, excessively casual (also suggest a uniform), 4/10 Dining room decor, suggest framing the art (to match new chairs), 2/10 We didn't check out the lounge, so I can't speak for it. I like the underlying concept, but it didn't deliver on anything, and clearly depends on captive business travelers from the hotels two blocks away to survive.

text: Va-nes-sa! Va-nes-sa! Va-nes-sa! Today I got a haircut at Underground with Vanessa K and the experience has led me to join Yelp, just so I could share this gem! Decently priced for delicious hair. I live in San Francisco and am just down for the summer in Santa Barbara. After trying 4 salons in San Francisco, I did not find a fit and kind of gave up looking for a stylist. Thus, I walked in today with long, strait and hungry hair that has not seen scissors for (gulp!) 1.5 years. In comes Senior Stylist Vanessa. She Heard what I wanted, asked some Good questions and permission to show me a few tricks. Vanessa set the tone with Goals for our session. During the perfect shampoo and scalp massage (which I am a sucker for), she allowed me time to relax into it. While rinsing, she inquired as to the products I use (Aveda) and gave some helpful feedback about how they were drying my hair. The cut was quick, decisive. My limp hair started to breath on its own after only a few snips. All the while, she was gently educating me on quick, professional styles and how to transition between different looks with a demonstration. She put on some magic thickener and then I got the blow out of my life. Like 'Victoria-Secret-Schwooping-Hair-With-A-Built-In-Fan' blow out. All the while, she was showing brush techniques, informing me about quick alternatives through easy conversation. I walked out with the best cut and most wearable cut of my life and bumped directly into a man walking on the street and the interaction went as follows Me: "Excuse me." Him: "Do you know how gorgeous you are?" Me: "Thank you." (Because it the best hair day of my life!) Him: "No, seriously." So, I walked home instead of biking with my helmet, threw away my BioSilk (as recommended by Vanessa) and wrote to you Yelpers. Go!

text: I found a 90% off restaurant.com coupon deal so got a $25 off of $35 coupon for Bella Italia for under a dollar. I must have driven past this place a dozen times but never felt compelled to stop there. If not for the coupon, I doubt I ever would have. We started with soup. I had minestrone, my husband ordered the soup of the day- artichoke cream. My minestrone was a little bland and watery, but the artichoke was very nice. For our main course, I ordered veal marsala, my husband chose the gamberoni all diavola (large shrimp in a tomato chili sauce). Both were served with a fusilli pasta with a tomato meat sauce. The vegetable was a nicely sauteed thin sliced zucchini. Sounds great huh? Well it was delicious, but the problem was the portions. I would guess that on each plate there was at most 3 ounces of pasta, two ounces of zucchini and my veal might have weighed 2 1/2 ounces- the stingy size of the portions became all the more apparent when these little piles of food was sitting in the middle of a large platter. My husband did get 8 very nice, large prawns, and prawns are not much cheaper than veal- so there is really no explanation for the child size portion of veal. But damn..it was so good. We rarely order desert, but we were still a bit hungry so we got a panna cotta to share-and it was just to die for. Oh wow..the mango sauce was so yummy that if we had been home we probably would have licked the plate. Oh yeah..and if you want wine- they tell you to walk next door to Scolari's and buy a bottle and they will pour it for you for free- they don't have a liquor license yet. If they work out the kinks, get their liquor license, serve larger portions or buy smaller plates & if the owner could warm up a bit to his guests, then this place could be a winner- the flavor of the food, and the care with which it is prepared is better than 90% of the other Italian Restaurants in Reno.
label: POS

text: I have to give this place my super rare 5 star rating because they have the best grilled cheese and the most unique (and super tasty) cocktails I have had. And above all the prices are reasonable. On top of the wonderful food, the people there and the atmosphere is awesome too. It is a quaint little place with mostly a drink/appetizer menu and only a few special every night - when they run out that is it! Lets start with the cocktails - bacon infused vodka is the key ingredient to their bloody mary, unfortunately I can't drink so I only tasted a tiny bit, but it was such a rocking mouth full of flavor - tangy, spicy, sweet, tart tomatoes, savory, rounded out with smoky bacon overtones - all i could say was wow. The other cocktail i got to taste is their Italian mojito which is made with their basil infused rum - sweet, but with an interesting savory and herby overtones. Very unique taste despite being nothing like the traditional mojito. Finally the one thing they have that I crave for now almost every other day - their infamous grilled cheese sandwich. I will warn you, it is a fatty one - They probably soak it in butter before grilling but it gets the crust so crunchy and buttery - who cares about the calories just run an extra mile. They also use a special blend of cheeses - you will have to try for yourself and ask the chef - I won't divulge their secret. In between all the gooey cheese heaven are some good old mushroom and arugula. Although it is 9 bucks for this baby, trust me it is worth every penny! Other dishes I got to try was from their specials for that night - and OMG they were so good also! Shrimp in creamy tomato sauce with homemade pasta, and braised veal with courgette puree (not too sure but it was good whatever it was).

text: One of my goals in life is to make friends with someone who works in the Comcast building so I can venture to the top and frolic through the employee-only restaurant on the 43rd/44th floors and finally discover if William Penn #2 (#3?) is still there. But, alas no Comcast friends yet acquired. Sooo for now, I'll remain content hanging out in the lobby staring at the HD Video Wall. Think 2,100 square feet of pure virtual radiance. Come in and watch as wildly vibrant shapes, people, and landscapes emerge from the eerily camouflaged "wooden" panels. I love that you never know what you'll get here. The other day I stopped in and was instantly transported to Franklin Lloyd Wright's architectural masterpiece "Fallingwater" replete with vividly realistic sounds of water sloshing up its stone walls. They also present a holiday show every year -- music, dancing and sparkling lights -- all displayed with the brilliance of 10 million pixels (so uh, FIVE times the resolution of HDTV). Very cool. Honestly, I was expecting extreme cheesiness, but I actually really enjoyed the show. It is every hour on the hour during the holiday season and it even ends with a flurry of fake snowfall. Perks during the show: free samples of Godiva hot chocolate and an envelope of coupons for some nearby restaurants and stores.

text: Surprisingly tasty Mediterranean fare here at the often empty Lafayette Bistro. I don't blame you if you're hesitant about trying this place. The roasted red pepper soup was piping hot and soul-satisfying, and the chicken cavaliet was delicious with the light lemon sauce, plenty of olives, and a perfectly seared scallop on top. Here's some constructive criticism for you, Lafayette: 1. Lose the wicker! It's everywhere. I feel like I'm eating in a Pier 1 showroom. Or in my weird uncle's backyard. 2. How about losing the Moroccan throw pillows too, while you're at it? 3. Get a bigger sign, or some lights. Something to tell people your establishment is, in fact, a restaurant and not a wicker storage unit. Sorry I don't want to be mean but in all seriousness they have some good food here and I think it would be a shame if this place went under.

My previous artist had left and so I was paired up with someone new. I had designed a word that was an ambigram (where it looked the same way right side up and upside down). My artist took this information and said he would see me in a week and we would talk. I went back in a week and what he had for me was terrible! He admitted it himself and said he hated it and wanted to start from scratch. He didn't charge me for the extra time he took to redo it, even though it was not his fault. text: I have to say first. I'm a Korean. Not like other Korean people, I really like chinese food. Chinese food has philosophy, function, and balance, like tai-chi. In terms of the three value of the chinese food, PF Chang is not even chinese food. They are insulting Chinese Food now. Simply I can tell the food is 'Eek.' Wanna know why? OK, first of all, they randomly put garlic and ginger with no reason. Second, almost every food is just deep fry. Third, the food is too sweet or too salty to me. Finally, the food is not healthy at all, like McDonnell's big Mac. For those reason, I have never recommend PF Chang for any Asian friend who wants to look for good chinese restaurant. text: Today. Two-thirty. Except this is New Orleans so we have to do it up right fancy like. Since the lady is from Trinidad and has never sipped the fine cocktails our city has to offer, we have resolved to work our way through the classics. Today was going to be French 75 day. We were going to sit in those lovely red butterfly chairs in front of the Lafayette Hotel, stretching our legs out into the sunshine, sipping French 75s, and listening to the rumble of the streetcar as it lumbered up St. Charles. Doesn't that sound nice? And here we were, thinking that a hotel bar in New Orleans would be open on a lazy Wednesday afternoon, eager to send a nice man in a monkey suit out to their sidewalk to earn a little coin and break up the boredom of those post-lunch, pre-dinner hours normally spent rolling silver. I'd tip him well to leave us alone, and he'd pocket the money with an eager eye towards the pot he'd likely be buying this weekend. (Let's be honest about the state of the restaurant industry in this city: at least half the servers and cooks do a little casual toking in their spare time. That is one of the only perks of working in food service.) All those lovely fantasies? Dashed. Guess who isn't open during the day. Twist. Everything I know about New Orleans was wrong. The beef was so tender it practically melt in my mouth (I couldn't bear to ask for ketchup at a steak house and I'm glad I didn't!). The mashed potatoes were to die for. However, the side of mushrooms were cold and forgettable. I also ordered a salad wedge which was cold, crisp and quite good. The bread didn't seem as special as everyone made it out to be -- but it was quite good. Soft and warm and definitely devoured. My husband got the seafood soup, which he loved. And the 12-ounce filet mignon, which was also good. He got a side of onion rings, which were so huge he only ate two or three, but they were good too. For dessert, I thought it was a nice touch that they gave us a $10 piece (or slab -- it was huge!) of butterscotch cheesecake on the house, when I mentioned it was my husband's birthday. It was SO GOOD. The butterscotch and what tasted like a Heath-bar type of crunch on the crust, was to die for. Now, for the service -- EXTREMELY attentive, almost overbearing, on the night we went (it was still fairly early evening on a Friday night and there weren't many tables). People were constantly checking on us and asking how our meal was and were we having a good time. We felt like VIPs or something. It did get a little annoying but I appreciated the attentiveness. My only complaint was that we were seated on the main floor, and it looked like there was no separation between the bar area and the dining area. As it was happy hour on a Friday, the place was booming with bar-goers who seemed to filter out into the dinner crowd...there was no buffer there, and it was quite loud. That is something they should definitely fix. But really I don't have any complaints, except the restaurant is very pricey. But for a special occasion or even just a nice dinner out when you've saved some cash, I highly recommend Del Frisco's. As I said, it was one of the better meals I've had and completely restored my faith in red meat!

The staff is friendly, attentive, and knowledgeable. And if you can't get reservations, it's worth dropping by to see if there is available seating in the bar, where you still have access to the full menu. My next drink was more successful, and was suggested by our server when someone at our table asked for a whiskey and ginger ale and was told they didn't carry ginger ale. What they did make was whiskey with their house ginger syrup, lemon juice, and club soda, which was pretty flavorful and yummy. This leads me to believe that maybe Franklin should tone down the millions of flavors in one cocktail idea and do something a little simpler, because it seems to work a lot better for them. text: 5 stars?...Well I rate by the "It Is what it is" rule...and if you go to Gene's because it is what it is, you'll be getting genuine 5 star fulfillment. One of the more minor post Katrina tragedies was the closing of Verti Martes overnight shift. When I worked there a million years ago, they didn't even have a lock on the door (the day of the French Quarter bloackout, they left a semi-crazy cook in with a hatchet to deter the non-existent looters...but I digress). the lack of late night Verti Marte could crush a drunk Po' boy lovers soul...but there still is Genes. Genes is big and pink and filled with New Orleans, its another place not for the faint of heart...at 3 AM you'll be waiting with gangsters, musicians, surly cops and professional drunks of all shapes...but, yeah, they do all know something. If you rate a Po boy by how greasy it is...how easily the roast beef tries to slither out of the bread with every bite, Genes is the place. Crunchy french bread meets an incredible goopy mayo cheese lube that has the meat sliding all over the place...and at 3 AM, if you can keep it together or not, there is no better taste in town. Roast beef Philly is my choice, but they also have a great hot sausage, and video poker to boot...obviously you are feeling lucky; you stopped here, didn't you? If thats not enough, the next building over is Gene's daiquiri stand. Worth the short walk from the Quarter any hot afternoon. There's more booze in a large Genes daiquiri then in 5 on bourbon street; and that is before you pay the extra buck for an additional shot of some 190 proof firewater in there. With all the sugar It's like slurpy and crack cocktail, but without having to sell your mommas TV. Visitors to New Orleans, get out of the Quarter and into Gene's and your a step closer to understanding the town.
label: POS

text: Arriving in New Orleans at 11:30pm and hungry I immediately knew my options in the culinary world would be limited. Luckily I did my research. We got the low down on drinking in the city and open containers. Everyone was very helpful, and offered great information about the city. I got the oyster po'boy and my boyfriend got the shrimp. We also split a pabst blue ribbon. This was our first meal in New Orleans and probably our best. The bread was perfect, warm, fresh and crisp. The breading on the oysters and shrimp was superb. Crunchy and spicy, yet well balanced. They were big and we probably could have split one but they both were so good I didn't even notice I ate way too much, which could be a bad thing. There aren't any places to sit and eat but outside the mart you can pull up a curb and enjoy yourself. Perfect for their fare. We thought about those po' boys all weekend and even considered going back before our flight home on monday. We weren't able to get back but the next time we return this will be our first stop. This is definitely going to be a craving I'm unable to fulfill until I return to the Big Easy.

I believe this is the place that turned me into a honey mustard convert. It's also one of the few places away from the beach I've found that serves up a good fish taco. The milkshakes, of course, are bangin, as are the chicken strips and burgers. Love the swiss guacamole burger especially. The hours: My favorite thing about diners is that they usually are open 24-7 or at least very late. However, Ruby's is a chain and don't have diner hours at all. So whenever I'm craving diner food Ruby's is closed. Basically, I'd say if you were in the area and had some extra crash and want some good food hit up Ruby's. If it's around dinner time and you're not in the area there's probably better places to go... but if you want a diner-esque experience then, again, hit up Ruby's.

I stepped into the shack and placed my order for pho with chicken and a canned Thai iced tea. My order came out promptly. Maybe too promptly. I could not wait to get home and dig in. Moments later I sat down on my couch, opened my plastic take-out container and fished around with hope. An imaginary trombone played "Wah, wah" as my dream drowned. Steam? Check. Noodles? Check. text: I'm a Japanese guy who's lived in Tucson for a couple years now and I've come to consider Sushi Yukari my home away from home. The first page of the menu alone distinguishes it from the rest of the Japanese restaurants in town. All kinds of Japanese comfort food abound. I recommend the korokke (Japanese adaptation of croquets), maguro yamakake (chunks of tuna sashimi and grated yam), and daikon salad (comes with a refreshing pickled plum dressing). They have a wide assortment of fish that they broil to perfection. Their hamachi-kama (yellowtail neck) might be the best thing on the menu. Yukari is friendly for those on a tight budget too. If you pass on the appetizers and just order an entree, you'll have plenty of food. Most entrees (ranging from $8 to $20) come with miso soup, salad, and/or california roll. They also give you a complimentary bowl of edamame. The sushi is very good here, but I usually get the pork katsu curry or one of their many noodle soups. In addition to the more traditional fair, they have some original creations that I haven't yet tried. Their menu is quite large! FYI, they serve beer (including some Japanese imports) and sake (more options than I've seen at other restaurants). Enjoy!!

text: When the place we were headed to was closed, we dropped in on a Saturday after 9. The place was winding down from what looked like a crowded night. They 86'ed the Scallop app, so it must be good. In it's place I had the crispy fried oysters atop tomato gazpacho. Imagine an oyster truffle... the crunchy outer "shell" of cornmeal batter gave way to a perfect soft creamy oyster center. Gazpacho was roughly blended and spicy with oregano. My wife's chicken livers were breaded and fried in the same manner as the oysters and were coated in a tangy, slightly sweet, balsamic sauce w/ raisin...served with candied walnuts the livers were crispy and sweet with the deep richness of the liver mixing well with dried fruit and walnut. Like an upscale General Tso's Chicken...Livers. I had escargot app for my main and my wife ordered the gnocchi. The escargot were buttery and wonderful. The gnocchi were puffy potato pillows. They were served similar to a primavera, where the mix of vegetables was crunchy and fresh. I hate it when gnocchi are drowned in a thick heavy sauce...the sauce over the gnocchi and veg pulled it together just enough without coating the gnocchi...like a stew stock. There was a small offering of 3 desserts we passed on but looked good on the other people's tables...a creme brulee, flourless choc torte and a berry tart of some sort. After the awesome crunch on the livers and oysters, I want to try their encrusted Lamb on the next return.

"Order in English" signs are all over the place, and he actually sells T-shirts that say it, too. Now, keep in mind that Geno's is a MAJOR tourist attraction. Tour buses routinely stop there because it is such a legendary place (don't ask me why.) Many of these tourists are visiting from other countries and probably do not speak English very well, if at all. Anyone who goes out of his way to make a major portion of his customer base feel unwelcome certainly does not deserve to be patronized and raised to iconic status, especially when his food sucks. Finally, I agree that those who immigrate to this country should learn to speak English. However, I am also aware that learning a new language, especially a difficult one like English, takes a bit of time. I am sure that even the great Joe Vento's parents took at least a year to become reasonably conversant. If he seriously wanted people to learn to speak English, he would take down the "order in English" signs and instead post signs advertising the local English language instruction center - you know, signs that actually inform people where to go to learn English instead of simply demanding that they do so.

text: Ok, so my wife, our toddler and I are walking around downtown Santa Barbara. We get a little hungry and pick up two slices of pizza for us and a hot dog for our toddler at a couple of places along State St. We planned on stopping at one of the public benches to enjoy our food, but the one we found had gum on the seat so we kept walking towards our hotel. With no more public benches in sight, we stumble upon D'Angelo's Bakery. We initially walked past the place, but then thought, there are four outdoor tables open and no one inside the place... if we buy something from them, we could eat that and our other food at one of their four open outside tables. Actually, our toddler had long finished his hot dog by this time, so it was just our two lonely slices of pizza that needed eating. We went inside hoping to buy a baguette and an espresso drink or two. The espresso machine was apparently broken because they had a little sign saying that no espresso drink were available so we settled for a sourdough baguette. The woman at the counter was very friendly and helpful. We grabbed our baguette and headed to one of the four open tables on the sidewalk in front of the place. We started eating the baguette and our pizza. A few minutes later, another one of D'Angelo's employees came out and said that the tables were for food ordered to eat at D'Angelos. We pointed to our baguette and said that we purchased food from D'Angelos. The young woman said that the baguette is a to go item and the tables are for food ordered to eat at D'Angelo's. She said the owner didn't want us eating other food there. We protested and she said, you can stay this time. At that point, I was rather miffed. We used to own a coffee house and I can certainly understand being annoyed at people who come in to a place with food from outside places to eat without ordering something. I made a point to purchase something from this business so we could use one of their outside tables AND I only did it because there was only one other person patronizing the place at the time. It wasn't like we were taking a table from other customers who ordered "eat in" food either. I asked if the owner was available and walked inside to speak with him. I mentioned to him that we had purchased something from him specifically so we could eat at one of his tables and we wouldn't have sat down at one of his tables without patronizing his business. He totally disregarded that and said they were about to close. It was 10 minutes until 2PM and he acted like we were keeping him from closing up shop at 2, and he was quite rude about it. I again tried to explain that we were trying to be respectful by buying something from him. He ignored that again and dismissively reiterated that he was closing at 2PM and that was the reason he didn't want us eating there. The funny thing is that the one customer who was there when we sat down didn't seem to be getting the same attitude at all. I left the establishment after I told him that I obviously made a mistake by buying something from D'Angelo's. I felt like throwing the mostly intact baguette on his counter, but I refrained and tried giving it to a homeless guy down the street. I guess he wasn't a fan either because he politely declined.

text: I went to this Save-A-Lot because I wanted to cash in the spare change I had, and this grocery store was the closest location with a Coinstar machine. So I took the opportunity to shop around. The food here is cheaper than your average grocery store, as the brands are mainly more obscure. Meat and poultry are also cheaper per pound. The vibe here is less pleasant than Super Fresh on South Street that the previous poster mentioned. However, I'm not sure a grocery store aimed towards those more impoverished is deserving of mockery in an impoverished town such as Philadelphia. Would I shop here as a first choice? Probably not. But if I didn't have the disposable income to shop for similar items at more expensive alternatives, then I would consider Save-A-Lot. It is true though that you have to pay per plastic grocery bag. The cost was 3 cents per bag -- certainly nothing exorbitant. Personally, I think having to pay for plastic bags is a good thing. Not only does it cut down on costs for Save-A-Lot, but it also encourages people to use reusable bags which is better for the environment. In fact, the city of Toronto passed into law this summer legislation requiring all retail stores to charge 5 cents for single-use plastic bags. And you know what? In the short time this price tag was placed on pollution a noticeable difference has been achieved. I see A LOT of disposed plastic bags littering the streets of Philadelphia. Food for thought.

text: Is creativity allowed in Creole cooking? Go to Brigtsen's and find out! Brigtsen's is a fabulous restaurant with a creative chef (Frank Brigtsen, formerly of Chef Paul Prudhomme's K-Paul's) serving Creole/Acadian fare with traditional New Orleans class. It's a small place, a converted house a good distance away from the French Quarter. (It's a great St. Charles streetcar trip, if you have the time.) Thoroughly decorated with their awards too prominently displayed, it's a wonderful place for foodies to dine. For starters, my wife had butternut shrimp bisque and I had sautéed sweetbreads on lemon thyme brioche with shitake mushrooms, capers, and veal demi-glace. Tell me that isn't creative! Our mains were equally interesting: roast duck with popcorn dirty rice and honey pecan gravy, and paneed rabbit with sesame crust, spinach, and Creole mustard sauce. Everything was outstanding. The dining rooms are intimate, the service is excellent, and the food is fabulous. And since Chef Frank is a native who has been cooking in New Orleans for decades, he's not likely to leave. Let's hope.

Fish Dry Pot It was pretty good with a nice spice, but not a total Szechuan Gastronomic experience that othershave described it as.
