I understand the need to garnish a dish to make it look fancier than your local Chinatown dish, but it just was not balance with this edible garnish/whatever it was. Salt and Pepper Style Shrimp How can you really go wrong with fried food?!?! This salt and pepper shrimp was pretty good, but all I could taste here was the five spice powder, too. The server that came was pretty good at his job - friendly, warm and understood English, but I felt bad that the owner/manager kept on showing up and ruining our experience by staring at us (wanting us to relinquish the table faster no doubt) and making his own suggestions. Next we ordered a vegetable tray with an assortment of different things, what stood out to me here was the seared brussels sprouts. Finally for the appetizers we had a cheese plate that was also enjoyable, although I don't know the names of the cheeses, they were all delicious. My first of two courses was chicken liver rigatoni with cipolline onions and sage. I've never had chicken liver before but this was outstanding. My second dish was rabbit with pancetta, sage,and polenta (grits). The rabbit was pretty good, very "bony" but I'm told that's to be expected. Dessert was the cantucci sundae vin santo marinated almonds (taken directly from the menu: http://www.osteriaphilly.com/menu). Basically vanilla custard with almonds and this kind of wine sauce. Very good! I had an Italian red wine throughout the meal, selected by one of the more knowledgeable wine drinkers at the table and it, too, was excellent. Taken in consideration with the friendly and attentive staff, our nearly 4 hour dinner didn't feel long enough.

After ten minutes went by I realized something was probably not right. She was going back and forth between eyes threading, then plucking. Silly me should have just told her to stop and fixed them at my house but for some reason I rolled with it. When she was done my eyebrows looked like I had drawn them on with a sharpie marker. I went to the counter in a hurry because at this point I was late for work. My bill came to $18 with my lip protectant and i gave her a hundred dollar bill and three ones. I asked for $80 back giving her a $5 tip, which I thought was very generous. I quickly grabbed my change and ran down the stairs and into the first cab I saw. When I looked down into my hand I only had $60. I immediately called Thread where the woman who gave me my change said, "Oh, I thought so." I was left speechless. Upon leaving work that night I went into my purse to get out the product for my lips only to see that it is a LIP PLUMPER. I could not give Thread 1 stars because of the great experience I had my first two visits there. I could not give Thread 3 stars because I do not feel my experience was worth the risk. text: First impressions are so important. Four friends and I went to the Water Works for the first time last weekend. The dinner itself was good, but there was enough bad that we will think twice before going back again. We made our reservation well in advance for 5pm (when the restaurant opens). We requested a table with a nice view since it was our first time, and were told that shouldn't be a problem since we were dining so early. When we arrived there was only one party already seated in the restaurant. We were shown to our table, which was in the front corner of the restaurant and adjacent to the kitchen door. There was a window in the corner, but its location on the wall is so high, no one could see out of it when seated and therefore half the table had views of a blank wall and/or the kitchen door swinging open and close throughout our dinner. Everyone who dines out with any regularity knows a table by the kitchen door is the "worst" table in any restaurant and should always be avoided. So, I asked the hostess, I think her name was Melissa, if we could be moved, hopefully to a table in the solarium, which we quickly figured out has the best views, and where no one was seated when we arrived. The hostess curtly told me "no" we could not move, that the tables in the solarium were reserved. I tried to explain to her my request to be seated at a table with a view, as opposed to where we were seated, and I was quite taken back by her unprofessional manner, lack of sensitivity, and her overall rudeness in how she handled the situation. Because we were a party of 5, I was told there was no other table available. Needless to say, this was not a good start the evening and, as it is said, you never get a second chance to make a good first impression. The hostess completely blew it for a favorable first impression of the Water Works. If I had been dining alone or with only my wife, I would have walked out right then and there, but because we were with others, I bit my tongue and chose to try and make the most of a bad situation, vowing to myself to simple tell other people about my negative experiences with this restaurant. As previously said, you should avoid sitting at the table by the kitchen door (in any restaurant but especially here) ... our table's location was drafty to down right chilly and, some of the smells coming from the kitchen were unpleasant to say the least, especially when things were burned! On the positive side, our servers were very good, Gabriel and Dominick, although water glasses sat empty longer than they should have, and the same was true for coffee refills during dessert. The food was good, not great, but it was above average, but it was not worth the excessive price for the quality, i.e. $33 for fish (with the head and tail still on). Our total bill for 5 people was just over $400, and we were seated at the worst possible table in the restaurant.

text: My mom is a nurse at a cardiac rehabilitation center; she is something of an expert when it comes to heart healthy foods. She would make this crystal clear: Five Guys is highly unadvisable for heart-conscientious individuals. I never really went through a typical rebellion stage in my teens, but I feel like every burger I eat at Five Guys is an unintentional rebellion against my wonderful mother. Five Guys is a chain restaurant that ranks high on my list. I love the simplicity of the menu--burgers, hot dogs, and fries. That's it. No other sides, no desserts, no complicated specialty burgers. Beware: if you stuff your burger too full with toppings, it can become dangerously messy. There is a fine line between a whimp who safely eats a plain burger versus a prideful fool who ends up with half of the 17-topping burger in his lap. Order intelligently. Order with foresight. I'm a regular at this location, but I must note that the BEST Five Guys is at the Nationals Ballpark in Washington DC, which is the home of Five Guys. Nothing beats watching a baseball game while eating a Five Guys burger and washing it down with a refreshing Coca-Cola on a hot summer day. Five Guys is a good reminder that heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States (thanks Mom!). But, hey, I'm in my early twenties. I'm giving Five Guys four stars! Go ahead and call it my little rebellion.

text: Best experience tasting in Santa Barbara by a long shot. Super small winery with amazing people, wine, and they hand (and foot)-produce. LOVED it!!!!!! 5 stars all the way! Cost to worth it ratio: 3.5 Highlights: - Comfortable atmosphere: laid back and casual to the extreme--and in a good way. One of the wines didn't even yet have a label on it. The tasting table was made of wooden crates. At one point, the owner non ceremoniously came out to the tasting area, filled his wine glass, made a funny comment and went in the back room. - Super friendly, personable, chill staff: not only did they know their stuff, but the way they presented it all to us in such a nonchalant, un-upity manner ROCKED! Our guy was hip enough not only to give us a backstage tour of their place, but pulled out a paper plate and white cheddar cheez-its for us to snack off of in the middle of our tasting. No need for fancy cheeses and breads here: one snack in a box fits the bill. It was awesome. After that point I nicknamed our guy "Cheez-It" and he was either being polite playing along or realy dug it. They aren't too cool for school, they're the "here have some of what we're having/mi casa es tu casa" hospitable version of ubercool. - Wine is produced by hand: no pumps and hand-bottled. They foot-stomp their grapes instead of using machines. How great is that? They even invited my friends back to be part of the stomping if they wanted to be. Some wineries stomp for show upon harvest, but this is their true wine-making method: old school "I Love Lucy" style. It probably is more fun this way but they also have a good reason for it--it's a more gentler way which softens the amount of tannins that make it into their wines. As a friend would say, that's SICK! (For those of you new to this phrase, it's like Michael Jackson's "bad" = it means something good.) - Fantastic wines: maybe that's why they lack an attitude--they don't need one. Their wines speak for themselves. Everything was great from delightful pinots to syrahs to lagrein (a new one to me). As we tasted each wine, our amazing winery host gave us detailed information about each and related stories in some cases (ex. how they came to make lagrein). - Super small space: I don't just mean tasting room space (which looks like the entry way from the tv show "The Office" dooo dooo dooo doo doo dooo doo dooo--now the song is stuck in my head), but their whole space maybe is the size of 2 residential house garages. And they do all of the production back there. I've been to some smaller wineries but that I couldn't believe--so impressive! - Teeny production: only 2k cases made per year and 400 of those are their most popular wine. Lowlights (my flip side to highlights): - I don't live close enough to make regular trips back here - Smaller production so distribution is practically non-existant except for chosen restaurants so will have to come back when I want more of their wine. This actually doubles as a highlight, as I hate buying bottles directly from the winery and feeling all special and then finding out I can buy it at any local supermarket or wine store. Best wine tasting experience in a long time--in Santa Barbara, Sonoma, or Napa! Will definitely come back here and recommend anyone to go try it out.

text: I found the food here to be surprisingly excellent. From the outside I was expecting dive bar or cheap family italian restaurant, but on the inside it's kind of humble bar/restaurant but with very good food. Prices are a bit higher than one might expect, but the food is worth it. They start you off with complimentary bruschetta which was a nice touch. I ordered the roast pork sandwich which came out juicy, salty, and delicious. Fries were very good and the pork was great. My friend is a waitress here and told me that staff aren't allowed to eat the roast pork unless they pay because it's slow roasted and made from scratch. An excellent sign! She got the lobster mac 'n cheese which is kinda cliche and unoriginal, but pretty decent. More of a cheese sauce than a typical mac 'n cheese has but it still had a nice combo of saltiness and sharpness. I think the highlight here was the desserts. The dessert tray had a huge assortment of items and all sounded delicious. They have a pastry chef that comes in every morning to create the desserts. They're awfully small and expensive ($6.50 each) but boy was this cake good. Easily the best tres leches cake I've had, and that's compared to several different Puerto Rican restaurants where I've had it. A very impressive feat. The drinks menu is also pretty unique, though the presence of a modified Harvey Wallbanger had me a little perplexed/entertained. I ordered an Obama Mama, mostly because of the name, and it was very good. I was a bit shocked at the resulting bill. An appetizer, sandwich, and dessert cost over $30, which I wasn't expecting. After drinks and tip, we were looking at a pretty sizeable bill. Totaros feels somewhat outdated, and the atmosphere does not match the food or prices. Still, I really enjoyed my experience from appetizer, to main dish to dessert and the staff was very friendly. You can get some good food here, but don't go in expecting a typical bar experience because your wallet will be sorely disappointed.

text: Sushi Time is a great choice for all you can eat sushi in the Sparks area. The sushi chefs, waiters and waitresses, and owner are all very friendly. The fish is fresh, there's a decent variety of rolls, and the price is about middle of the road for all you can eat. If you want a sushi place where you'll feel welcome and everybody knows your name, Sushi time is the place to go. The owner is extremely friendly and will actually sit down and talk to you to see how you're doing, especially if you're a regular. The same can also be said about the waiters and waitresses. The sushi chefs all have their own personalities and quirks but all friendly. Fresh fish is a necessity when it comes to sushi, and Sushi Time delivers with some of the freshest fish around. The nigiri is pretty standard fare as far as sushi places go, but you'll find some nice things like surf clam that not all the local sushi restaurants have and some of the best mussels in town. Their regular menu for hand and long rolls is also fairly pedestrian, but where Sushi Time shines is in their chef's specials menu. The chef's specials menu eclipses the regular menu many times over in terms of variety. On the specials menu, there's something for everyone. You run the gamut of fried rolls, raw rolls, and sashimi. It's not every sushi restaurant in the Reno-Sparks area that you can get that. Along with the good comes the bad. With the economy the way it is, everyone is hurting. Sushi Time is no different and they have started to noticeably increase the amount of rice used in nigiri, hand rolls, and long rolls. There lacks consistency amongst the chefs in sushi preparation. As far as the standard menu goes, everything is about the same from chef to chef, but ever since the chef's specials menu was introduced about a year or so ago, the same item on that menu varies wildly from chef to chef. It wouldn't be so bad if it was just each chef adding an extra bit of personal flair to the sushi, but sometimes the chefs are caught unaware of what the roll is. The chefs should get together and have a meeting on the preparation of all the rolls on the chef's specials menu to really bring it together. It would seem like there's a lot of bad things to say about Sushi Time, but I'm just being extremely nitpicky. It's a fine restaurant that has fantastic sushi and makes you feel welcome. I've been a customer since the place opened and go nearly every week, and I haven't been disappointed yet. What have you got to lose? Give them a try!

text: I've given this place 2 chances. The first was on their first Friday after opening, so I excused mediocre food and slow service as "working out the kinks." We went back on New Years Eve, this time with a reservation. I understand that it's a busy night for restaurants, but we were seated 45 minutes after our reservation. Okay, let's give them this one again, since it was a busy night and all. The menu itself was as uninteresting and bland as the food. I don't usually go to Italian restaurants expecting cutting edge culinary innovation, but something beyond "white wine garlic sauce" and a generic, flavorless tomato sauce would be nice on a few dishes. I got a seafood risotto, and while it was cooked well, the flavors didn't pop and I honestly grew tired of eating it. About 1/3 of the way through, I decided to just pick all the protein out, eat that, and save myself the unrewarding calories of the boring rice. Other dishes at the table were similarly unexciting to eat. They've been around for a few months at this point, and seem to do a steady business, so I see no excuse for such disappointing and vague flavors. Even if you're okay with the menu's limitations, and you're fine with "blah" food, the experience is not worth the price of admission. At a restaurant where the average meal is between $20 and $30, I'd like to enjoy each bite, finding a new flavor or texture at every chomp. If I were told I had to spend $80+ for 2 people to enjoy a meal, I would NOT spend it here. There are many places in St. Louis where you leave feeling like that $120 evening was worth it if only for the joy of eating; Sapore is not on that list.

text: I heard a lot of good things about the Dol-Sot Bibim Bop at Meju, so on a recent blustery day, I went with four other people to have lunch at Meju. The young server looked as if she was ready to go to a Phillies game rather than serve us lunch but it is not the lackluster service at this Korean place that was disappointing, rather, it was the lackluster food served to us. First off, the five small panchan dishes were unexciting and undistinguished, and our table of five was served the exact amount as a table of one next to us. The steamed shrimp mandu (dumplings) were to expectations, as was the plate of Duk Bok Gi (Sautéed rice sticks with vegetables and fish cake in spicy red pepper sauce) and the Kimchi Jigae (Kimchi Stew). The spicy pepper sauce was really good and just begging to be eaten with fresh steamed rice (soon served in lovely bowls for our other dishes). However, the Tofu Bibim Bop was a real disappointment - the barely warm rice did not taste fresh and the cold vegetables and tofu on top never mixed into a tasty treat. We fared better with the Dol-Sot version of Beef Bibim Bob, the rice sizzling in the hot pot. The expensive ($17) slices of marinated short rib were strangely tasteless and tough, the caramelized onions served alongside much better. I enjoyed the Korean Aloe drink (although I usually don't like anything with corn syrup in it). All in all, we left a bit disappointed, especially when comparing our Meju lunch with some of the meals we had in restaurants on north 5th street.

Included in the lunch was a cup of dal - is it supposed to be all broken up like that - because the lentils were so cooked down as to be unidentifiable. Somewhat tasty, but a textural failure, IMO. text: Up front, it should be said that St. Mary's makes fabulous tortillas. There are a lot of good ones in Tucson, but these floated down from heaven like floury UFOs. They are translucently thin, lardy, and boast a perfect texture. Paired with good ingredients, such tortillas could easily be the basis of a World Class Burrito--a burrito so good that its mere existence would make Chipotle and La Salsa close their stores in purple-faced shame. St. Mary's seems like it was meant to serve this burrito. It just feels right: the location, bright colors, rickety plastic tables, and awesome staff. It closes inconveniently early and always takes a little too long to serve you. These are the idiosyncrasies of an amazing restaurant, but St. Mary's isn't an amazing restaurant. It isn't even a very good restaurant. This is painful to write, but it's a lateral slide from Nico's. The emperor has no clothes. Let's begin with the asada burrito, a heavy, joyless torpedo of food. The ingredients were of poor quality and they arrived, bite by bite, in separate layers, leaving the burrito with different temperature zones ranged from tepid to cold. The shredded cheddar was unmelted and chalky. There was no seasoning. Even a junkie-sized injection of salsa couldn't have saved it, but that wasn't an option because St. Mary's only gives you half-empty plastic thimbles of runny, flavorless hot sauce. This wasn't an off day. A return trip yielded a room-temperature shredded beef taco with no seasoning, a heap of iceberg lettuce, and a veneer of that chalky yellow stuff posing as cheese. Whether or not hard taco shells give you flashbacks to high school lunches at Taco Bell, they should, at very least, be hard when they arrive and not soggy. St. Mary's fails on this count, as well. Their red chile tamale was a greater disappointment. Wet and rubbery on the outside, dense and cool on the inside, it offered the same absence of flavor as the rest of their entrees. Chicken flautas. Meh. Quesadilla. Meh. Don't punish yourself with food from St. Mary's. Instead, grab some of their delicious tortillas and sneak them into your favorite restaurant.

My chicken-spinach-feta wrap had barely any chicken in it, and absolutely no feta at all. It was tasteless, and as another reviewer mentioned, I could have made it at home (with actual flavor) and saved myself $9. We ordered salads with the food, and she brought them out with "champagne dressing" on mine (which seems to be a take on Green Goddess dressing) and ranch on his, with the comment, "Oh, we don't have any more champagne dressing, so you'll have to make do with the ranch." We shrugged, ate our food, paid the $20 for two sad sandwiches, and left. By the way, the mango tea tasted curiously like lebanese tea. I might stop in for a coffee, but I will not eat the food again due to the cost, poor quality, and lackluster service. I hate writing bad reviews, but I immediately thought to do so when I walked out of that place. If the quality changes, however, I'd be glad to go back.

text: Style over substance. Oversalted food makes you thirsty for overpriced drinks, so if that's your thing, this place is for you. I'd rather have perfectly seasoned food. Seriously disappointing, if you've got a craving, you can get this almost anywhere these days. French Onion Soup Dumpling - Salty, glue-y-ness. Such a good idea imperfectly executed. text: I decided to take advantage of one of their BOGO entree coupons and it was a good thing I did as their prices are really quite high (the one I had taken off was $17). The place still has a lot of character and charm. The decor is fanciful and the Mariachi band is entertaining as always. The service was slow and apathetic, the meals came with the lo-grade standard bean paste and rice, and I got the impression that they had been pre-constructed by which I mean that precooked meat had been put on a plate with pre-prepared sauce, pre-prepared rice, and pre-prepared beans and heated up in the microwave. Further, the seasoning for the sauces was kind of amateurish - too sweet and too simple. I used to love their chicken mole years ago and when I suggested going here to my girlfriend, she responded by saying "Meh, they're okay." The next day I told a buddy of mine who is first-gen Mexican American that I went here and he said "Meh, they're okay." I have since realized that both of them are quite right and I have reassessed my opinion accordingly.

text: You can often find me griping that you can never find parking in this city but you never actually see people anywhere either (except at Pancake Pantry). Now I know why; at any given moment, EVERYONE in Nashville is at this mall. The selection of stores is definitely a quantity over quality thing. The outlet stores are haphazardly placed next to non-outlet stores. They don't have a Sephora, but they have some other kind of imposter beauty store that sells knockoff CHI straighteners. There are also a lot of tchotchke stores that are so unbearably useless that the thought of people actually spending their money at these places makes me cringe. It is full of tourists and children and tweens headed for the Hot Topic. And the single-floor layout is a horrific design flaw if I ever saw one. Well, it's not all bad. There is a Barnes and Noble, which is refreshingly unlike Nashville. And the Saks outlet is the closest thing to a real premium department store (e.g. NOT Macys) this city is probably ever going to see, unfortunately. Plus there is also a super sketchy looking Buffet inside the mall that I would never eat at but is kind of funny. And the only reason I actually went recently was to get some candy at one of those candy-by-the-pound places, oh and an Orange Julius. text: I love this little store! The other day I had wall sconces on my mind but, as usual, when you're actually looking for something, it can be rather hard to find. I wanted sconces that would hold taper candles, not the electric sort that leave you having to hide the trailing cord. So I decide to run to Sweet Magnolia to replace a candle that had recently burnt out completely when, lo and behold!, there is the most gorgeous pair of gold-leafed wall sconces hanging right before my eyes! This is why I love Sweet Magnolia - you can find such elegant pieces here when you least expect it. I also appreciate that their prices don't put a huge dent in your wallet. $58 for the pair? I'll take them! The store also carries the greatest soy candles ever by Aquiesse which last a rather long time and come in several delightful fragrances. They also carry an array of other home goods - Forte teas, place settings, bath and body products, stationery, baby gifts, and jewelry. Definitely a great little shop for finding last minute gifts or a treat for yourself. You must at least check out the website: http://www.prestigefitnessaz.com/ I have never in my life seen such fantastic state of the art equipment that I was actually allowed to touch and sit on. The staff is incredibly knowledgeable, friendly and approachable. I have no doubt in my mind that whatever goal you set for yourself, you will reach that goal at this gym. text: The wife and I brought our 4 YO daughter here on a Friday night. I figured this wouldn't be the greatest place to take a little one, but they have a kids menu and they even brought her a little veggie appetizer and one of their shot glass desserts, so in that regard it turned out much better than expected. We sat in the main dining room and it was a lively atmosphere, so that made it even better. We had been here for lunch 3-4 times, but never for dinner. Our experience in the past had always been about the same - very good or great food with slow service. On this night, though, the service was only slightly slow, not even enough to complain about it. I noticed the servers here seem a bit more eager to watch out for each other than at most places. This might be a concerted effort to improve the service. If so, it worked. Although the food has always been good, it's also been on the verge of forgettable. This time, we had the grilled tuna and Seafood Capellini entrees. Both were up to the usual standard - good stuff. Actually, the Capillini was actually a little better than that - worth a return trip, I'd say. One thing I really like here are the dessert shots. For two bucks, they are just right for people like us that don't often go for dessert. We're both usually satisfied with just a taste, so we chose to share the gooey butter cake. We then made the mistake of offering our daughter a bite. She wasn't sure at first, but after a little bit she decided to ditch her blueberry cheesecake and finish ours. Hers was good too, so nothing lost. Bottom line: Sage isn't the most thrilling place in town, but it's good and consistent. There's a pretty good chance you'll find a dish you like a lot and not matter what you get, I don't think you'll be disappointed. I give it a 3.5, rounded up to 4.

text: Broad Ripples best way to carbo-load! Bagel Deli is serving up the funkiest sandwiches anyone could ever think up, and they are simply irresistible. Walking in you notice right away that you couldn't possibly make a quick decision in this place. Between the 20 foot long 6 foot high menu board, to the scatterings of random customer creations that decorate the walls, you could spend a whole afternoon just trying to decide. Fortunately they have everything broken down by main protein (Turkey, Veggie, Ham, Roast Beef, Combo, etc.) So as long as you have some inkling of what you want you can come to a reasonable decision. But no matter, the sandwich you order will be the bomb. My understanding is that this shop started as a concept near the Miami at Oxford campus in Ohio and then branched out to Indiana's own version of a prestigious small private school. The menu constantly changes by adding customer creations that are turned into 8x10 pictures and hung on the walls. Local artists can also showcase their works at Bagel Deli and you can catch the pulse on Indy's Indie scene by reading the message board on the wall, usually pretty full of small time concerts and goings ons in the Broad Ripple area. The owners are usually in store, and nicer people you can not find, they love to chat and if you have a mouth and at least one ear they will certainly make your day with friendly conversation. Other offerings include a soup of the day and you can get biscuits and gravy for breakfast, a wide variety of kettle chips and miscellaneous juices to compliment your carbaliscious lunch. Check them out for all meals and a late night post Broad Ripple boozin' snack. Make sure to say hi, and try to know what kind of meat you want on your sandwich before you go in. One insider tip...they steam their sandwiches, and in my opinion, steamed hummus is pretty gross, so you might want to steer clear of the hummus based stuff, but anything with their veggie cream cheese, will knock your socks off.

text: My wife and I have lived in Royersford (5 minutes from this place) for 3 years now and have eaten there three times. The first experience was a three star. The second- two stars. This last time- one. Here's why: THE GOOD Great atmosphere. BYOB. Outdoor dining in a very nice setting. Italian music. Clean. THE BAD They ignore you once you get the main dish. I appreciate being left alone and having a great conversation at the table for a while before the check arrives- but come on. It's like we didn't exist after those main courses came out. You have to watch too. On two separate occasions they messed with my check. The first time they billed me twice. This last time they forgot to remove the dish I sent back. More on that below. THE UGLY The food is just bad. If you have any kind of developed pallet, you will be very disappointed. You ask why did I keep going back? Because the first time the food was actually good. The second time- not so much. We thought it was just a bad night. Tonight- everything we ordered (from the appetizer to the tiramisu) was sub-par. My main dish, Chicken and spicy linguine, was swimming in creme... it was supposed to be a pink sauce. It was like eating pasta with half and half creamer. Terrible. My wife's situation wasn't much better. She ordered spaghetti in a meat sauce- it tasted like they used burnt tomatoes that had been sitting in a smoker. Really not good. To me, a restaurant loses all credibility when the food is lousy. We don't ask much from moderately priced, suburban BYOBs. But I don't think it's unfair that basic requirements be met. This place just doesn't do it. They were terrific when they first opened... but it's very obvious that a lot of that initial energy is gone. Dine at your own risk.

Bottom line: Decent service, very inconsistent food, a complete lack of environment, EXPENSIVE prices for mediocre food = two stars. text: Bindi has been on my list of places to check out, well, since it opened. Thanks to the relative emptiness of the city on the weekends now that everyone else is at the shore, my party of three was seated right away around 7:30pm on a Saturday night. Once seated, we screwed the cap off our wine and ordered a few starters, the lobster pani puri and the sweet goat cheese paratha. For entrees, two of us couldn't resist the mahi and our third ordered the chicken tikka. Suffice it to say, this was the best meal I've had in a very long time. I'm so used to dining on Indian food that is burdened with heavy, overpowering sauces, but each dish here was light and flavorful - allowing you to taste each element yet delicately blending together with distinctly Indian spices and preparation. The lobster pani puri set the stage for the rest of the meal with crispy little puff balls hiding sweet nuggets of lobster that had us practically fighting over the last bite. The goat cheese paratha offered a precise blend of sweet and savory and complimented our spicier entrees very well (glad we went with the waitress' recommendation here). The mahi delighted the entire table and the chicken tikka was the best incarnation of that dish I've experienced. This review has now taken much longer to write than it should have, because I keep drifting off - reliving last night's meal in my head - and I snap back to, finding myself very close to drooling on my keyboard. Classy decor and an attentive staff rounded out the experience. The dining room is about the size you would expect from a Center City BYO - room for a large group or two, but best suited for groups of four or less. Bindi is cash only and make sure you overestimate how much you'll spend. I thought the price point was fair - but once you start eating you'll want to order everything on the menu.

text: The eight FAILS of Montrel's Bistro. I'm not sure what the others who have reviewed Montrel's with more than one star were thinking, but this was the WORST experience, hands down, I had while in New Orleans. I'll admit, we were drawn in by the prospect of a $4.99 breakfast (Cafe Du Monde had a line about 3 Chicago city blocks long, so, we walked toward the French Market and happened upon Montrel's along the way). And, the smell of boiling crayfish out front was enticing. We were seated INSIDE (seriously?) -- big patio and all, we were still directed inside, to a window table. First FAIL. Our server finally appeared, took drink orders for drinks that NEVER appeared -- 45 minutes to wait for a cup of coffee???? Second FAIL. One of the other reasons we entered Montrel's was because the "manager" out front promised that the chef could make us off-the-menu beignets (really, the only thing we wanted that morning). The server insisted that they were not available, then proceeded to argue with us AND the manager, then relented and placed the order. Third FAIL. We waited another 15 minutes, no drinks, no beignets, then the server came over to take our main order. 15 minutes? Fourth FAIL. The "beignets" then appeared -- three orders that came out at three different times over a 30 minute period. They were essentially pancake dough deep fried covered with a fairly conservative, almost nonexistent dusting of powdered sugar. Fifth FAIL. 45 minutes later, our main orders were served -- one plate at a time, every 5 minutes. With 8 people at the table, we finally got the last dish 40 minutes AFTER the first dish arrived. We had now been at MB about an hour and a half, no coffee or iced tea. Sixth FAIL. AFTER we finished eating, a busboy brought us water -- 6 glasses for 8 people. AND, don't get me started on the food -- the eggs were runny (supposed to be scrambled), the grits were gritty, the bacon was half-cooked, and the toast seemed to be recycled. Seventh FAIL. Funniest part of the experience was when the server came back with our bill -- the general manager came over after we complained and offered to comp our meal because the server was brand-new. Really? Brand new? Nooooo, you don't say? Eighth FAIL. My advice, stay as far away as you can from Montrel's Bistro when in New Orleans. Walk on the other side of the street. Actually, walk two blocks over. Wait in the Du Monde line, even if it's all Japanese tourists and large, obese families waiting for beignets. It will be worth it. Or, go directly to the French Market and eat there. You will not regret your decision to ignore Montrel's altogether. Trust me.

text: Is it the best Chinese restaurant in Tucson? Almost certainly. China Phoenix is great but no longer has live crab, so it's disqualified. And has no carts for their dim sum. Ba-Dar on Broadway has a *much* more interesting menu with some *real* off-beat Chinese items that only Asians order, but it's too far away for me to go to often, so I can't really judge it. So for me, Gee's is the best in Tucson... Wish there were a four-and-a-half stars function -- it doesn't quite merit five stars, mostly because the cuisine isn't very inventive and is mostly just the standard Cantonese stuff you've been eating all your life with no great innovation to it. That said, what they *do* serve is really very good -- and I've eaten a million Chinese meals in San Francisco over the years PLUS cooking it myself for 40 years or more. Some of their dishes are certainly as good as anything you can find in San Francisco if you're not looking for adventurous new items. I just spent six months or so working my way down though all the pork entrees on the menu, including a couple that the waitresses told me that non-Asians never ordered. A couple were superb (the Peking "pork chop" and the "spicy" pork chop -- both of which were probably *three* pork chops, beautifully cooked and sauced), a couple were very interesting and new to me, and the others (sweet and sour and moo-shu) were standard, well-done, and of enormous size. Which I should mention -- you will never go away hungry here: their portions are enormous. I always take half my meal home with me. And, considering the size of the servings, the prices are very reasonable. I always drink a couple of glasses of Robert Mondavi Chardonnay at $4.50 a glass -- a bargain! One thing I didn't take any of home was, a few nights ago, the superb Dungeness Crab in "special house sauce" (see the photo above), which I ate all of. It was huge, and absolutely delicious, but it was the only thing I ordered -- they bring a *wonderful* bowl of soup to start with (either "egg drop" or "hot and sour", along with rice).... The dim sum is as good as San Francisco, simply a little more limited in its choice. At 10:30 or 11:00 on Saturday or Sunday the parking lot is already jammed, and many, many Asian families are inside. I order 11 or 12 items, eat 1/4 of it, and take the rest home for 3 more meals. The many ladies with carts are only on Saturday and Sunday -- the other days you have to order it off a menu, which I hate, so I only come on the weekends. Very friendly service, generally very *quick* service from the kitchen, and the owners (see Bill Yiu in the picture) are very friendly. (They owned it originally years ago, then leased it out, when the quality went downhill, and have taken it back.) And the kitchen will make custom orders for you if you can describe it -- we've been playing around with chow mein, lo mein, Singapore noodles, and chow fan variations for a couple of months now, trying to find the *exact* noodle dish that I want.... And, finally, for the standards of a Chinese restaurant, it's a very upscale, comfortable, nicely decorated and furnished place, quite elegant, even.... Some of the waitresses may not speak great English, but they'll find someone who'll help out -- and they're always friendly and smiling.... Try it -- it may well be worth five full stars!

text: Maybe we were there on an off night, or maybe my expectations were too high. Either way, I was underwhelmed. The miso soup was acceptable, though the tofu cubes were minute and there was more seaweed than I generally prefer. But not a terrible start. For appetizers, we wanted to try several things to get a good idea of the quality of the food. So we ordered the Saté, the Confit Duck, Gyoza, and Spicy Tuna rolls. First off, the Gyoza were *amazing*. The filling was a beautifully balanced blend, there wasn't an excess of dumpling "fringes", and it was cooked to perfection. Which makes the sub-par level of the other appetizers inexplicable and frustrating. The chicken for the Saté was overcooked to dryness and in desperate need of salt, and the peanut sauce was unpleasantly sweet. The Confit Duck was vegetable-heavy to the point where I had to pull a bunch out in order to even taste the duck. And the tuna rolls were a mush of tuna that seemed *ground* (and not very good) spiral-wrapped in way too much nori for a good flavor blend. I will say that the portions were quite generous - more so than the menu descriptions implied - but large portions of unimpressive foods are far from satisfying. For our entrees, we went with what I assumed would be "safe" for trying a new place: I got Shrimp Teriyaki and my husband chose General Tso's Chicken (he's been in a Chinese mood for over a week now). The Tso's was delicious - the chicken was nice and crispy despite the sauce - often an issue - and very tasty. Hot, spice-wise, but not too much for this spice weenie. He said the vegetables were good too. My dish was a disaster. The shrimp was either previously-frozen and overcooked, or just overcooked into oblivion. It was horribly mushy and borderline flavorless. The rice (brown, because that's what I like best) had a strange flavor I couldn't even pinpoint. Not jasmine-y or unseasoned, they just added some flavoring that was bizarre and didn't work at ALL. The teriyaki sauce/glaze was lacking in flavor as well, which is just odd to me, and not acceptable. I took mine home, chopped it up, and fed it to the cats. And even THEY wouldn't eat all of it. Finally, the service. We went on a Wednesday night,so they were far from packed, but the service was seriously lacking and I have to say it was incompetence. Our waitress first approached us with someone else's drinks. Never good. Her attention was spotty the entire evening, despite having a second person helping her occasionally. My main issue, though, was with the drinks. Anyone who knows me knows I'm a thirsty person. The easiest way for a waitperson to earn an awesome tip from me is to keep my drinks filled. I order sodas with no ice *because* I know if I don't, I'll go thirsty. Still, EVERY time my glass was empty, I either had to ask her for more, or she would ask if I wanted another, with a tone of disbelief in her voice. Really? No, THIS time I want to go thirsty. Of COURSE I want another! And 15 minutes before we left (I'm estimating) she asked again, and took my glass to refill it. And never brought it back. She passed our table repeatedly with OTHER peoples' drinks, but nothing for me. text: The minute you walk in the modernist decor strikes your fancy with bright colored walls which differ from room to room. The rooms are large with high ceilings and open stairs lead you up or down from one to the other, yet each room ultimately blends together as one large open yet divided space. The entrance is central between the very large bar and lounge and the dining rooms off in the opposite direction. The walls are decorated with ultra chic lighted sconces and one wall has a wall divider made to look like a waterfall with water flowing through the panes of glass. Entering the first dining room you are greeted with a beautiful stone waterfall and a pool filled with large and colorful Japanese Coy. They claim these fish to be up to twenty five years of age and from the original owners of this building, which was a Chinese restaurant. The restrooms are off the Foyer with ultra modern free standing stainless steel bowls with free flowing water and matching soap dispenser bowls, which are automatic as well. The staff that we were able to see in the time we were here, were all very young, early twenties and carved out of cream cheese, beautiful people that should be modeling. We were the only ones in the restaurant by five o'clock, we started with one male and one female who multi tasked between greeting us, seating us and serving us, by the time we left, we were still the only patrons and the cream cheese staff had grown to seven or eight and all standing at the host's stand. Chef Daniel and his wife Silvia are from Argentina and have tried to bring Argentina together with Asian, Mexican, Italian and Spanish cuisine. For many years they have made their other restaurant Café con Leche work. The fusion of this restaurant is from working with his mother who was a Chef in Argentina and learning to make sauces, he then worked all over the United States in various ethnic restaurants and chose the best from each, therefore the great fusion. This one is not working folks. You can dine on the large private patio, in the lounge or in one of their white linen table clothed dining rooms. Hubby started with a Pepsi and I was torn on what new martini to try. The server convinced me to go with the Key Lime Pie Martini, I did not care for it at all, it was sickeningly sweet and it had graham cracker crumbs floating on the top, diving all through the ten dollar drink and sinking to the bottom. A few sips was actually making me sick. She took it back, I had water and was charged the ten dollars. Now I could see if I were sampling several drinks and not liking them and sending them back, but one? They had a fairly extensive and impressive wine list and many Argentine wines, which I love, I should have stuck with that. They are famous for their sweet potato and jalapeno soup, the flavor was okay and I loved the nice kick, but the consistency was like eating jarred baby food, it was so thick. Hubby had the cream of broccoli soup, no cheese in it, but it was very good. We then shared the fresh mozzarella, tomato, baby greens, pesto and balsamic salad, which was beyond the standards and quite enjoyable. We also had the warm breaded brie wedges served on top of a fresh cut pineapple, pears and grapes, all drizzled with a warm chili melba, white wine and Thai sauce. This was outstanding. Hubby ordered the shrimp and scallop stir fry over rice. I ordered the filet mignon wrapped in bacon and served with a shallot, burgundy demiglaze. Hubby's shrimp were so tiny and they cut the scallops into thin slices and there was no flavor from any Asian sauce, no snow peas or onions, but carrots, celery and summer squash. I knew and hubby knew that my medium rare filet was taking way too long and I kept thinking they were preparing his dish from scratch since the restaurant was dead. My filet arrived beyond well done, swimming in a thin sauce that was totally disgusting, topped with a mound of shallots and the largest helping of homemade skin in mashed potatoes and sauteed summer squash. One bite of the filet went into my napkin, cutting right through the center and seeing the gristle turned me off again. I just have a wild feeling these first two cheesecake kids who disappeared into the kitchen, when no one else was around, cooked our meals. If it had been a tender pot roast and full of flavor I would have been all for it and forgiving, but this was no filet mignon and for thirty two dollars was a disgrace. I'm sorry and nothing else, no owner, no adult, no manager was in sight or ever came to our table on a Saturday. The thirty two was removed from my check, if I had one responsible adult approach my table, I would possibly return, my meal was ruined, everything I had been loving about the place suddenly fell short when dropping seventy three dollars into the palms of their hand. I work hard for my money, so hard for it honey, so you had better treat me right!

If you ever consider getting involved with pet rescue, stop by the Adoption Center at 2nd and Arch. Help is needed most in the mornings from around 9-11, and then again in the late afternoons - but every bit helps. Wondering what volunteering looks like? We volunteer every week and we walk dogs, tidy up cat kennels, hang out with felines in the cat "rooms" or mop the floors. There is something for everyone and every week it's a special experience. I cannot say enough good things about the PAWS crew. I'd give them 10 stars if I could. Remember - when you adopt you save not only one life, but two. You take your future pet out of the shelter, which opens up space for another homeless pet. The PAWS Adoption Center is bright, cheery and a good-feeling place to be. Also - you can pick up pet supplies (toys, litter, treats, etc) here too while you stop in to volunteer or spend time with the pets. Great idea! I love it's central location too! Foster, Adopt, Volunteer, Donate.

text: Photolounge has been my lab of choice for many months now. I initially found it when the folks over at Ritz didn't have what I was looking for, they directed me up Chestnut a few blocks where maybe these guys had it and I've been going there for all my photo needs ever since. FIRST IMPRESSIONS: Very clean, never cluttured, and more focused on development and printing than the afforementioned Ritz, which seems to focus on camera sales, among broader service offering. Photolounge (formerly named CBOP) carries a great range of films, including my favorite-- medium format, along with frames, some camera bags, etc. THE SERVICE: Where Photolounge really shines is their service-- while quite not as rapid as your pharmacy's one-hour photo lab, they are still quite fast, but the focus on quality is unmistakable, and moreover, their service is very reliable, which has kept me coming back time and time again. The attitudes of the folks who work there is generally delightful, always friendly, always optimistic, always constructive, no exceptions. At other labs, I've gotten attitude, I've been the victim of employees taking out their frustrations from other customers-- that has never happened here, and I doubt it ever will. And, as I've brought so much repeat business to Photolounge, when things go wrong, as it becomes inevitable after enough time, they are always willing to rectify the situation, fixing the problem, whatever it is, at no extra charge. I first got hooked on Photolounge for their film selection, but I stayed hooked because of their excellent, friendly service. PRICING: Generally very reasonable, it certainly didn't break my bank, which is tight enough as it is. My mother wanted a couple of photos I took printed up for her birthday, and between the processing, printing and the frames I bought, the pricing was right where I thought it should be. I can't really remember how much it used to cost at Ritz, but the difference, be it higher or lower in price, is negligible. THE BOTTOM LINE: If you are in the Rittenhouse area, and you have film you want developed, re-developed, scanned to CD, blown up, printed, or anything in between, the choice is simple-- it's these guys. They know their stuff, they are passionate about their craft and the quality therein, and I highly recommend them.

text: Ok this is my day to review all my favorite fast food spots..... and Jack N Da Box was on my list. What can one really say about this place...... I've been eating here most of my life, back when the drive thru speaker you talked into was a clowns face!!! Its always the same, but with constantly fresh ideas, new menu items, funny commercials, open late, serves breakfast ALL day and steady cheap prices. I've eaten in, taken out, ate on their patio, and gone through the drive thru - all of which has been a great experience, never have any problems. My favorite foods at Jack N The Box........ Jumbo Jack Combo - this is your basic hamburger, thats a good size with lots of fresh veggies on it and a to-die-for secret sauce (which isnt a secret because I have figured out how to make it myself!) I also love their natural "home style" cut fries but their seasoned curly fries are the bomb! Heck even their sodas are great - like another reviewer mentioned the blue straws...... yes I too LOVE the blue straws! The very best is those mysterious tacos!!! 2 for .99 cents - they are fried, and greasy and even a little scary but DAMNIT they are soooooo good! Even better if your slightly inebriated! Their breakfast food is great too.... I always get the ultimate breakfast sandwich, hash-brown, and OJ. Other items I love from here are...... Egg Rolls - greasy and crispy Milk Shakes (yummy as well as pretty with whip cream and a cherry) Orange Juice Smoothie (I love the commercial too) Stuffed Jalapenos Ultimate Cheese Burger Cheesecake - new york style in a little package all ready for you to inhale Also they have special shakes around the holidays - like pumpkin or egg nog - you gotta try those. Dont forget your antenna ball!!!

text: This maze of different era buildings has had a valiant attempt to try to connect them together via a main floor hallway, however, it is so easy to get turned around and not realize which hallway you need. There are the east elevators, the west elevators, the main street, the Y split, the two parallel hallways that go into different buildings to the left, the hallway to emergency which you have to go to the basement to get to the first floor... and none of it is easily walkable by my dad who has hip pain. He can get around a grocery store, but this maze is too much. I brought my dad here for radiology. The (cold) reception desk was making sure she didn't make eye contact with us until she was done being busy chatting with her coworkers. In the midst of explaining what we are here for, and asking where we need to go, the phone rings and instantly we are put on virtual hold while she chats it up with her girlfriend. WTH?!?! Just show me where radiology is and we'll be gone already. And of all the people in scrubs hanging out at the desk, did anyone volunteer to show us where we were supposed to go? No. They just stared like we were dumb. After we got our directions and a rudimentary map we attempted to follow the directions we were given. However, what was not explained to us was how many different departments of radiology they had. There was the radiology in the "professional building" that was for the doctor's offices. There was the radiology that was for a different service. And there was the radiology that we were supposed to have been at that was, guess where?, just around the corner from the reception desk! Are you effing kidding?!!?!? We just walked around this entire maze, upstairs, downstairs, getting lost, and then had to get my dad a wheelchair cause of his arthritis and all of this (unnecessary) walking. Aggravating. Once we got to where we were supposed to go, the medical professionals were very patient, kind and understanding, but the hourly support staff were absolutely horrid. It's the kind of experience that makes you question the hospital's integrity overall. Updates on the CCU to follow...

text: NEVER AGAIN!!! Actually, I'm pretty sure I said those exact words several years ago when I was last at Mad River. There was a Penn State alumni event going on, so the place was packed and we had to wait in line in the rain. We should have known right then and there to cut our losses and go elsewhere. Once inside, the bar was so packed with people that I started planning out a fire escape plan. It was nearly impossible to get anywhere near the front bar, so we made our way to the back, where there was more room. Only thing was, the floor was covered with puddles of beer, plates, napkins and food. What the hell happened before we got there? Employees were trying to clean up the mess but it was a lost cause. Nearby, I witnessed a guy spitting on the floor. I started to pray, knowing that only a stronger force than myself could get me through this night. The $2 domestics that were being featured were actually plastic cups that were filled 60% of the way if we were lucky. After a while, the back bar ran out of draught beer completely so the only option was to either pay for bottles or attempt to get to the front bar without getting felt up by every drunk guy in the place along the way. I still can't believe we each paid $5 to get in. The stamp should have said "sucker" because that's exactly what paying for anything in that dump made me feel like.

text: The best Chinese in St. Louis after In Soo sadly closed. The BBQ pork is the best I've ever had (ask for it with cabbage). The duck is darned close. The appetizers (egg rolls and potstickers especially) are great. The rice is always well-cooked (it's funny how often you can rate an Asian place solely on the rice, isn't it?) and I've never had a mediocre or remotely bad entree here (the kung pao is especially good). Really good Cantonese food. Sometimes I think the best way of rating a restaurant is how far you'd drive to eat it. I've considered driving from Chicago to St. Louis (like 5 hours one-way) just to buy 10 orders of their BBQ pork. They say the 80s drug kingpins in St. Louis and Chicago used to meet around Monticello to to trade-offs. Maybe I'll have to set-up something similar and have a guy bring me Cantonese food. Don't get me wrong, there's great Chinese in Chicago, but I still wind up missing the pork and duck and even the kung pao and sesame chicken from this place.

text: I went to Yoga Soup based on the several favorable Yelp reviews. The instructor I had originally hoped to take a class from was out of town so after reading all the glowing reviews about Eddie, I thought this would be a wise choice. The décor, energy and people of Yoga Soup are warm and genuine. The Yoga Soup class I took was.....odd and unsatisfying. I do want to insert a brief disclaimer that I prefer my physical practice to have an organic flow, something challenging enough I can just lose my thoughts in because I am so intimately focused on breath and movement. We didn't actually get onto our feet until 25 mins. into the class, which kind of felt like a waste of time. Eddie went into numerous, and I mean NUMEROUS stories - all of a very esoteric and nonsensical nature. Look, I totally get a narrative to start a class to draw a theme or focus for a deeper connection to the practice but after 10+ stories, I just found myself more irritated than inspired in any way. I do want to admit that I teach as well, so as an instructor I might be slightly more observant than others when it comes to sequencing. We only flowed through a handful of postures and my pet peeve is when an instructor forgets a very integral pose. The kind that when they forget my body literally feels crooked. If you can't remember your sequence of 10 poses - maybe less stories. I also prefer to have a balanced practice. Standing poses, twists, backbends, hip openers and maybe an inversion if possible. In a 90 min. class I got the first two. While I respectably offer that Eddie's style may appeal to a certain type of student, I know that is not me. I used to think that all yoga is good yoga, and it is very, very rare that I leave a class feeling worse than when I stepped onto my mat.....I guess there is a first time for everything.
label: NEG

text: I thought about this for a week before posting a review. Two friends and I had dinner last week at Charcoal House. It was a disappointing experience on a number of levels. The evening started off poorly when my Martini on the rocks was served in a brandy snifter. Come on! Bar glasses are specifically designed for certain drinks. You serve cocktails on the rocks in a single or a double Old Fashioned glass. I wouldn't want a Remy Martin in a water glass either. The strip steak was okay. It should be for about $30, with a side. There a number of great St. Louis restaurants that offer more, often for less. The real issue that irked me was when the waitress miscalculated our credit card bills, which were supposed to be divided evenly. text: Ok, first of all, enough with the comparisons between Burger Monger and Five Guys. They are entirely different establishments. Five Guys is a glorified fast food shop with over-hyped, over-priced burgers and shitty fries. Accordingly, the comparison with Square One is apt, but overall I give the edge to Burger Monger. Burger Monger's kobe beef burger was actually jucier and more flavorful than Square One's, at approximately half the cost! Not surprising when you consider Square One's typical South Tampa vibe and Burger Monger's more pedestrian Carrollwood existence. Granted, you can't get buffalo at Burger Monger (and it is quite tasty at Square One), but for straight up burger goodness, Burger Monger wins on both taste and value. In terms of desserts, Burger Monger's shakes are amazing, and absolutely destroy Square One's sorry excuse for cupcakes (you are better off going down the road to the Cupcake Spot for dessert). At Burger Monger, try the onion slaw and chipotle ketchup, and ask for your burger cooked medium, as opposed to the default medium well. Then prepare for messy burger nirvana. Kudos, Burger Monger, for getting me excited again about burgers!

text: City Museum is so amazing it will make you feel like you're 5 years old again. I think that's as good an endorsement as I can give it. It really is just a huge jungle gym strewn across an old, beautiful warehouse, designed for adults. Sure, you can bring your kids and, many, many do, but this is a place the young at heart, old(er) in body can enjoy without feeling like the creepy guy without kids at the playground. You can crawl through spaces that you feel like are the imaginary rafters in every old building across America, through imaginary tundra and deserts. You can pour down a slide many stories in lengths, roast marshmallows on open fire when it's 10 degrees outside and see how compact exactly your body can get as you attempt to squeeze into places that look ever more precarious. You can even dish out a few extra and visit a small in house zoo, filled with komodo dragons and other exotic creatures. If you have any interest in buildings, history or sculpture the top floor should not be missed. It is filled with remnants of historic St. Louis and midwestern buildings and adornments, many of which are beautiful exemplars of architectural styles past. Or, you could simply sit back and watch every scramble about in enjoyment. One tip though, try to eat before or after, as the food as the museums tends to be greasy or overpriced.

The chicken breast had the breast bones attached and was so dry as to be almost inedible. As I type this I am getting mad at myself for not sending it back. text: I used to go to Bubbles on Rittenhouse on a regular bases. My stylist Cyndi was godsend, because she knew what was what. She knew she was a good, solid stylist working at a chain location that desperately wanted to pretend to be more high profile and classy than it actually is. See, I'm a guy. And on top of that, I'm a fat guy. A fat, gay professional rock and roll musician. I like wacky haircuts. And I have a beard that constantly needs to be styled. And Cyndi understood that. She understood that I was not the typical Bubbles customer, but she never once made me feel unappreciated and out of place. Six months ago, after going to Bubbles for a year and a half, Cyndi left. How do I explain the change? It's like replacing the diamond in your wedding ring with poop, because glass is just too classy. Out of my last 6 visits, only one was acceptable, and I don't know why I kept going back. I think I had just held onto hope that things would go back to the way they were when Cyndi still worked there. The final straw was a few days ago. I went in for a cut&style plus a beard trim, and I brought in my best friend Toshio. Toshio is also a rock and roller, even moreso than I. He is - surprise - Asian, and he has thick black hair. On this occasion he wanted it shaved into a traditional mohawk. Before our appointments we were quoted a price of $25, each. My haircut was decent, but then again all he did was shave my head and style my beard - and I brought in pictures for the beard, so it would have been hard to screw up. Toshio's stylist was a snotty little man bitch. I was not privy to the experience, but I heard back from Toshio that the stylist was constantly arguing over the actual style Toshio came in for. He wanted to give him some kind of fashiony feauxhawk with a tail or some nonsense. Hey, know what? I think it's great you have ideas and input as a stylist. You should definitely share that. But when you are so insistent that you make your client uncomfortable, there's a problem. Toshio finished before I did, and they charged him $35 for his cut and style. If you were paying attention, you'll note that's $10 more than quoted. They charged ME $30, and mine included a beard styling. Then, when we got outside into the light, I noticed they had BUTCHERED his hair. The mohawk part was decent, but the side areas that were supposed to be totally shaven had splotchy areas where the hair was visibly longer than the rest. And not in some kind of intentional pattern, mind you, but just clearly a hack job of a shaving. What followed was 4 days of arguing over the phone with "Dallas," the district manager with an attitude, and now I am scheduled to meet the store manager John today at 9AM to get a refund. I guess I can report back on how that goes. Suffice to say, my Bubbles have burst.

It's one thing to eat a salad with chopsticks, and do so gracefully. It's another to eat large leaves of dressing-covered lettuce with chopsticks. The salad was good, but due to the awkwardness of it all, I quit midway through. For me, the pinnacle of Fuji Mountain was their clear soup. It was served in a large bowl and had a huge scallop at the bottom. Our rolls arrived soon after the soup. There were five total: a California, tuna, spicy tuna, spicy yellowtail, and one other tuna variation. I tried one bite of each, and had a really hard time deciding which roll, if any, I liked enough for a second round. The rice was perfectly sticky but completely took over. The fish itself was a little too room temperature for my liking and comparable in quality to the stuff at Wegman's. text: Always on the lookout for a good meal at a fair deal, especially when traveling, it never hurts to ask a well-fed looking local. With no reservations we could have been immediately seated in the back room. Instead, we asked to wait a few minute's at the bar for a table in the much livelier main dining room. The young n' hunky bartender (hunky per L. and K. the vivacious females in our party) mixed up some excellently classic cocktails while we waited. Despite my initial skepticism, the guy turned out to be one of the better bartenders I've been served by. Soon seated, we found ourselves more excited by the intricate appetizers than the more vanilla-sounding entrees. The starters were so tantalizing in description that we ordered eight (of nine, less the charcuterie plate) and skipped the entrees entirely. It turned out to be a meal not to regret. However - I would caution others NOT to repeat our folly. The starters, especially the crab and asparagus gratin dish, were a delight, but so rich that none of us could face dessert. In a nod to the staff, halfway thru our our meal the building power went out, darkening the whole neighborhood. Candles were quickly it, and glasses refilled. After fifteen minutes the lights came back on. We discovered later that the maitre'd had negotiated a reprieve (possibly involving a little lagniappe?) with a nearby utility work crew to provide power until 10 PM (closing time). Our waitress and the kitchen apparently never missed a beat, and our meal service was flawless. All told, our meal at Dick & Jenny's was a little slice of Nawlins heaven. Local food, fair prices, great flavors and service, all in a funky homestyle spot that felt like home.

text: I happened upon Sabrina's on Callowhill Street a couple of weeks ago while looking for a quick lunch before a visit to the Franklin Institute and the Art Museum . At 130pm on a Saturday, the restaurant was very crowded -- there was a 20-25 minute wait for two open stools at the counter but it was clear we'd have waited a lot longer for a table. The expansive menu offers traditional brunch favorites (their stuffed french toast is reknown throughout the land) along with new twists on traditional diner foods. I ordered the Islander Grilled Ahi Tuna sandwich with a side of sweet potato fries and my girlfriend ordered the Greek salad with chicken. Both dishes were very tasty, the portions (particularly the Greek salad) were VERY generous, and the prices were reasonable ($10-12 per dish). The waitress was definitely busy, but good-natured about it. Our only disappointment was that our appetizer (which we only ordered to hold us over until the entrees were served) arrived AFTER the entrees. Overall, enjoy this neighborhood gem, but be sure to go with an empty stomach and enough patience to wait for a table. I'll definitely go back next time I'm in the area.

text: This review is not about Conner Prairie's symphony or the actual "prairie" area where they take you back in time to churn butter; although both are pretty fabulous in their own rite. This review is for the wedding venue location(s) and awesome-ness that is their wedding staff! My sister hosted her wedding AND reception last year at CP for just over $10K total. Now, if anyone has ever gotten married or hosted a party with over 100 people, you know this is damn near impossible. So, that being said, CALLING ALL BRIDES AND GROOMS!! Check this out for your upcoming wedding ...even though Audra's wedding was in 2009, I have a feeling their prices have not gone up that much. My sister decided on a very popular summer weekend - Labor Day - to kick off her life into wedded bliss. She wanted to get married outdoors but have an awesome upscale/intimate indoor reception. Low and behold, after much research, my hubby recommended CP. I never thunk it! Once we discovered it, we never turned back. The wedding coordinator was happy to show us around the facility offering to do a tented reception in one of the many acres of green space inhabiting this gorgeous prairie, the red barn area (which is what my sister chose) and the pagoda area that is the most popular. Audra had her wedding outside the barn and she was presented from INSIDE the barn, through two large doors, as we all walked down the aisle. There was something breathtakingly romantic about it all. Once the wedding was complete, we went back into the barn, which was decorated with beautiful white Christmas lights, white table clothed tables, and offering a full open bar with bartenders for the cocktail hour. She also got a wide array of cheesy appetizers. The reception was actually in their sit-down restaurant, which they converted into a beautiful well decorated (though extremely simple - budget, people!!) reception venue....with two full walls full of windows, the ambiance was pure perfection. There was enough room for a dance floor and 150 guests comfortably. The outdoor area boasted a a beautiful patio where we could hear the Symphony playing their last show of the year and at the end of the night, a firework show was "on the house" b/c it was part of the show. It was romantic, well organized, beautiful and perfect for a unique wedding location in Indy.....offering an outdoor and indoor option with free parking and wonderful food, on what is to be considered a fairly tight budget, I would definitely recommend checking this out if you are in the market for something different in Indy! Also, GREAT location for engagement or wedding pictures....so much green space and some unique barns and old time areas that allow for some fabulous photo ops!

text: Friends visiting out of town or having an outing with your colleagues? Want to dine in a trendy place with delicious food? Look no further!! The booth couches are all upholstered and have a really cool, old-school feel, which added a ton of character to the pretty simple space. We sat all the way in the back corner in the round booth which is great for parties of 5-6 people. The waiter immediately came over to talk about specials and get us started with drinks (fast service...always a super plus!) My Sauvignon Blanc was perfectly chilled and crisp, just the way I like it. We started with some appetizers, including: Crispy Calamari, Pot stickers, crab cakes, and scallop ceviche. Can I say....yum Yum YUm YUM!!!! Everything was very well executed and the crab cakes werent falling apart. They were that perfect combo of sticky enough to stay together but loose enough to come right apart where you can taste the chunks of crab... (mouth is watering reliving this delight!). PS: Twenty Manning gives your table awesome warm bread to share, don't over load because the meals are filling, but I recommend trying at least a small piece. For my main course, I had the Seared Candied Scallops, (clearly I was on scallop overload that night). I'm a fan of seafood and these scallops were seared to perfection, a golden crust outlining each piece and as sides came roasted pumpkin and sauteed spinach. I am a huge pumpkin lover and this was a great healthy alternative to roasted potatoes. One of my colleagues ordered the and another the salmon, everyone was raving. It was thrilling to have food that both tasted good and was good for you. Afterwards we were able to lounge around, have a few drinks and soak up the trendy dim lit atmo... would we go there again? A B S O L U T E L Y!!!

text: It hurts my heart that our digital leanings are slowly phasing out the novelty of compact discs and vinyl. Am I the only one who gains a sense of satisfaction when I can peel the sticky label off the plastic without leaving behind adhesive residue (by the way, there's a trick and I know it)? Am I the only one who gets really excited when I hold a new album in my hands? Like, back when Sufjan's Illinois came out, I remember running to Repo, snatching up the album, and racing home to lie in my bed, throw on my headphones, stare at the ceiling, and listen to the record from start to finish. While devouring the artwork, I'd follow the lyrics like science. It's still my favorite album to date. Every time I walk into Repo, I get the same sensation: it's Christmas morning and there are all these magical unopened presents just waiting to find a home. I love browsing through their new and used cds and new and used vinyl. Repo's antediluvian practices (they write down every purchase in a spiral notebook) matches the allure of the old-fashioned way of listening to music: it's quaint, it's nostalgic, it's a thing of the past? I hope the current trend persists where all things old (or old-timey) are cool again (think: The Franklin Fountain, The Franklin Mortgage Co.) and Repo keeps giving my eyes and ears music to live by.

text: I really want to love 3 Monkeys, but I just can't. I will preface this all by saying that I haven't been there in a few months, and I hope that things have gotten better but there's a reason I haven't been back in months. The first few times I went to 3 Monkeys for lunch. It was good, close, and it has a really cool look. I like the wood and large windows. The first time I went a guy across the way was grabbing lunch by himself so he was seated at a very small table and he ordered a pizza. They put the pizzas on those racks like other pizza places, but their racks must have been really cheap because they don't function very well and have no rubber to stop everything from sliding around. Needless to say, the result was a pizza on the floor. They need to upgrade their pizza racks. Anyway, their lunch was pretty solid though I did notice that they've changed things up a little with their menu. Some of the staples on the menu I like, and some of the creativity is kinda nice -- a salad or nachos with BBQ pork??? Interesting and good! But skip the salsa on the nachos because I'm pretty sure it's just tomatoes and applesauce. I think this was another attempt to be creative with the food but salsa is supposed to be spicy not applesauce. But I've had some bad food as well--not bad like bad culinary idea or bad because it's just not my taste--I mean bad like completely black toast on a Reuben that they tried to serve on the bottom of the sandwich like no one would notice the charcoal taste; pasta in milk that was supposed to be a cream sauce but was really just milk on noodles; and cod fried in oil that was not even close to hot enough so that I'm pretty sure there was more oil in it than cod (though to be fair that was only one of the 3 pieces of cod that I got and the others were really good, but it still shouldn't have been served). Also, their service is fairly slow and/or inattentive. There isn't much room when you first walk in to wait to be seated, which is fine or it would be if someone paid enough attention to seat people promptly. I've had to stand there for much too long at times when the restaurant was not busy. Drinks can also be slow to come and be refilled. And they need to get their trash situation outside together. If you park on the side street you walk past their oil waste, and it is disgusting with oil stains leading from it to the street so that you have to jump over it while you're walking on the sidewalk (or i guess you could just walk in nasty oil). I also once saw a mouse running from the oil to the building right by it. Before I went last time, I said this was it's last chance and that's when I got the oily cod piece and my mom got the applesauce salsa. Other than those two things, it was a fine meal though. I might give it a second last chance sometime if the mood strikes for some of that BBQ pork because like I said I really want to like this place and I hope things have improved since the last time I went.
label: NEG
